# How to choose an open-source alerting platform

"Alerting platform" means the last layer of monitoring: once the data exists, **who evaluates it, how noise is cut, and who gets told**. Collection and storage are out of scope here, and so is visualization. The open-source choices at this layer are few, but they differ a lot. First the tools are sorted into three kinds, then six questions are asked of each.

## Three kinds of tool[​](#three-kinds-of-tool "Direct link to Three kinds of tool")

| Kind              | What it does                                                                       | Examples                                                 |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Alerting engine   | Runs queries itself, evaluates, cuts noise, delivers                               | Prometheus + Alertmanager, Grafana Alerting, Nightingale |
| Aggregation layer | Receives alerts other systems already produced; deduplicates, correlates, delivers | Keep, Alerta                                             |
| On-call delivery  | Schedules, escalations, phone wake-ups                                             | Mostly commercial; Grafana OnCall OSS is archived        |

Step one is deciding which layer you lack. Data with no alerts yet: an engine. Three systems each already alerting: an aggregation layer. Alerts accurate enough but nobody answering the phone: on-call delivery.

## Do rules live in files or in a UI?[​](#do-rules-live-in-files-or-in-a-ui "Direct link to Do rules live in files or in a UI?")

In the Alertmanager world, rules are Prometheus YAML managed by reload and GitOps, with no UI editing and no permission model. Grafana Alerting and Nightingale both configure in the UI and both export and import. Ownership differs: Grafana uses folders and org roles, with fine-grained RBAC in Enterprise; Nightingale uses business groups, which are also the permission boundary and decide who can see, who can edit and where mutes apply. If only SREs maintain rules, files plus GitOps are the leanest option; if product teams configure their own, a UI and a permission boundary are hard requirements.

## Looking for an Alertmanager UI?[​](#looking-for-an-alertmanager-ui "Direct link to Looking for an Alertmanager UI?")

Most people who search for an Alertmanager UI want one of two things, and they have different answers.

* **A better view of firing alerts.** Alertmanager's built-in web UI (port 9093) lists alerts and lets you create silences. [karma](https://github.com/prymitive/karma) adds grouping and a dashboard across several Alertmanagers, and Grafana can add Alertmanager as a data source to browse alerts and manage silences. All of these sit on top of Alertmanager and leave it unchanged.
* **Editing rules and routing without touching YAML.** None of the tools above do this: Prometheus rules and `alertmanager.yml` stay files. To manage rules, routing and mutes in a UI with per-team permissions, the alerting layer itself has to move. Grafana Alerting does that inside Grafana; Nightingale does it as a standalone engine that queries Prometheus directly, and [Migrating from Prometheus + Alertmanager](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-alertmanager.md) shows how `alertmanager.yml` maps onto it. Nightingale does not receive alerts from Alertmanager, so it replaces that layer rather than sitting on top of it.

## Is the data in one place or several?[​](#is-the-data-in-one-place-or-several "Direct link to Is the data in one place or several?")

Alertmanager only handles alerts evaluated by Prometheus (Loki alerts go through its own ruler). Grafana Alerting spans any data source it supports alerting on. Nightingale registers Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Elasticsearch, Loki, ClickHouse, MySQL and others, <!-- -->10+<!-- --> types, so metric, log and SQL rules all live in one place. Keep and Alerta do not query data; they only receive alerts.

## What cuts the noise: grouping, inhibition, mutes, subscriptions[​](#what-cuts-the-noise-grouping-inhibition-mutes-subscriptions "Direct link to What cuts the noise: grouping, inhibition, mutes, subscriptions")

This is where the three engines differ most.

* **Alertmanager**: label-based grouping into one message (`group_by`), cross-rule inhibition (`inhibit_rules`), one-off silences, recurring mute intervals on routes. A clean model, all in config files.
* **Grafana Alerting**: embeds an Alertmanager, so grouping and silences match, but Grafana-managed alerts do not support inhibition rules.
* **Nightingale**: no label grouping, one event per notification. Noise is cut by merging at the rule level (one rule covers every series its query returns), fixed and recurring mutes (optionally muting notifications while keeping the event), subscription rules (conditional copies, timeout escalation) and event pipelines (processors that rewrite, drop or call back). Cross-rule inhibition has no declarative form; it is a pipeline rewrite.
* **Keep / Alerta**: deduplication and correlation are their main job, on alerts some other system produced.

If the on-call flow depends on seeing a group of alerts in one message, the Alertmanager family fits better. If events must be routed to different people by business condition and rewritten before delivery, Nightingale fits better.

## How does the on-call person get woken up?[​](#how-does-the-on-call-person-get-woken-up "Direct link to How does the on-call person get woken up?")

Among the open-source engines only Nightingale ships phone and SMS media types, alongside DingTalk, Feishu, WeCom, Slack, Telegram and others, <!-- -->20<!-- --> channels in total. Alertmanager receivers are email, Slack, PagerDuty and webhooks first; Grafana contact points cover the main chat tools and also lack phone and SMS. None of the three has a schedule: on-call rotation in the open-source world is mostly left to commercial products, and Grafana OnCall OSS was archived in March 2026.

## Who can change a rule, and where is the boundary?[​](#who-can-change-a-rule-and-where-is-the-boundary "Direct link to Who can change a rule, and where is the boundary?")

Alertmanager and Prometheus have no authentication or permissions; isolation happens at the deployment level. Grafana OSS has org roles and folder permissions. Nightingale has users, teams and business groups; rules, mutes, subscriptions and targets belong to a business group, and data sources can be granted per group. When several product teams share one alerting platform, this question usually decides.

## What can AI do here?[​](#what-can-ai-do-here "Direct link to What can AI do here?")

Alertmanager has no built-in AI. Grafana Assistant is Cloud-only; OSS relies on the LLM plugin and a separate MCP server. Nightingale runs an AI assistant and <!-- -->74<!-- --> MCP tools in-process across <!-- -->13<!-- --> toolsets, read tools on by default, write tools off, no delete tools; clients such as Claude Code and Cursor connect to the `/mcp` endpoint directly and inherit the user's token permissions. Keep applies AI to alert correlation.

## One table[​](#one-table "Direct link to One table")

| Dimension                 | Prometheus + Alertmanager | Grafana Alerting            | Nightingale                           | Keep                                   | Alerta            |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Kind                      | Engine                    | Engine                      | Engine                                | Aggregation                            | Aggregation       |
| Where rules live          | YAML files                | UI + provisioning           | UI + import/export                    | Does not evaluate                      | Does not evaluate |
| Data sources              | Prometheus                | Any alerting-capable source | 10+<!-- --> types: metrics, logs, SQL | Receives alerts                        | Receives alerts   |
| Grouping into one message | Yes                       | Yes                         | No                                    | Correlation                            | Correlation       |
| Cross-rule inhibition     | Yes                       | No                          | Pipeline rewrite                      | Correlation rules                      | Correlation rules |
| Phone and SMS             | Third party               | Third party                 | Built in                              | Third party                            | Third party       |
| Permission model          | None                      | Roles + folders             | Business-group RBAC                   | Yes                                    | Yes               |
| Built-in AI               | None                      | Cloud only                  | Assistant + MCP                       | Alert correlation                      | None              |
| License                   | Apache-2.0                | AGPL-3.0                    | Apache-2.0                            | Open core with an enterprise directory | Apache-2.0        |

## Recommendations by team profile[​](#recommendations-by-team-profile "Direct link to Recommendations by team profile")

* **Small team, all data in Prometheus, comfortable with GitOps**: Prometheus + Alertmanager. Fewest components, cleanest model.
* **Heavy Grafana users, moderate alert volume, contact points suffice**: Grafana Alerting. One system fewer.
* **Several data sources, product teams configuring their own rules, phone and SMS and chat tools required, AI-assisted investigation wanted**: Nightingale. Full comparisons: [Nightingale vs Prometheus + Alertmanager](https://n9e.github.io/comparisons/prometheus-alertmanager.md) and [Nightingale vs Grafana Alerting](https://n9e.github.io/comparisons/grafana-alerting.md).
* **Three monitoring systems already alerting, want one inbox**: an aggregation layer such as Keep or Alerta. Nightingale is not one.
* **Coming from Zabbix**: start with [Zabbix alternatives](https://n9e.github.io/comparisons/zabbix-alternatives.md), then [Nightingale vs Zabbix](https://n9e.github.io/comparisons/zabbix.md).

## Questions[​](#questions "Direct link to Questions")

**Is an alerting platform the same thing as a monitoring system?**

No. A monitoring system usually has four layers: collection, storage, visualization and alerting. This page is about the last one only: evaluation, noise reduction, delivery. Prometheus is storage plus evaluation, Grafana is visualization plus an alerting module, Nightingale is an engine built for the alerting layer alone.

**Can Nightingale receive alerts from Alertmanager or Zabbix?**

No. Nightingale is an alerting engine that runs its own queries; it has no inbound alert endpoint. To consolidate alerts other systems already produce, look at aggregation layers such as Keep or Alerta.

**Is there a UI for Alertmanager?**

Alertmanager ships a web UI for viewing alerts and creating silences, and karma or Grafana add richer alert dashboards on top. None of them edit alert rules or routing; those stay in YAML files. If you want rules, routing and mutes managed in a UI with permissions, the alerting layer itself has to change, for example to Grafana Alerting or Nightingale.

**Do the open-source editions have phone and SMS?**

Nightingale does; phone and SMS are built-in media types in its open-source edition. Alertmanager and Grafana OSS have neither and rely on third parties such as PagerDuty; Grafana OnCall OSS was archived in March 2026.

Based on each project's public documentation and open-source edition as of October 2026; a guide, not a verdict. Nightingale figures come from build-time data. If something here is out of date, open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/n9e/n9e.github.io/issues).

# Nightingale vs Prometheus + Alertmanager

Prometheus stays. The exporters stay. The Grafana panels stay. Alertmanager is the only component this comparison actually replaces: rules move from YAML into the UI, the routing tree is flattened into notification rules, and silences become mute rules with a business-group boundary.

[Try live demo](https://play.n9e.io/api/n9e/auth/demo-login)[Install in 5 minutes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md)

## The 30-second version

* **Stay on Prometheus + Alertmanager if**

  the team is comfortable with GitOps, the rule count fits in one head, and webhooks into PagerDuty or a similar on-call tool are all the delivery you need. The pair is mature and adds no components; nothing here says switch for its own sake.

* **Move to Nightingale if**

  rules must be maintained in a UI by teams who are not SREs, permissions have to follow business groups, someone has to be phoned rather than webhooked, or the data is no longer only in Prometheus: logs in Elasticsearch, business metrics in MySQL.

* **Run both if**

  you want evidence first. Register Prometheus as a data source and Nightingale evaluates the same rules while Alertmanager keeps delivering; switch one notification channel at a time and back out of any step in about a minute.

Their way

Rules live in YAML and ship through GitOps.

The Nightingale way

Rules live in the UI, scoped by business group.

## Where it shines

Prometheus remains one of the best time-series foundations available, and Alertmanager’s grouping and silencing model is genuinely clean. At moderate scale, with a GitOps-comfortable team and a rule count you can hold in your head, the pair is enough and adds no components.

## When Nightingale fits better

Nightingale earns its place when rules must be maintained by teams who are not SREs, when permissions need to follow business groups, when someone has to be phoned at 3am, or when the data is not all in Prometheus.

## Signs it is time to switch

* Rules must be maintained by teams who are not SREs
* Someone has to be phoned at 3am, not just webhooked
* The data is no longer all in Prometheus

```
- alert: MysqlReplicaLag  expr: mysql_slave_lag_seconds > 30  for: 5m  labels: { team: dba }route:  receiver: dba-webhook  group_by: [alertname]
```

Nightingale · alert rule

* Name

  MySQL replica lag

* Condition

  mysql\_slave\_lag\_seconds > 30, for 5m

* Business group

  DBA

  Phone, SMS, DingTalk

* You

  Create in one sentence: page the DBA group by phone when mysql-prod replica lag stays above 30s for 5 minutes

* Nightingale AI

  PromQL and threshold drafted. I will not guess the business group; pick one from the list and I will create the rule.

Based on the publicly documented capabilities of each project’s open-source edition as of August 2026. We try to state what the other tools are good at — advice you cannot trust is worth nothing to a community.

## How the objects map

Take a rules.yml and an alertmanager.yml apart, and here is where each piece lands. The entry-by-entry mapping, the method for flattening the routing tree and the four asymmetries are in the migration guide.

| Prometheus / Alertmanager                 | Nightingale                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Alerting rules in rules.yml               | Alert rules; paste the whole file into “Import Prometheus alert rules”                     |
| Recording rules                           | Untouched, Prometheus keeps computing them                                                 |
| receivers\[]                              | Notification media plus a notification config inside a notification rule                   |
| The route tree                            | Flattened: every root-to-leaf path becomes one notification config with its matchers ANDed |
| group\_by / group\_wait / group\_interval | No equivalent; one event per notification                                                  |
| inhibit\_rules                            | No declarative equivalent; rewrite as a drop processor in an event pipeline                |
| Silence                                   | Mute rule, which must belong to a business group                                           |
| Alertmanager cluster                      | Several alert engine instances shard the rules; no gossip needed                           |

Two traps: a notification config with no severity ticked matches nothing, not everything; and an event that lacks a label never matches, even for != and !\~, whereas Alertmanager treats a missing label as an empty string.

[From Prometheus + Alertmanager<!-- --> →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-alertmanager.md)[Coexistence and rollback plan<!-- --> →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/coexistence.md)

## Questions about this comparison

Do I have to replace Prometheus?

No. Prometheus keeps scraping and storing; Nightingale registers it as a data source and runs instant queries against it on a schedule, so nothing has to move. Thanos, Mimir and VictoriaMetrics connect the same way.

Can alertmanager.yml be converted automatically?

The alert rules can: paste rules.yml into Rules → Import → Import Prometheus alert rules. Routes, receivers and silences are rebuilt entry by entry following the migration guide, because Nightingale uses flat notification rules rather than a routing tree.

Can Nightingale receive webhooks from Alertmanager?

No. Nightingale has no inbound alert endpoint, only metric write endpoints, so Alertmanager cannot sit in front of it as a forwarder during a transition. Rules are rebuilt inside Nightingale.

What happens to Alertmanager grouping?

Nightingale sends one event per notification and does not batch alerts into one message by label. Noise is cut at the rule level instead (one rule covers every series the query returns), plus mute rules and subscriptions. If your on-call flow depends on grouped messages, accept that difference before you switch.

Do I have to stop Alertmanager to switch?

Only as the final step. Everything before it runs with Prometheus and Alertmanager untouched: import rules disabled, enable one business group as a canary, compare in parallel, then remove the alerting rules from rule\_files and stop Alertmanager last.

# Nightingale vs Zabbix

Zabbix is built around hosts and items: it collects, stores and alerts on its own. Nightingale is built around queries: it evaluates on the Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or Elasticsearch you already run, and Categraf fills only the gaps. This is not one product beating another; two architectures fit two kinds of infrastructure.

[Try live demo](https://play.n9e.io/api/n9e/auth/demo-login)[Install in 5 minutes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md)

## The 30-second version

* **Stay on Zabbix if**

  the estate is mostly network gear, SNMP and IPMI, you lean on auto-discovery and LLD, and the team has years of Zabbix experience. Two decades of work in that space has no complete open-source substitute.

* **Move to Nightingale if**

  metrics already live in Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics, logs in Elasticsearch or Loki, Kubernetes and cloud services outnumber racks, or you keep both a Zabbix agent and exporters running just to get one alert.

* **Run both if**

  you want to migrate in batches. Categraf and the Zabbix agent coexist on the same host; let Nightingale deliver to one dedicated channel first, compare what fired each day, and never stop Zabbix.

Their way

Collect everything with its own agents, then alert on that.

The Nightingale way

Alert on the stores you already fill; collect only where nothing does.

## Where it shines

Two decades of work show in traditional IT monitoring: network gear, SNMP, agent-based collection and auto-discovery are its home ground, and the hiring pool knows it well.

## When Nightingale fits better

If your telemetry already lives in Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or ElasticSearch, Nightingale reads it directly instead of asking you to pour it into a second collection stack.

## Signs it is time to switch

* Telemetry already lives in Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or ElasticSearch
* Kubernetes and cloud services outnumber network gear
* You maintain two collection stacks to get one alert

Based on the publicly documented capabilities of each project’s open-source edition as of August 2026. We try to state what the other tools are good at — advice you cannot trust is worth nothing to a community.

## How the objects map

What each kind of Zabbix object is called in Nightingale, and which have no equivalent at all. The full table and the rebuild order that keeps Zabbix running throughout are in the migration guide.

| Zabbix              | Nightingale                                                                                                 |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Zabbix server       | Nightingale plus a time-series store (the embedded TSDB is on by default; move to an external one at scale) |
| Zabbix agent        | Categraf, or exporters you already run; both coexist on one host                                            |
| Host / host group   | Target (ident) / business group, which is also the permission boundary                                      |
| Template            | A component in the template center, 83 built in; import is a one-time copy                                  |
| Item                | No equivalent; what is collected is decided in the collector config                                         |
| Trigger             | Alert rule; one covers every object the query returns                                                       |
| Low-level discovery | No equivalent; as many series as the query returns, that many objects                                       |
| Action + media type | Notification rule + notification media + message template                                                   |
| Maintenance         | Mute rule                                                                                                   |

Nightingale has no importer for Zabbix templates or triggers and cannot read its XML or YAML. Coming from Zabbix is a rebuild, not a move; the good news is that it is smaller than it looks: built-in components replace most templates, and one rule replaces a whole set of triggers.

[From Zabbix<!-- --> →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-zabbix.md)[Coexistence and rollback plan<!-- --> →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/coexistence.md)

## Questions about this comparison

Can Nightingale read Zabbix data directly?

No. Nightingale data sources are query backends such as Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and Elasticsearch; the Zabbix history and trends tables are not among them. Leave the history in Zabbix as a read-only archive; nothing needs to be moved.

Can Zabbix templates be imported?

Not mechanically. The template center ships 83 components covering operating systems, databases, middleware and Kubernetes, so most standard Zabbix templates have a counterpart; custom triggers are rewritten one by one using the merge method in the guide.

Can Nightingale monitor switches and routers?

It can collect them, but it is not home ground. Categraf has an SNMP plugin that polls OIDs and Nightingale alerts on the result, but there is no network auto-discovery or mature device template library like Zabbix has. For device-heavy estates, keep Zabbix on the devices and put Nightingale on cloud and applications.

How do the six Zabbix severities map?

Down to three: Disaster and High become S1, Average and Warning become S2, Information and Not classified become S3. Information is lost in that step, so compare severities against this mapping during the parallel run.

Does Zabbix have to stop during the migration?

Never. Install Categraf, settle the storage, import built-in templates, translate the remaining triggers, build notifications, move maintenance windows, compare in parallel, then stop the Zabbix actions first and the agents a week later. Rolling back is disabling the Nightingale rules in bulk.

# Open-source Zabbix alternatives: pick by scenario, not by ranking

Searching for "Zabbix alternatives" returns ten-item lists with two sentences per tool. This page goes the other way: first why you want to leave, then where your data and objects would go, then one honest paragraph per candidate, including where it does not fit. Nightingale (n9e, 夜莺) is our own project; it appears only in the rows where it genuinely belongs.

## Why people leave Zabbix[​](#why-people-leave-zabbix "Direct link to Why people leave Zabbix")

Three common reasons, and one counter-example that gets skipped too often.

* **The database becomes the bottleneck.** The `history` and `trends` tables grow with hosts times items; partitioning, the housekeeper and TimescaleDB are all ways of fighting that. Metric time-series stores were built for exactly this data.
* **The environment went cloud-native.** Kubernetes pods appear and vanish by the minute; a host-and-item model needs discovery and agents to keep up, and the metrics for these environments usually already live in Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics. Collecting them again with Zabbix means running two collection stacks.
* **The alerting layer has new requirements.** Noise reduction, permissions by business group, phone and SMS, chat tools, self-healing, AI-assisted investigation. Zabbix can do parts of it, but through script media types and outside systems.

The counter-example: **if the estate is mostly network gear, SNMP and IPMI, the team has years of Zabbix experience and the system runs stably, there is no reason to move.** Two decades of work in that space has no complete open-source substitute.

## Three questions before switching[​](#three-questions-before-switching "Direct link to Three questions before switching")

1. **Where is the data now?** If metrics are already in Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics and logs in Elasticsearch or Loki, the replacement should read those stores rather than collect again. If the data exists only inside Zabbix, the replacement needs its own collection.
2. **What are you monitoring?** Switches, routers and out-of-band IPMI are one world; Kubernetes, cloud databases and microservices are another. The first is about discovery and device templates, the second about query languages and multiple data sources.
3. **Who maintains the alert rules?** SREs only: config files plus GitOps are enough. Product teams: a UI and a permission boundary are hard requirements.

## Choose by scenario[​](#choose-by-scenario "Direct link to Choose by scenario")

| Your situation                                                                      | Better fit                                     | Why                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mostly network gear, SNMP, IPMI                                                     | Stay on Zabbix; LibreNMS for pure network      | Discovery and device template libraries are their home ground |
| Metrics already in Prometheus / VictoriaMetrics, lots of Kubernetes                 | Nightingale, or Prometheus + Alertmanager      | Alert on the stores you have; no second collection stack      |
| The team already lives in Grafana, modest alert volume                              | Grafana Alerting                               | One system fewer                                              |
| Product teams configure rules in a UI, permissions by business group, phone and SMS | Nightingale                                    | Those are the things it is built around                       |
| Unified APM with traces, metrics and logs                                           | SigNoz                                         | OpenTelemetry-native                                          |
| A few dozen hosts, want charts right after install                                  | Netdata; or Nightingale with its embedded TSDB | Zero-config start                                             |
| Traditional IT, just want a nicer interface                                         | Checkmk Raw                                    | Same model family as Zabbix, lowest concept migration cost    |

## The seven candidates, one at a time[​](#the-seven-candidates-one-at-a-time "Direct link to The seven candidates, one at a time")

### Prometheus + Alertmanager (Apache-2.0)[​](#prometheus--alertmanager-apache-20 "Direct link to Prometheus + Alertmanager (Apache-2.0)")

The de facto standard for cloud-native metrics: pull model, exporter ecosystem, PromQL. Rules live in YAML and are evaluated by Prometheus; Alertmanager groups, inhibits, silences and routes. It shines exactly where Zabbix struggles: dynamic environments, service discovery, high-cardinality labels. The price is no UI for rules, no permission model, and webhook-first delivery with phone, SMS and most chat tools left to third parties. At moderate scale with a GitOps-comfortable team it is the leanest choice.

### Nightingale (Apache-2.0)[​](#nightingale-apache-20 "Direct link to Nightingale (Apache-2.0)")

An open-source alerting engine hosted by the China Computer Federation's open-source committee. It does not need the data moved: Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Elasticsearch, ClickHouse and other sources (<!-- -->10+<!-- --> types) are registered and queried in place; Categraf fills the gaps, with <!-- -->83<!-- --> built-in integrations bundling collector config, dashboards and rules. Rules are configured in the UI, business groups are the permission boundary, phone, SMS, DingTalk, Feishu and WeCom are among <!-- -->20<!-- --> built-in channels, and an AI assistant with <!-- -->74<!-- --> MCP tools runs in-process. Not its ground: network device discovery, Zabbix-style multi-step escalation ladders, and it is not an aggregation layer, so it cannot receive alerts from other systems. Full comparison: [Nightingale vs Zabbix](https://n9e.github.io/comparisons/zabbix.md).

### Grafana Alerting (AGPL-3.0)[​](#grafana-alerting-agpl-30 "Direct link to Grafana Alerting (AGPL-3.0)")

Grafana's built-in unified alerting: rules across many data sources, an Alertmanager-style notification policy tree, contact points for the main chat tools. If the team already lives in Grafana it is the one-system-fewer option. Watch the OSS permission granularity (fine-grained RBAC is Enterprise), the lack of phone and SMS contact points, and the fact that Grafana OnCall OSS was archived in March 2026 with on-call living in Grafana Cloud. See [Nightingale vs Grafana Alerting](https://n9e.github.io/comparisons/grafana-alerting.md).

### Checkmk Raw Edition (GPL-2.0)[​](#checkmk-raw-edition-gpl-20 "Direct link to Checkmk Raw Edition (GPL-2.0)")

The same generation of model as Zabbix: agents plus automatic service discovery, thousands of check plugins, complete SNMP and traditional-IT coverage, and a more modern interface. It is the lowest-cost move when what you want is "a nicer Zabbix". Raw is the open-source edition; the CMC core and several features are commercial.

### Netdata (GPL-3.0)[​](#netdata-gpl-30 "Direct link to Netdata (GPL-3.0)")

Per-second collection, auto-configured dashboards, usable minutes after a single-host install, low footprint. Good for a few dozen machines and teams that want to see charts first; often used alongside Zabbix rather than instead of it. Multi-node views and long retention go through Netdata Cloud, which has free and paid tiers.

### LibreNMS (GPL-3.0)[​](#librenms-gpl-30 "Direct link to LibreNMS (GPL-3.0)")

SNMP-centred network monitoring: discovery, device templates, topology, traffic graphs, alert rules. If Zabbix is mainly your switch-and-router view, LibreNMS is the closest open-source replacement; it is not a general metrics or log alerting platform.

### SigNoz (Apache-2.0)[​](#signoz-apache-20 "Direct link to SigNoz (Apache-2.0)")

An OpenTelemetry-native observability platform with traces, metrics and logs in ClickHouse and built-in alerting. It solves unified APM rather than infrastructure monitoring; "Zabbix alternative" only holds when what you really want is APM.

## What moving from Zabbix to Nightingale involves[​](#what-moving-from-zabbix-to-nightingale-involves "Direct link to What moving from Zabbix to Nightingale involves")

It is a rebuild, not a move: Nightingale has no importer for Zabbix templates or triggers. The work is smaller than it looks, because one Nightingale rule covers every series its query returns; the thousand trigger sets a template generates on a thousand hosts are usually one rule. The order: install Categraf (the Zabbix agent stays), settle the storage, import built-in templates, translate the remaining triggers, build notifications, move maintenance windows, compare in parallel, then stop Zabbix actions first and agents a week later. Every step verifies on its own; rolling back is disabling the Nightingale rules in bulk. Step by step: [From Zabbix](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-zabbix.md) and [Coexistence and rollback plan](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/coexistence.md).

## Questions[​](#questions "Direct link to Questions")

**Can Nightingale read Zabbix data directly?**

No. Nightingale data sources are query backends such as Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and Elasticsearch; the Zabbix history and trends tables are not among them. Leave the history in Zabbix as a read-only archive; nothing has to be moved.

**How long does leaving Zabbix take?**

It depends on the number of custom triggers. Built-in templates cover most of the standard ones; custom triggers and notification actions are rewritten one by one. The usual approach is one business group at a time, each running in parallel for a week or two, with Zabbix never stopping.

**Is there one open-source tool for both network gear and cloud-native alerting?**

None is home ground on both sides. In practice the work is split: Zabbix or LibreNMS keeps the switches, routers and IPMI, Nightingale or Prometheus takes Kubernetes and applications, and notifications land in the same channels.

**Did the Zabbix license change?**

Yes. Zabbix 7.0 moved from GPL-2.0 to AGPL-3.0. Nothing changes for internal deployments; if you embed it in a service offered to others, read the AGPL network clause.

NOTIFICATIONS

## Notification channels

DingTalk, WeCom, Feishu, email and phone/SMS work out of the box. Slack, Telegram, Discord, PagerDuty and Jira come with built-in message templates — create the media type and send. Anything else goes through a webhook with a custom body.

* ![Slack logo](https://n9e.github.io/img/logos/slack.png)Slack
* ![PagerDuty logo](https://n9e.github.io/img/logos/pagerduty.png)PagerDuty
* Email

COLLECTORS

## How data gets in

Nightingale does not collect data itself. The templates above are written for Categraf, but any collector that speaks Prometheus Remote Write can feed it.

### CategrafRecommended

One agent for operating systems, middleware, databases and cloud providers. Every built-in template ships its collector config for Categraf.

[Categraf docs](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf.md)

<!-- -->

[ →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf.md)

### Telegraf / Datadog Agent

Keep what is already running; point its output at the Nightingale Remote Write endpoint.

[Collector setup](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/collector-config.md)

<!-- -->

[ →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/collector-config.md)

### Exporters

node\_exporter, mysqld\_exporter and the rest of the Prometheus ecosystem, scraped by Categraf or Prometheus and written in.

[Collector config](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/collector-config.md)

<!-- -->

[ →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/collector-config.md)

### Remote Write directly

Your own programs or the OpenTelemetry Collector push straight to /prometheus/v1/write.

[Verify data arrives](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md)

<!-- -->

[ →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md)

# Prometheus alert rules with runbooks

238 Prometheus alert rules for 8 services, including Kubernetes, Linux, MySQL and Redis. Every rule has a PromQL condition, a severity, a duration and runbook steps. Free to download as Prometheus rules files.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

An alert rule is only half the job: when it fires at 3 a.m., someone needs to know what to check first. This library collects 238 PromQL alert rules from Nightingale's integration templates, and every one of them comes with runbook steps written for the person on call. The rules use standard exporter metric names (node\_exporter, kube-state-metrics, mysqld\_exporter and so on), so they work with plain Prometheus as well as with Nightingale.

| Service                                                             | Rules | Metrics from                                      | Download                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Kubernetes](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes.md)       | 77    | kube-state-metrics, cAdvisor (kubelet), apiserver | [`kubernetes.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes.yml)       |
| [Prometheus](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus.md)       | 30    | Prometheus's own /metrics, Prometheus Operator    | [`prometheus.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus.yml)       |
| [Linux](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/linux.md)                 | 76    | node\_exporter, Categraf, Telegraf                | [`linux.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/linux.yml)                 |
| [MySQL](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/mysql.md)                 | 11    | mysqld\_exporter, Categraf                        | [`mysql.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/mysql.yml)                 |
| [Redis](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/redis.md)                 | 12    | redis\_exporter, Categraf                         | [`redis.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/redis.yml)                 |
| [Elasticsearch](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/elasticsearch.md) | 11    | elasticsearch\_exporter, Categraf                 | [`elasticsearch.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/elasticsearch.yml) |
| [MongoDB](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/mongodb.md)             | 8     | mongodb\_exporter                                 | [`mongodb.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/mongodb.yml)             |
| [Windows](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/windows.md)             | 13    | windows\_exporter, Categraf                       | [`windows.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/windows.yml)             |

## Rule format[​](#rule-format "Direct link to Rule format")

* Each page lists every rule with its PromQL condition, severity, `for` duration and runbook steps, grouped by the collector that produces the metrics.
* Each `.yml` file is a standard Prometheus rules file and passes `promtool check rules`. Severity is a `severity` label (critical / warning / info), the summary is in `annotations.summary`, and `annotations.runbook_url` links to the rule page.
* Thresholds are starting points, not recommendations for every environment. Review them before you enable a rule.

## Why the runbooks matter[​](#why-the-runbooks-matter "Direct link to Why the runbooks matter")

A rule without a runbook moves the investigation to whoever is on call. The steps here say what to look at first (the log before the last restart, the exit code, the slow query list, the replication thread state) and what usually fixes it, so the alert carries its own first response.

## Sources and license[​](#sources-and-license "Direct link to Sources and license")

Rule expressions are partly adapted from community collections: [kubernetes-mixin](https://github.com/kubernetes-monitoring/kubernetes-mixin) (Apache-2.0), [kube-prometheus](https://github.com/prometheus-operator/kube-prometheus) (Apache-2.0), [awesome-prometheus-alerts](https://github.com/samber/awesome-prometheus-alerts) (CC BY 4.0). Runbook steps and the remaining rules come from [Nightingale's integration templates](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/tree/main/integrations) (Apache-2.0).

## Related[​](#related "Direct link to Related")

* [Integrations](https://n9e.github.io/integrations.md): collector config and dashboards for each service
* [Alert rules in Nightingale](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/overview.md)
* [Rule design practices](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/best-practices.md)

# Elasticsearch alert rules for Prometheus: 11 rules with runbooks

11 ready-to-use Elasticsearch alert rules in PromQL, each with severity, duration and runbook steps. Metrics from elasticsearch\_exporter, Categraf. Download as a Prometheus rules file or import into Nightingale.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Elasticsearch alert rules for cluster health turning yellow or red, JVM heap usage climbing, disk space running low or out, unassigned, initializing and relocating shards, pending cluster tasks, and an index that has stopped receiving new documents. The exporter group uses prometheus-community/elasticsearch\_exporter metric names; the Categraf group runs the same checks on Categraf-collected metrics.

## At a glance[​](#at-a-glance "Direct link to At a glance")

* **11 rules**, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a `for` duration and runbook steps
* **Metrics from**: elasticsearch\_exporter, Categraf
* **Download**: [`elasticsearch.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/elasticsearch.yml), a standard Prometheus rules file (`groups:` format), checked with `promtool check rules`
* Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

## Rule list[​](#rule-list "Direct link to Rule list")

| Rule                                              | Severity | For |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------- | --- |
| Elastic Cluster Red status                        | Critical | —   |
| Elastic Cluster Yellow status                     | Warning  | —   |
| Elasticsearch disk out of space of the instance   | Critical | 2m  |
| Elasticsearch disk space low of the instance      | Warning  | 2m  |
| Elasticsearch Heap Usage Too High of the instance | Critical | 2m  |
| Elasticsearch Heap Usage warning of the instance  | Warning  | 2m  |
| Elasticsearch initializing shards of the instance | Warning  | 15m |
| Elasticsearch no new documents of the instance    | Warning  | 5m  |
| Elasticsearch pending tasks of the instance       | Warning  | 15m |
| Elasticsearch relocation shards of the instance   | Warning  | 15m |
| Elasticsearch unassigned shards of the instance   | Critical | —   |

## Prometheus exporter (11)[​](#prometheus-exporter-11 "Direct link to Prometheus exporter (11)")

All rules in this group also apply unchanged to instances collected by Categraf, which produces the same metric names.

### Elastic Cluster Red status[​](#elastic-cluster-red-status "Direct link to Elastic Cluster Red status")

Critical · — · Trigger:

```
elasticsearch_cluster_health_status{color="red"} == 1
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_cluster/health?level=indices to find the indices that are red;
2. Run GET \_cluster/allocation/explain to see exactly why the primary shard cannot be allocated;
3. The usual cause is a node dropping out — bring the node back so shards recover automatically;
4. If the node's data is genuinely corrupted, restore the index from a snapshot with POST \_snapshot/\<repo>/\<snap>/\_restore.

### Elastic Cluster Yellow status[​](#elastic-cluster-yellow-status "Direct link to Elastic Cluster Yellow status")

Warning · — · Trigger:

```
elasticsearch_cluster_health_status{color="yellow"} == 1
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_cluster/allocation/explain to find why the replica shards cannot be allocated;
2. On a single-node cluster, set the index replica count to 0: PUT \<index>/\_settings {"index.number\_of\_replicas":0};
3. On a multi-node cluster, check whether a node dropped out or a disk watermark is blocking allocation;
4. Once handled, confirm the health goes back to green.

### Elasticsearch disk out of space of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-disk-out-of-space-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch disk out of space of the instance")

Critical · 2m · Trigger:

```
elasticsearch_filesystem_data_available_bytes / elasticsearch_filesystem_data_size_bytes * 100 < 10
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_cat/allocation?v to find the nodes that are short on disk;
2. Delete or archive expired indices (DELETE \<index>), or use ILM to move cold data to cold nodes;
3. After freeing disk, lift the read-only block by hand: PUT \_all/\_settings {"index.blocks.read\_only\_allow\_delete":null};
4. Longer term, expand the disk or add data nodes.

### Elasticsearch disk space low of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-disk-space-low-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch disk space low of the instance")

Warning · 2m · Trigger:

```
elasticsearch_filesystem_data_available_bytes / elasticsearch_filesystem_data_size_bytes * 100 < 20
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_cat/allocation?v to check the disk watermark on each node;
2. Clean up expired indices or adjust the ILM policy to roll data to cold nodes earlier;
3. Review whether the cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.\* thresholds match your actual capacity;
4. Schedule expansion early so it never drops to flood stage and turns indices read-only.

### Elasticsearch Heap Usage Too High of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-heap-usage-too-high-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch Heap Usage Too High of the instance")

Critical · 2m · Trigger:

```
(elasticsearch_jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} / elasticsearch_jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="heap"}) * 100 > 90
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_nodes/stats/jvm to identify which node is under heap pressure;
2. Run GET \_cat/indices?v\&s=store.size:desc to find the largest indices and close or archive the unused ones;
3. Run GET \_tasks?actions=*search*\&detailed to find large aggregations or deep pagination queries and cancel them;
4. Longer term, set the heap to half of physical memory (never above 31G), or add nodes to spread the load.

### Elasticsearch Heap Usage warning of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-heap-usage-warning-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch Heap Usage warning of the instance")

Warning · 2m · Trigger:

```
(elasticsearch_jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} / elasticsearch_jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="heap"}) * 100 > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Compare against elasticsearch\_jvm\_gc\_collection\_seconds\_count to see whether old GC is becoming more frequent;
2. Run GET \_cat/indices?v\&s=store.size:desc to check whether any index has grown sharply recently;
3. Run GET \_nodes/stats/indices/fielddata to inspect fielddata and query cache usage;
4. Plan capacity or cleanup ahead of time so it does not climb to 90% and trigger full GC.

### Elasticsearch initializing shards of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-initializing-shards-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch initializing shards of the instance")

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
elasticsearch_cluster_health_initializing_shards > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_cat/recovery?v\&active\_only=true to see whether recovery is still making progress;
2. If it is stuck, run GET \_cluster/allocation/explain to find the reason (insufficient disk, saturated node bandwidth);
3. Temporarily raise indices.recovery.max\_bytes\_per\_sec if the recovery throttle is the bottleneck;
4. Confirm no node is repeatedly dropping out and causing shards to be rebuilt over and over.

### Elasticsearch no new documents of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-no-new-documents-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch no new documents of the instance")

Warning · 5m · Trigger:

```
rate(elasticsearch_indices_docs{es_data_node="true"}[5m]) == 0
```

Runbook:

1. First confirm this cluster is genuinely expected to receive continuous writes, otherwise disable this rule;
2. Check that the upstream writers (Filebeat/Logstash/application bulk clients) are alive and whether their logs show rejected bulk requests;
3. Run GET \_cat/thread\_pool/write?v to see whether the write thread pool's rejected counter is growing;
4. Confirm the indices have not been made read-only (a disk watermark triggers read\_only\_allow\_delete).

### Elasticsearch pending tasks of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-pending-tasks-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch pending tasks of the instance")

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
elasticsearch_cluster_health_number_of_pending_tasks > 10
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_cluster/pending\_tasks to see the queued tasks and their priorities;
2. Run GET \_cat/master?v to confirm the master is not flapping;
3. Run GET \_cat/shards to count total shards and check whether a large number of tiny indices is bloating the cluster state;
4. Reduce the shard count (merge small indices, tune ILM) and, if needed, scale the master nodes separately.

### Elasticsearch relocation shards of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-relocation-shards-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch relocation shards of the instance")

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
elasticsearch_cluster_health_relocating_shards > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_cat/recovery?v\&active\_only=true to see whether the relocation is still progressing;
2. If it has stalled, run GET \_cluster/allocation/explain to check whether a disk watermark or an allocation filter is blocking it;
3. Confirm whether someone triggered a large reroute by hand, or whether nodes are joining and leaving;
4. If needed, temporarily raise cluster.routing.allocation.node\_concurrent\_recoveries and the recovery throttle.

### Elasticsearch unassigned shards of the instance[​](#elasticsearch-unassigned-shards-of-the-instance "Direct link to Elasticsearch unassigned shards of the instance")

Critical · — · Trigger:

```
elasticsearch_cluster_health_unassigned_shards > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run GET \_cluster/allocation/explain to get the exact reason the shards are unassigned;
2. If a node dropped out, bring it back into the cluster first;
3. If the replica count exceeds the number of available nodes, lower index.number\_of\_replicas;
4. If a disk watermark was hit, free disk space first and then run POST \_cluster/reroute?retry\_failed=true.

## How to use these rules[​](#how-to-use-these-rules "Direct link to How to use these rules")

* **With Prometheus or vmalert**: download [`elasticsearch.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/elasticsearch.yml), add it to `rule_files` (or `-rule` for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a `severity` label (critical / warning / info), and `runbook_url` points back to this page.
* **With Nightingale**: the same rules ship in the [Elasticsearch](https://n9e.github.io/integrations/elasticsearch.md) integration template. Open the integration center, [import the rules into a business group](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md), and enable them one by one. Nightingale keeps the runbook with each alert and can evaluate the rules against Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and other data sources.

## Sources and license[​](#sources-and-license "Direct link to Sources and license")

The runbook steps and the remaining rules come from Nightingale's integration templates ([Elasticsearch](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/tree/main/integrations/Elasticsearch), Apache-2.0). Corrections are welcome as pull requests there.

* [Write a metric rule in Nightingale](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/metric-rules.md)

# Kubernetes alert rules for Prometheus: 77 rules with runbooks

77 ready-to-use Kubernetes alert rules in PromQL, each with severity, duration and runbook steps. Metrics from kube-state-metrics, cAdvisor (kubelet), apiserver. Download as a Prometheus rules file or import into Nightingale.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Alert rules for Kubernetes clusters built on the metrics every cluster already exposes: kube-state-metrics for object state, cAdvisor through the kubelet for container resources, and the apiserver, kubelet, scheduler and controller-manager endpoints for the control plane. They cover crash-looping and unready pods, stuck rollouts, replica mismatches, failed jobs, resource overcommit, quota pressure, certificate expiry and control-plane outages. Most rules keep the alert names used by kubernetes-mixin and kube-prometheus (KubePodCrashLooping, KubeNodeNotReady, KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn…), so they match the names you already see in Alertmanager.

## At a glance[​](#at-a-glance "Direct link to At a glance")

* **77 rules**, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a `for` duration and runbook steps
* **Metrics from**: kube-state-metrics, cAdvisor (kubelet), apiserver
* **Download**: [`kubernetes.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes.yml), a standard Prometheus rules file (`groups:` format), checked with `promtool check rules`
* Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

## kube-state-metrics, cAdvisor and control plane (77)[​](#kube-state-metrics-cadvisor-and-control-plane-77 "Direct link to kube-state-metrics, cAdvisor and control plane (77)")

### Deployment Pod availability below 70% (replicas above 9 pods)[​](#deployment-pod-availability-below-70-replicas-above-9-pods "Direct link to Deployment Pod availability below 70% (replicas above 9 pods)")

Critical · 1m · Trigger:

```
kube_deployment_status_replicas_unavailable and kube_deployment_status_replicas_available{} / kube_deployment_status_replicas{} * 100 < 70 and kube_deployment_status_replicas{} > 9
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl describe deploy \<name> -n \<ns> for Conditions and Events;
2. Run kubectl get pod -n \<ns> -l \<selector> to see the state and reason of the unready Pods;
3. Common causes are insufficient resources for scheduling, image pull failures, and failing readiness probes;
4. Follow the Pod's specific state; for resource shortage, add nodes or lower requests.

### Job failed[​](#job-failed "Direct link to Job failed")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
kube_job_status_failed{} > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl get job \<job> -n \<ns> for the failure count, then kubectl logs job/\<job> for the reason;
2. Run kubectl describe job for Events and whether it gave up after exhausting backoffLimit;
3. After fixing the root cause, kubectl delete job and resubmit, or let the CronJob run again on schedule;
4. Confirm whether the failure has downstream impact (missing output, skipped cleanup) and redo it manually if needed.

### Pod startup timeout[​](#pod-startup-timeout "Direct link to Pod startup timeout")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{} == 1
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl describe pod \<pod> -n \<ns> and use the Event timestamps to see whether it is stuck pulling the image, mounting a volume, or in an init container;
2. For slow pulls, check image size and registry bandwidth, and consider pre-warming images or a local registry;
3. For slow mounts, check the PV/CSI driver state;
4. If the application itself starts slowly, optimise startup and set a sensible readiness probe initialDelaySeconds.

### Pod state abnormal[​](#pod-state-abnormal "Direct link to Pod state abnormal")

Critical · 1m · Trigger:

```
kube_pod_status_phase{phase=~"Pending|Unknown|Failed"} > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl get pod \<pod> -n \<ns> -o wide for STATUS and READY, then kubectl describe pod for Events;
2. Pending usually means insufficient resources or scheduling constraints (affinity, taints, unbound PVC); for ImagePullBackOff check the image address and pull credentials;
3. Running but not Ready — check the readiness probe and kubectl logs \<pod> for startup errors;
4. Confirm whether the replica count is now too low to carry traffic, and scale healthy replicas first if so.

### Pod restarting frequently[​](#pod-restarting-frequently "Direct link to Pod restarting frequently")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{}[5m]) > 3
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl logs \<pod> -n \<ns> --previous to see the log before the last exit — this is the key step;
2. Run kubectl describe pod for the exit code and Events: 137 usually means OOM or killed, 1/2 usually means the application failed to start;
3. For config or dependency problems (unreachable database, missing ConfigMap/Secret), fix the dependency first;
4. For OOM, compare resources.limits.memory against actual usage, or fix the application's memory leak.

### Container CPU usage exceeds 80%[​](#container-cpu-usage-exceeds-80 "Direct link to Container CPU usage exceeds 80%")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
100 * (sum(rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{id!="/"}[2m])) by (pod_name,namespace,container) / sum(label_replace(kube_pod_container_resource_limits_cpu_cores{},"pod_name","$1","pod","(.*)")) by (pod_name,namespace,container)) > 80 and sum(label_replace(kube_pod_container_resource_limits_cpu_cores{},"pod_name","$1","pod","(.)")) by (pod_name,namespace,container) != 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl top pod \<pod> -n \<ns> --containers to compare actual usage against the limit;
2. Check the CPUThrottlingHigh metric to confirm whether it is already being throttled;
3. For genuine growth, raise resources.limits.cpu or scale out with an HPA;
4. For abnormal usage, capture a CPU profile in the application rather than papering over it with more quota.

### Container memory usage exceeds 80%[​](#container-memory-usage-exceeds-80 "Direct link to Container memory usage exceeds 80%")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
(sum(container_memory_working_set_bytes{id!="/"}) BY (instance,name,container,pod_name,namespace) / sum(container_spec_memory_limit_bytes{id!="/"} > 0) BY (instance,name,container,pod_name,namespace) * 100) > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl top pod \<pod> -n \<ns> --containers to compare usage against the limit;
2. Check the history curve to tell a steady climb (likely a leak) from a normal traffic peak;
3. For normal peaks, raise resources.limits.memory with headroom;
4. For a steady climb, capture a heap profile in the application — raising the quota only postpones it.

### Node CPU usage exceeds 90%[​](#node-cpu-usage-exceeds-90 "Direct link to Node CPU usage exceeds 90%")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
100-cpu_usage_idle{cpu="cpu-total"} > 90
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl top node for the overall picture and kubectl top pod -A --sort-by=cpu for the biggest consumers;
2. Check whether too many high-load Pods landed on this node and drain some if needed;
3. Check whether Pod requests are set too low, causing overcommit;
4. If the cluster is running hot overall, add nodes.

### Node memory usage exceeds 90%[​](#node-memory-usage-exceeds-90 "Direct link to Node memory usage exceeds 90%")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
mem_used_percent > 90
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl top node and kubectl top pod -A --sort-by=memory to find the biggest consumers;
2. Check for Pods without a memory limit growing without bound;
3. Use kubectl drain to move some Pods off, confirming the target nodes have headroom;
4. Review the kubelet eviction thresholds, and add nodes if the cluster is tight overall.

### Node not ready[​](#node-not-ready "Direct link to Node not ready")

Critical · 1m · Trigger:

```
kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready",status="true"} == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl describe node \<node> for Conditions and Events to tell MemoryPressure, DiskPressure and a lost kubelet apart;
2. Log in to the node and check kubelet and the container runtime (systemctl status kubelet containerd);
3. Use journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 to locate the problem;
4. If the node cannot recover soon, run kubectl drain so the Pods move promptly instead of waiting for the eviction timeout.

### Node disk usage exceeds 90%[​](#node-disk-usage-exceeds-90 "Direct link to Node disk usage exceeds 90%")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
disk_used_percent > 90
```

Runbook:

1. On the node run df -h to find the mount point, usually /var/lib/docker or /var/lib/containerd;
2. Run crictl rmi --prune or docker system prune to clean unused image layers — the fastest win;
3. Check whether a Pod is writing large amounts of data to an emptyDir or hostPath;
4. After cleaning, confirm the kubelet DiskPressure taint was removed automatically.

### KubeClientCertificateExpiration-S2[​](#kubeclientcertificateexpiration-s2 "Direct link to KubeClientCertificateExpiration-S2")

A client certificate used to authenticate to the apiserver is expiring in less than 7.0 days.

Warning · — · Trigger:

```
apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_count{job="apiserver"} > 0 and on(job) histogram_quantile(0.01, sum by (job, le) (rate(apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_bucket{job="apiserver"}[5m]))) < 604800
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubeadm certs check-expiration (kubeadm clusters) or openssl x509 -noout -dates to confirm the expiry;
2. On kubeadm clusters run kubeadm certs renew all and restart the control plane components;
3. kubelet client certificates usually rotate automatically — if not, check the rotateCertificates setting and CSR approval;
4. After renewal, verify the components loaded the new certificate (restart them) and re-check every node.

### KubeClientCertificateExpiration-S1[​](#kubeclientcertificateexpiration-s1 "Direct link to KubeClientCertificateExpiration-S1")

A client certificate used to authenticate to the apiserver is expiring in less than 24.0 hours.

Critical · — · Trigger:

```
apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_count{job="apiserver"} > 0 and on(job) histogram_quantile(0.01, sum by (job, le) (rate(apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_bucket{job="apiserver"}[5m]))) < 86400
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubeadm certs check-expiration (kubeadm clusters) or openssl x509 -noout -dates to confirm the expiry;
2. On kubeadm clusters run kubeadm certs renew all and restart the control plane components;
3. kubelet client certificates usually rotate automatically — if not, check the rotateCertificates setting and CSR approval;
4. After renewal, verify the components loaded the new certificate (restart them) and re-check every node.

### AggregatedAPIErrors[​](#aggregatedapierrors "Direct link to AggregatedAPIErrors")

An aggregated API {{ $labels.name }}/{{ $labels.namespace }} has reported errors. The number of errors have increased for it in the past five minutes. High values indicate that the availability of the service changes too often.

Warning · — · Trigger:

```
sum by(name, namespace)(increase(aggregator_unavailable_apiservice_count[5m])) > 2
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl get apiservice to see which APIService is False;
2. Run kubectl describe apiservice \<name> for the specific error;
3. If the backing service is down, check its Deployment/Service health (commonly metrics-server);
4. For certificate problems, verify the CA bundle configuration.

### AggregatedAPIDown[​](#aggregatedapidown "Direct link to AggregatedAPIDown")

An aggregated API {{ $labels.name }}/{{ $labels.namespace }} has been only {{ $value | humanize }}% available over the last 10m.

Warning · 5m · Trigger:

```
(1 - max by(name, namespace)(avg_over_time(aggregator_unavailable_apiservice[10m]))) * 100 < 85
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl get apiservice to identify the APIService;
2. Run kubectl -n \<ns> get pod to check its backing Pods;
3. Read that Pod's logs for startup or runtime errors;
4. After recovery, verify with something like kubectl top node that the functionality is back.

### KubeAPIDown[​](#kubeapidown "Direct link to KubeAPIDown")

KubeAPI has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery.

Critical · 15m · Trigger:

```
absent(up{job="apiserver"} == 1)
```

Runbook:

1. On the control plane node, check the kube-apiserver process/static Pod state and logs;
2. For multi-replica deployments, confirm whether only some instances are down and whether the load balancer removed the faulty ones;
3. Common root causes are unavailable etcd, expired certificates and resource exhaustion;
4. Restore etcd and certificates first — apiserver usually recovers on its own.

### KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn-S1-120s[​](#kubeapierrorbudgetburn-s1-120s "Direct link to KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn-S1-120s")

The API server is burning too much error budget.

Critical · 2m · Trigger:

```
sum(apiserver_request:burnrate1h) > (14.40 * 0.01000)

and

sum(apiserver_request:burnrate5m) > (14.40 * 0.01000)
```

Runbook:

1. Look at the apiserver error code and latency distribution to tell read from write degradation;
2. For write degradation, check etcd disk latency first — that is the most common root cause;
3. For read degradation, look for clients doing wide LIST calls (full enumeration without a resourceVersion);
4. Rate limit the offending client and consider enabling APF (API Priority and Fairness).

### Deployment replicas mismatch[​](#deployment-replicas-mismatch "Direct link to Deployment replicas mismatch")

### StatefulSet replicas mismatch[​](#statefulset-replicas-mismatch "Direct link to StatefulSet replicas mismatch")

```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl get pod -n \<ns> -l \<selector> and check by ordinal which replica is stuck;
2. Run kubectl describe pod to check whether its PVC bound successfully — this is the most common sticking point for stateful services;
3. For storage problems, check the PV/StorageClass and the CSI driver;
4. For application problems check kubectl logs; once fixed, the StatefulSet continues automatically.

### DaemonSet has unready Pods[​](#daemonset-has-unready-pods "Direct link to DaemonSet has unready Pods")

```

Runbook:

2. Compare node taints against the DaemonSet's tolerations — a taint mismatch is the most common cause;

### HPA scaling failed[​](#hpa-scaling-failed "Direct link to HPA scaling failed")

```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl describe hpa \<name> -n \<ns> and read the reason in Conditions;
2. ScalingLimited means it hit the min/max boundary; FailedGetScale means the target workload has a problem;

### Pod in Failed state[​](#pod-in-failed-state "Direct link to Pod in Failed state")

Pod {{ $labels.pod }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} has failed.

Warning · 5m · Trigger:

```
kube_pod_status_phase{job="kube-state-metrics",phase="Failed"} == 1
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl get pod \<pod> -n \<ns> -o wide for STATUS and READY, then kubectl describe pod for Events;
2. Pending usually means insufficient resources or scheduling constraints (affinity, taints, unbound PVC); for ImagePullBackOff check the image address and pull credentials;
3. Running but not Ready — check the readiness probe and kubectl logs \<pod> for startup errors;
4. Confirm whether the replica count is now too low to carry traffic, and scale healthy replicas first if so.

### Job failed[​](#job-failed-1 "Direct link to Job failed")

```

1. Run kubectl get job \<job> -n \<ns> for the failure count, then kubectl logs job/\<job> for the reason;
2. Run kubectl describe job for Events and whether it gave up after exhausting backoffLimit;
3. After fixing the root cause, kubectl delete job and resubmit, or let the CronJob run again on schedule;

### CPUThrottlingHigh[​](#cputhrottlinghigh "Direct link to CPUThrottlingHigh")

{{ $value | humanizePercentage }} throttling of CPU in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} for container {{ $labels.container }} in pod {{ $labels.pod }}.

Info · 15m · Trigger:

```
sum(increase(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{container!="", }[5m])) by (container, pod, namespace)

  /

sum(increase(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{}[5m])) by (container, pod, namespace)

  > ( 25 / 100 )
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl top pod \<pod> -n \<ns> --containers and compare against resources.limits.cpu;
2. Note that runtimes like Java that do not detect the cgroup limit may spawn too many threads and worsen throttling — check the JVM version and flags;
3. Raise limits.cpu, or scale out horizontally with an HPA;
4. A limit far above the request is easily squeezed by overcommit — consider bringing them closer together.

### KubeClientErrors[​](#kubeclienterrors "Direct link to KubeClientErrors")

### KubeCPUOvercommit[​](#kubecpuovercommit "Direct link to KubeCPUOvercommit")

Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted CPU resource requests for Pods by {{ $value }} CPU shares and cannot tolerate node failure.

Warning · 10m · Trigger:

```
sum(namespace_cpu:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum{job="kube-state-metrics",}) by (cluster) - (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster)) > 0

and

(sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster)) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl describe node | grep -A5 'Allocated resources' to sum up allocation per node;
2. This is a capacity planning signal rather than an immediate outage — assess whether there is still headroom to absorb a node failure;
3. Check for Pods with requests set far above actual usage; lowering them frees a lot of schedulable capacity;
4. If headroom is genuinely insufficient, add nodes.

### KubeletDown[​](#kubeletdown "Direct link to KubeletDown")

Kubelet has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery.

Critical · 15m · Trigger:

```
absent(up{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} == 1)
```

Runbook:

1. On the node run systemctl status kubelet to check the process;
2. Use journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager to find the exit or error reason;
3. Common causes are expired certificates, config errors and an unavailable container runtime;
4. After recovery, confirm the node is Ready again and check whether Pods were wrongly evicted meanwhile.

### KubeletPlegDurationHigh[​](#kubeletplegdurationhigh "Direct link to KubeletPlegDurationHigh")

The Kubelet Pod Lifecycle Event Generator has a 99th percentile duration of {{ $value }} seconds on node {{ $labels.node }}.

Warning · 5m · Trigger:

```
node_quantile:kubelet_pleg_relist_duration_seconds:histogram_quantile{quantile="0.99"} >= 10
```

Runbook:

1. On the node run crictl ps and crictl info to gauge container runtime responsiveness;
2. Check whether the node has too many containers and whether disk IO is saturated — these are the main causes of slow PLEG;
3. For a stalled runtime, consider restarting containerd (briefly affects that node);
4. If it persists, reduce the Pod density on that node.

### KubeletPodStartUpLatencyHigh[​](#kubeletpodstartuplatencyhigh "Direct link to KubeletPodStartUpLatencyHigh")
