# MySQL alert rules for Prometheus: 11 rules with runbooks

11 ready-to-use MySQL alert rules in PromQL, each with severity, duration and runbook steps. Metrics from mysqld\_exporter, Categraf. Download as a Prometheus rules file or import into Nightingale.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

MySQL alert rules for the failures that page people in practice: an instance that is down or has just restarted, slow queries piling up, connections approaching max\_connections, too many running threads, InnoDB log waits, open files nearing the limit, and replication problems (IO or SQL thread stopped, replica lag). The exporter group uses mysqld\_exporter metric names (`mysql_global_status_*`, `mysql_slave_status_*`); each rule comes with the first commands to run, such as SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST and pt-query-digest, when it fires.

## At a glance[​](#at-a-glance "Direct link to At a glance")

* **11 rules**, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a `for` duration and runbook steps
* **Metrics from**: mysqld\_exporter, Categraf
* **Download**: [`mysql.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/mysql.yml), a standard Prometheus rules file (`groups:` format), checked with `promtool check rules`
* Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

## Rule list[​](#rule-list "Direct link to Rule list")

| Rule                                                                        | Severity | For |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | --- |
| More than 60% of the connections in MySQL are in a running state            | Warning  | 2m  |
| More than 80% of MySQL files open                                           | Warning  | 2m  |
| MySQL connection count has exceeded 80%                                     | Warning  | 2m  |
| Mysql has just restarted. Please be advised - exporter                      | Info     | —   |
| MySQL slow queries are piling up                                            | Warning  | 2m  |
| MysqlInnodbLogWaits - exporter                                              | Warning  | —   |
| MysqlSlaveIoThreadNotRunning - exporter                                     | Critical | —   |
| MysqlSlaveReplicationLag - exporter                                         | Critical | 1m  |
| MysqlSlaveSqlThreadNotRunning - exporter                                    | Critical | —   |
| The MySQL instance is down                                                  | Critical | —   |
| Mysql has opened a large number of file handles. Please be aware - categraf | Warning  | 2m  |

## Prometheus exporter (10)[​](#prometheus-exporter-10 "Direct link to Prometheus exporter (10)")

9 of the 10 rules in this group also apply unchanged to instances collected by Categraf, which produces the same metric names.

### More than 60% of the connections in MySQL are in a running state[​](#more-than-60-of-the-connections-in-mysql-are-in-a-running-state "Direct link to More than 60% of the connections in MySQL are in a running state")

Warning · 2m · Trigger:

```
avg by (instance) (mysql_global_status_threads_running) / avg by (instance) (mysql_global_variables_max_connections) * 100 > 60
```

Runbook:

1. Run SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST to see which SQL statement and which table the piled-up threads are concentrated on;
2. Run SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS to check for lock waits or deadlocks;
3. KILL the offending SQL to stop the bleeding, then add indexes or apply rate limiting;
4. Check whether an upstream traffic spike or a slow dependency is keeping connections from being released.

### More than 80% of MySQL files open[​](#more-than-80-of-mysql-files-open "Direct link to More than 80% of MySQL files open")

More than 80% of MySQL files open

Warning · 2m · Trigger:

```
avg by (instance) (mysql_global_status_innodb_num_open_files) / avg by (instance)(mysql_global_variables_open_files_limit) * 100 > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Run SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Open\_files' and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'open\_files\_limit' to confirm the current level;
2. Raise open\_files\_limit in my.cnf and raise the system ulimit -n and the systemd LimitNOFILE to match;
3. Check whether table\_open\_cache is set too large and inflating the handle count;
4. Check whether a large number of partitioned or small tables are being accessed at once.

### MySQL connection count has exceeded 80%[​](#mysql-connection-count-has-exceeded-80 "Direct link to MySQL connection count has exceeded 80%")

More than 80% of MySQL connections are in use

Warning · 2m · Trigger:

```
avg by (instance) (mysql_global_status_threads_connected) / avg by (instance) (mysql_global_variables_max_connections) * 100 > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Run SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST and group connections by source host to find the application with an abnormal connection count;
2. Tell a traffic spike apart from an application connection pool leak (many long-lived Sleep connections piling up);
3. As an emergency measure raise max\_connections, checking free memory at the same time to avoid an OOM;
4. For the root cause, cap the application connection pool and shorten wait\_timeout.

### Mysql has just restarted. Please be advised - exporter[​](#mysql-has-just-restarted-please-be-advised---exporter "Direct link to Mysql has just restarted. Please be advised - exporter")

MySQL has just been restarted, less than one minute ago

Info · — · Trigger:

```
mysql_global_status_uptime < 60
```

Runbook:

1. Check the error log (the file pointed to by SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log\_error') to tell a crash, an OOM kill and a manual restart apart;
2. If it was an OOM, compare innodb\_buffer\_pool\_size against the machine's physical memory and lower it;
3. If the restart was unplanned, check whether systemd or the container orchestrator is repeatedly restarting it;
4. After the restart, confirm replication resumed automatically and application connection pools reconnected.

### MySQL slow queries are piling up[​](#mysql-slow-queries-are-piling-up "Direct link to MySQL slow queries are piling up")

MySQL slow queries are piling up over the last 5 minutes

Warning · 2m · Trigger:

```
increase(mysql_global_status_slow_queries[5m]) > 10
```

Runbook:

1. Run SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST to find long-running SQL and KILL \<id> to stop the bleeding if needed;
2. Use mysqldumpslow -s t -t 10 \<slow\_log> or pt-query-digest to find the top slow queries;
3. Run EXPLAIN on the queries you found to inspect the plan, then add indexes or rewrite them;
4. If the noise comes from long\_query\_time being set too low, tune that parameter instead of ignoring the alert.

### MysqlInnodbLogWaits - exporter[​](#mysqlinnodblogwaits---exporter "Direct link to MysqlInnodbLogWaits - exporter")

MySQL innodb log writes stalling

Warning · — · Trigger:

```
rate(mysql_global_status_innodb_log_waits[15m]) > 10
```

Runbook:

1. Raise innodb\_log\_buffer\_size (typically doubling the 16M default up to 64M\~256M);
2. Check whether innodb\_log\_file\_size is too small and causing frequent checkpoints;
3. Run iostat -x 1 to see whether the disk holding the redo log is already at full utilization;
4. Check for large transactions writing too much data at once and split them into smaller batches.

### MysqlSlaveIoThreadNotRunning - exporter[​](#mysqlslaveiothreadnotrunning---exporter "Direct link to MysqlSlaveIoThreadNotRunning - exporter")

MySQL Slave IO thread not running

Critical · — · Trigger:

```
mysql_slave_status_master_server_id > 0 and ON (instance) mysql_slave_status_slave_io_running == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G on the replica and read Last\_IO\_Error;
2. The usual causes are the primary being unreachable, an invalid replication account, or the required binlog having been purged — fix the network, reset the account with CHANGE MASTER TO, or rebuild the replica from a backup respectively;
3. Then run START SLAVE IO\_THREAD and confirm Slave\_IO\_Running=Yes;
4. Take read traffic off this replica before you start.

### MysqlSlaveReplicationLag - exporter[​](#mysqlslavereplicationlag---exporter "Direct link to MysqlSlaveReplicationLag - exporter")

Critical · 1m · Trigger:

```
mysql_slave_status_master_server_id > 0 and ON (instance) (mysql_slave_status_seconds_behind_master - mysql_slave_status_sql_delay) > 30
```

Runbook:

1. Run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G and read Seconds\_Behind\_Master together with the event the SQL thread is currently applying;
2. On the primary, run SHOW PROCESSLIST to check for a large transaction or a bulk DML loading data;
3. If the replica applies single-threaded, enable parallel replication (slave\_parallel\_workers / slave\_parallel\_type=LOGICAL\_CLOCK);
4. If the lag keeps growing, move read traffic back to the primary or to another replica.

### MysqlSlaveSqlThreadNotRunning - exporter[​](#mysqlslavesqlthreadnotrunning---exporter "Direct link to MysqlSlaveSqlThreadNotRunning - exporter")

MySQL Slave SQL thread not running

Critical · — · Trigger:

```
mysql_slave_status_master_server_id > 0 and ON (instance) mysql_slave_status_slave_sql_running == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G on the replica and read Last\_SQL\_Error to identify the event it is stuck on;
2. If it is a conflict that can be safely skipped (such as a duplicate primary key), verify the data is consistent, then run SET GLOBAL sql\_slave\_skip\_counter=1 followed by START SLAVE SQL\_THREAD;
3. If the primary and replica data have already diverged, rebuild the replica from a backup instead of blindly skipping;
4. Take read traffic off this replica before you start.

### The MySQL instance is down[​](#the-mysql-instance-is-down "Direct link to The MySQL instance is down")

Critical · — · Trigger:

```
mysql_up == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Log in to the host and run systemctl status mysqld or docker ps to confirm the process is alive;
2. If it is alive, connect by hand with mysql -h\<host> -P\<port> -u\<user> -p to tell a hung instance apart from a network or account problem;
3. If it is not running, read the tail of the error log to identify the cause (OOM, full disk, corrupted data files) before starting it — do not blindly restart;
4. If replication is in use, immediately assess whether to fail over, and confirm the application has taken this node out of rotation.

## Categraf (1)[​](#categraf-1 "Direct link to Categraf (1)")

For hosts and instances collected by Categraf; metric names follow Categraf plugins.

### Mysql has opened a large number of file handles. Please be aware - categraf[​](#mysql-has-opened-a-large-number-of-file-handles-please-be-aware---categraf "Direct link to Mysql has opened a large number of file handles. Please be aware - categraf")

More than 80% of MySQL files open

Warning · 2m · Trigger:

```
avg by (instance) (mysql_global_status_open_files) / avg by (instance)(mysql_global_variables_open_files_limit) * 100 > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Run SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Open\_files' and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'open\_files\_limit' to confirm the current level;
2. Raise open\_files\_limit in my.cnf and raise the system ulimit -n and the systemd LimitNOFILE to match;
3. Check whether table\_open\_cache is set too large and inflating the handle count;
4. Check whether a large number of partitioned or small tables are being accessed at once.

## How to use these rules[​](#how-to-use-these-rules "Direct link to How to use these rules")

* **With Prometheus or vmalert**: download [`mysql.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/mysql.yml), add it to `rule_files` (or `-rule` for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a `severity` label (critical / warning / info), and `runbook_url` points back to this page.
* **With Nightingale**: the same rules ship in the [MySQL](https://n9e.github.io/integrations/mysql.md) integration template. Open the integration center, [import the rules into a business group](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md), and enable them one by one. Nightingale keeps the runbook with each alert and can evaluate the rules against Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and other data sources.

## Sources and license[​](#sources-and-license "Direct link to Sources and license")

The runbook steps and the remaining rules come from Nightingale's integration templates ([MySQL](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/tree/main/integrations/MySQL), Apache-2.0). Corrections are welcome as pull requests there.

## Related[​](#related "Direct link to Related")

* [Monitor MySQL with Nightingale](https://n9e.github.io/integrations/mysql.md): collector config, dashboards and metric reference
* [Write a metric rule in Nightingale](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/metric-rules.md)
* [All alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules.md)

# Prometheus alert rules for Prometheus: 30 rules with runbooks

30 ready-to-use Prometheus alert rules in PromQL, each with severity, duration and runbook steps. Metrics from Prometheus's own /metrics, Prometheus Operator. Download as a Prometheus rules file or import into Nightingale.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Rules that watch Prometheus itself: a bad configuration reload, failing or missed rule evaluations, a notification queue backing up, no connection to Alertmanager, remote write falling behind, TSDB compactions or reloads failing, scrape and label limits being hit, and the Prometheus Operator failing to reconcile. When these fire, every other alert you rely on may be silently missing, so they are worth routing to the people who own the monitoring stack rather than to application teams.

## At a glance[​](#at-a-glance "Direct link to At a glance")

* **30 rules**, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a `for` duration and runbook steps
* **Metrics from**: Prometheus's own /metrics, Prometheus Operator
* **Download**: [`prometheus.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus.yml), a standard Prometheus rules file (`groups:` format), checked with `promtool check rules`
* Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

## Prometheus self-monitoring (30)[​](#prometheus-self-monitoring-30 "Direct link to Prometheus self-monitoring (30)")

### ConfigReloaderSidecarErrors[​](#configreloadersidecarerrors "Direct link to ConfigReloaderSidecarErrors")

Errors encountered while the {{$labels.pod}} config-reloader sidecar attempts to sync config in {{$labels.namespace}} namespace. As a result, configuration for service running in {{$labels.pod}} may be stale and cannot be updated anymore.

Warning · 10m · Trigger:

```
max_over_time(reloader_last_reload_successful{namespace=~".+"}[5m]) == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl logs \<pod> -c config-reloader -n \<ns> for the specific error;
2. It is usually a config syntax error causing the reload to be rejected;
3. Validate with promtool check config / amtool check-config;
4. After fixing, confirm the reload succeeded and verify the new config on Prometheus's /config page.

### PrometheusOperatorListErrors[​](#prometheusoperatorlisterrors "Direct link to PrometheusOperatorListErrors")

Errors while performing List operations in controller {{$labels.controller}} in {{$labels.namespace}} namespace.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
(sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_list_operations_failed_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[10m])) / sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_list_operations_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[10m]))) > 0.4
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl logs -n \<ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error;
2. For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources;
3. For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule);
4. For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.

### PrometheusOperatorNodeLookupErrors[​](#prometheusoperatornodelookuperrors "Direct link to PrometheusOperatorNodeLookupErrors")

Errors while reconciling Prometheus in {{ $labels.namespace }} Namespace.

Warning · 10m · Trigger:

```
rate(prometheus_operator_node_address_lookup_errors_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0.1
```

Runbook:

1. Run kubectl logs -n \<ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error;
2. For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources;
3. For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule);
4. For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.

min by (cluster,controller,namespace) (max_over_time(prometheus_operator_ready{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) == 0)

Warning · 10m · Trigger:

```
(sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_reconcile_errors_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]))) / (sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_reconcile_operations_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]))) > 0.1

### PrometheusBadConfig[​](#prometheusbadconfig "Direct link to PrometheusBadConfig")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to reload its configuration.

Critical · 10m · Trigger:

```
# Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see

# https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details.

max_over_time(prometheus_config_last_reload_successful{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Find the config parse error line in kubectl logs or the instance log;
2. Validate locally with promtool check config prometheus.yml;
3. On Kubernetes the config is usually generated by the Operator — check ServiceMonitor/PrometheusRule for invalid fields;
4. After fixing, confirm /-/reload succeeded and the /config page shows the new configuration.

### PrometheusDuplicateTimestamps[​](#prometheusduplicatetimestamps "Direct link to PrometheusDuplicateTimestamps")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is dropping {{ printf "%.4g" $value }} samples/s with different values but duplicated timestamp.

Warning · 10m · Trigger:

```
rate(prometheus_target_scrapes_sample_duplicate_timestamp_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Find the duplicated targets on the /targets page (the same instance appearing under several jobs);
2. Check whether ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor selectors are too broad and overlapping;
3. Tighten the selectors so each target is scraped by exactly one job;
4. After fixing, confirm the discard counter stops growing.

### PrometheusErrorSendingAlertsToAnyAlertmanager[​](#prometheuserrorsendingalertstoanyalertmanager "Direct link to PrometheusErrorSendingAlertsToAnyAlertmanager")

{{ printf "%.1f" $value }}% minimum errors while sending alerts from Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} to any Alertmanager.

Critical · 15m · Trigger:

```
min without (alertmanager) (

  rate(prometheus_notifications_errors_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring",alertmanager!~``}[5m])

/

  rate(prometheus_notifications_sent_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring",alertmanager!~``}[5m])

)

* 100

> 3
```

Runbook:

1. Check whether the Alertmanager instances are healthy and reachable;
2. Confirm Alertmanager discovery on the Prometheus /status page;
3. If the queue is full, check whether Alertmanager processing is stuck or the alert volume spiked abnormally;
4. After recovery, confirm Alertmanager actually received the alerts so nothing fails silently.

### PrometheusErrorSendingAlertsToSomeAlertmanagers[​](#prometheuserrorsendingalertstosomealertmanagers "Direct link to PrometheusErrorSendingAlertsToSomeAlertmanagers")

{{ printf "%.1f" $value }}% errors while sending alerts from Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} to Alertmanager {{$labels.alertmanager}}.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
(

  rate(prometheus_notifications_errors_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])

/

  rate(prometheus_notifications_sent_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])

)

* 100

> 1
```

Runbook:

4. After recovery, confirm Alertmanager actually received the alerts so nothing fails silently.

### PrometheusHighQueryLoad[​](#prometheushighqueryload "Direct link to PrometheusHighQueryLoad")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} query API has less than 20% available capacity in its query engine for the last 15 minutes.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
avg_over_time(prometheus_engine_queries{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) / max_over_time(prometheus_engine_queries_concurrent_max{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0.8
```

Runbook:

1. Check the query engine concurrency and queue metrics on the /status page;
2. Use topk-style queries or the query log to find the heaviest queries;
3. The usual root causes are high-cardinality labels and over-wide time ranges — narrow the range and reduce group by dimensions;
4. If it stays high after tuning, scale Prometheus or use federation/sharding.

### PrometheusLabelLimitHit[​](#prometheuslabellimithit "Direct link to PrometheusLabelLimitHit")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has dropped {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} targets because some samples exceeded the configured label\_limit, label\_name\_length\_limit or label\_value\_length\_limit.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_target_scrape_pool_exceeded_label_limits_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Find the rejected targets and the specific reason on the /targets page;
2. On the target side, work out why the label count is so high — usually high-cardinality data (user ID, request ID) was made into labels;
3. Fix the metric design at the source, or drop the excess labels with metric\_relabel\_configs;
4. If more labels are genuinely needed, raise label\_limit after assessing the cardinality impact.

### PrometheusMissingRuleEvaluations[​](#prometheusmissingruleevaluations "Direct link to PrometheusMissingRuleEvaluations")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has missed {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} rule group evaluations in the last 5m.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_rule_group_iterations_missed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Check the log for rule evaluation timeout errors;
2. Find the rule group with the longest evaluation time, usually recording rules with heavy queries;
3. Split the rule group, lengthen evaluation\_interval, or optimise the queries in the rules;
4. If resources are short, scale Prometheus.

### PrometheusNotConnectedToAlertmanagers[​](#prometheusnotconnectedtoalertmanagers "Direct link to PrometheusNotConnectedToAlertmanagers")

max_over_time(prometheus_notifications_alertmanagers_discovered{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) < 1
```

Runbook:

1. Check whether the Alertmanager instances are healthy and reachable;
2. Confirm Alertmanager discovery on the Prometheus /status page;
3. If the queue is full, check whether Alertmanager processing is stuck or the alert volume spiked abnormally;
4. After recovery, confirm Alertmanager actually received the alerts so nothing fails silently.

### PrometheusNotificationQueueRunningFull[​](#prometheusnotificationqueuerunningfull "Direct link to PrometheusNotificationQueueRunningFull")

Alert notification queue of Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is running full.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
# Without min_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see

# https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details.

(

  predict_linear(prometheus_notifications_queue_length{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m], 60 * 30)

>

  min_over_time(prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])

)
```

Runbook:

1. Check whether the Alertmanager instances are healthy and reachable;
2. Confirm Alertmanager discovery on the Prometheus /status page;
3. If the queue is full, check whether Alertmanager processing is stuck or the alert volume spiked abnormally;
4. After recovery, confirm Alertmanager actually received the alerts so nothing fails silently.

### PrometheusNotIngestingSamples[​](#prometheusnotingestingsamples "Direct link to PrometheusNotIngestingSamples")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is not ingesting samples.

Warning · 10m · Trigger:

```
(

  rate(prometheus_tsdb_head_samples_appended_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) <= 0

and

  (

    sum without(scrape_job) (prometheus_target_metadata_cache_entries{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}) > 0

  or

    sum without(rule_group) (prometheus_rule_group_rules{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}) > 0

  )

)
```

Runbook:

1. Check on the /targets page whether every target is down;
2. Check that service discovery is working (the /service-discovery page);
3. If a config error left the target list empty, treat it as a configuration problem;
4. This is total monitoring blindness and should be the highest priority.

### PrometheusOutOfOrderTimestamps[​](#prometheusoutofordertimestamps "Direct link to PrometheusOutOfOrderTimestamps")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is dropping {{ printf "%.4g" $value }} samples/s with timestamps arriving out of order.

Warning · 10m · Trigger:

```
rate(prometheus_target_scrapes_sample_out_of_order_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Identify which target is reporting out-of-order data;
2. The usual root causes are an unsynchronised clock on the target, or metrics aggregated from multiple sources with mixed timestamps;
3. Correct the target machine's clock first (chronyc);
4. For Pushgateway-style setups, review how the pusher handles timestamps.

### PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures[​](#prometheusremotestoragefailures "Direct link to PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} failed to send {{ printf "%.1f" $value }}% of the samples to {{ $labels.remote\_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}

Critical · 15m · Trigger:

```
(

  (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_failed_samples_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]))

/

  (

    (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_failed_samples_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]))

  +

    (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_succeeded_samples_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]))

  )

)

* 100

> 1
```

Runbook:

1. Check the Prometheus log for remote\_write or tsdb errors;
2. For remote write failures, confirm remote storage availability and credentials, and check for throttling;
3. For local storage failures, check disk space and permissions — a corrupted TSDB may require clearing the WAL;
4. Confirm the queue backlog is draining; if not, raise queue\_config or reduce the write volume.

### PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind[​](#prometheusremotewritebehind "Direct link to PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} remote write is {{ printf "%.1f" $value }}s behind for {{ $labels.remote\_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}.

Critical · 15m · Trigger:

```
# Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see

# https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details.

(

  max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])

- ignoring(remote_name, url) group_right

  max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])

)

> 120
```

Runbook:

1. Check the Prometheus log for remote\_write or tsdb errors;
2. For remote write failures, confirm remote storage availability and credentials, and check for throttling;
3. For local storage failures, check disk space and permissions — a corrupted TSDB may require clearing the WAL;
4. Confirm the queue backlog is draining; if not, raise queue\_config or reduce the write volume.

### PrometheusRuleFailures[​](#prometheusrulefailures "Direct link to PrometheusRuleFailures")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to evaluate {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} rules in the last 5m.

Critical · 15m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_rule_evaluation_failures_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Check the log for the failing rule name and error;
2. Common causes are a query syntax error in the rule, a reference to a non-existent metric, or an oversized result;
3. Validate the rule files with promtool check rules;
4. After fixing, confirm the rule shows ok on the /rules page.

### PrometheusScrapeBodySizeLimitHit[​](#prometheusscrapebodysizelimithit "Direct link to PrometheusScrapeBodySizeLimitHit")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} scrapes in the last 5m because some targets exceeded the configured body\_size\_limit.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_target_scrapes_exceeded_body_size_limit_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Find the rejected targets on the /targets page;
2. curl that target's /metrics by hand to see the actual size and whether the metric count has ballooned;
3. High-cardinality metrics are the usual cause — fix at the source or drop with metric\_relabel\_configs;
4. If a higher limit is genuinely needed, raise body\_size\_limit.

### PrometheusScrapeSampleLimitHit[​](#prometheusscrapesamplelimithit "Direct link to PrometheusScrapeSampleLimitHit")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} scrapes in the last 5m because some targets exceeded the configured sample\_limit.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_target_scrapes_exceeded_sample_limit_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Find the rejected targets and their sample counts on the /targets page;
2. Run curl /metrics | wc -l by hand to confirm the actual scale;
3. High-cardinality metrics are the main cause — reduce label dimensions at the source or drop unneeded metrics with metric\_relabel\_configs;
4. If a higher limit is genuinely needed, raise sample\_limit after assessing storage and query impact.

### PrometheusSDRefreshFailure[​](#prometheussdrefreshfailure "Direct link to PrometheusSDRefreshFailure")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to refresh SD with mechanism {{$labels.mechanism}}.

Warning · 20m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_sd_refresh_failures_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[10m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Check the log for service discovery errors;
2. For Kubernetes SD, check that Prometheus's RBAC covers the required resources;
3. For other SD types (Consul, file, …), check backend reachability and credentials;
4. After fixing, confirm the target list is updated on the /service-discovery page.

### PrometheusTargetLimitHit[​](#prometheustargetlimithit "Direct link to PrometheusTargetLimitHit")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has dropped {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} targets because the number of targets exceeded the configured target\_limit.

Warning · 15m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_target_scrape_pool_exceeded_target_limit_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the current target count against the limit on the /targets page;
2. Check whether the ServiceMonitor selector is too broad and picking up unwanted targets;
3. Tighten the selector or split across multiple Prometheus instances by business domain;
4. If more targets are genuinely needed, raise target\_limit and size the resources accordingly.

### PrometheusTargetSyncFailure[​](#prometheustargetsyncfailure "Direct link to PrometheusTargetSyncFailure")

{{ printf "%.0f" $value }} targets in Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} have failed to sync because invalid configuration was supplied.

Critical · 5m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_target_sync_failed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[30m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Check the log for the specific target sync error;
2. It is usually a relabel misconfiguration producing an invalid target address;
3. Review recently changed ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor configurations;
4. After fixing, confirm the targets are healthy again on the /targets page.

### PrometheusTSDBCompactionsFailing[​](#prometheustsdbcompactionsfailing "Direct link to PrometheusTSDBCompactionsFailing")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has detected {{$value | humanize}} compaction failures over the last 3h.

Warning · 240m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_tsdb_compactions_failed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[3h]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Check the log for compaction errors;
2. The most common cause is insufficient disk space — confirm the free space first;
3. A corrupted block may need its directory deleted (losing that time range);
4. After fixing, confirm subsequent compactions complete successfully.

### PrometheusTSDBReloadsFailing[​](#prometheustsdbreloadsfailing "Direct link to PrometheusTSDBReloadsFailing")

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has detected {{$value | humanize}} reload failures over the last 3h.

Warning · 240m · Trigger:

```
increase(prometheus_tsdb_reloads_failures_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[3h]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Check the log for reload errors and which block is involved;
2. It is usually a corrupted block or a permissions problem;
3. For permissions, fix the data directory owner; a corrupted block can only be deleted (losing that time range);
4. After fixing, restart Prometheus and confirm the data is queryable.

## How to use these rules[​](#how-to-use-these-rules "Direct link to How to use these rules")

* **With Prometheus or vmalert**: download [`prometheus.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus.yml), add it to `rule_files` (or `-rule` for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a `severity` label (critical / warning / info), and `runbook_url` points back to this page.
* **With Nightingale**: the same rules ship in the [Kubernetes](https://n9e.github.io/integrations/kubernetes.md) integration template. Open the integration center, [import the rules into a business group](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md), and enable them one by one. Nightingale keeps the runbook with each alert and can evaluate the rules against Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and other data sources.

## Sources and license[​](#sources-and-license "Direct link to Sources and license")

Many rule expressions are adapted from [kube-prometheus](https://github.com/prometheus-operator/kube-prometheus) (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps and the remaining rules come from Nightingale's integration templates ([Kubernetes](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/tree/main/integrations/Kubernetes), Apache-2.0). Corrections are welcome as pull requests there.

## Related[​](#related "Direct link to Related")

* [Monitor Kubernetes with Nightingale](https://n9e.github.io/integrations/kubernetes.md): collector config, dashboards and metric reference
* [Write a metric rule in Nightingale](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/metric-rules.md)

# Redis alert rules for Prometheus: 12 rules with runbooks

12 ready-to-use Redis alert rules in PromQL, each with severity, duration and runbook steps. Metrics from redis\_exporter, Categraf. Download as a Prometheus rules file or import into Nightingale.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Redis alert rules for high memory usage, a rising eviction rate, rejected connections, too many client connections, a falling cache hit ratio, high command or ping latency, and an instance that has just restarted. The exporter group uses oliver006/redis\_exporter metric names; the Categraf group covers the same checks for instances collected by Categraf.

## At a glance[​](#at-a-glance "Direct link to At a glance")

* **12 rules**, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a `for` duration and runbook steps
* **Metrics from**: redis\_exporter, Categraf
* **Download**: [`redis.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/redis.yml), a standard Prometheus rules file (`groups:` format), checked with `promtool check rules`
* Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

## Rule list[​](#rule-list "Direct link to Rule list")

| Rule                                                      | Severity | For |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | --- |
| High Redis client connection count - exporter             | Warning  | 1m  |
| High Redis eviction rate - exporter                       | Warning  | 1m  |
| High Redis latency - exporter                             | Warning  | 1m  |
| High Redis memory usage rate - exporter                   | Warning  | 1m  |
| Low Redis hit rate - exporter                             | Warning  | 1m  |
| Redis connection refused - exporter                       | Warning  | —   |
| Redis has just been restarted, please be aware - exporter | Info     | —   |
| High Redis eviction rate                                  | Warning  | 1m  |
| High Redis memory usage rate                              | Warning  | 1m  |
| High Redis Ping latency (above 100 milliseconds)          | Warning  | 1m  |
| Low Redis hit rate                                        | Warning  | 1m  |
| Redis connection refused                                  | Warning  | —   |

## Prometheus exporter (7)[​](#prometheus-exporter-7 "Direct link to Prometheus exporter (7)")

1 of the 7 rules in this group also apply unchanged to instances collected by Categraf, which produces the same metric names.

### High Redis client connection count - exporter[​](#high-redis-client-connection-count---exporter "Direct link to High Redis client connection count - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
(redis_connected_clients / redis_config_maxclients) > 0.85
```

Runbook:

1. Use CLIENT LIST grouped by source address to find the application holding the most connections;
2. Tell a scale-out apart from a connection pool leak (many idle connections never released);
3. As an emergency measure run CONFIG SET maxclients \<larger value> and check the system ulimit -n to match;
4. For the root cause, cap the application connection pool and enable connection reuse.

### High Redis eviction rate - exporter[​](#high-redis-eviction-rate---exporter "Direct link to High Redis eviction rate - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
rate(redis_evicted_keys_total[5m]) / sum without (db) (redis_db_keys) > 0.1
```

Runbook:

1. Use INFO memory to compare used\_memory against maxmemory and confirm whether it has topped out;
2. Use redis-cli --bigkeys to find abnormally large keys and clean up or split them;
3. Confirm maxmemory-policy matches expectations (allkeys-lru for a pure cache; data you cannot afford to lose must not be left evictable);
4. If capacity is genuinely insufficient, scale up memory or shard.

### High Redis latency - exporter[​](#high-redis-latency---exporter "Direct link to High Redis latency - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
sum without (cmd) (rate(redis_commands_duration_seconds_total[5m])) / rate(redis_commands_processed_total[5m]) > 0.25
```

Runbook:

1. Run SLOWLOG GET 10 to find the slowest commands;
2. Focus on O(N) commands such as KEYS, HGETALL and SMEMBERS and on big-key operations, switching to SCAN or batched processing;
3. Check INFO persistence to see whether an RDB/AOF rewrite fork is causing the stall;
4. Check whether the host CPU is saturated or the machine is swapping.

### High Redis memory usage rate - exporter[​](#high-redis-memory-usage-rate---exporter "Direct link to High Redis memory usage rate - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
redis_memory_max_bytes > 0 and (redis_memory_used_bytes / redis_memory_max_bytes) > 0.85
```

Runbook:

1. Check used\_memory\_rss and the fragmentation ratio mem\_fragmentation\_ratio in INFO memory — enable activedefrag if fragmentation is high;
2. Use redis-cli --bigkeys / --memkeys to find big keys and split them or add TTLs;
3. Check whether keys without an expiry are piling up;
4. Confirm maxmemory-policy, then scale up memory or shard as needed.

### Low Redis hit rate - exporter[​](#low-redis-hit-rate---exporter "Direct link to Low Redis hit rate - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total[5m])

/

(rate(redis_keyspace_misses_total[5m]) + rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total[5m]))

< 0.9
```

Runbook:

1. First rule out a cold start after a restart or scale-out (check redis\_uptime\_in\_seconds);
2. Compare the growth of keyspace\_hits and keyspace\_misses in INFO stats to tell unwarmed new keys apart from heavy eviction;
3. If an eviction alert fired at the same time, treat it as insufficient memory (scale up or clean up big keys);
4. Review the cache key design and whether the TTL is too short on the application side.

### Redis connection refused - exporter[​](#redis-connection-refused---exporter "Direct link to Redis connection refused - exporter")

Warning · — · Trigger:

```
(rate(redis_rejected_connections_total[5m])) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Compare connected\_clients from INFO clients against CONFIG GET maxclients;
2. Use CLIENT LIST grouped by source address to find the application leaking connections;
3. As an emergency measure run CONFIG SET maxclients \<larger value>, confirming the system ulimit -n is high enough;
4. For the root cause, cap the application connection pool and enable connection reuse.

### Redis has just been restarted, please be aware - exporter[​](#redis-has-just-been-restarted-please-be-aware---exporter "Direct link to Redis has just been restarted, please be aware - exporter")

Info · — · Trigger:

```
redis_uptime_in_seconds < 600
```

Runbook:

1. Check the Redis log to tell an OOM kill, a crash and a manual restart apart;
2. If the system OOM killer was involved, compare maxmemory against free host memory and lower maxmemory;
3. Confirm the RDB/AOF loaded correctly and the data is complete (check rdb\_last\_load\_keys\_loaded in INFO persistence);
4. After the restart, watch the hit rate and the backend database load, and warm the cache if needed.

## Categraf (5)[​](#categraf-5 "Direct link to Categraf (5)")

For hosts and instances collected by Categraf; metric names follow Categraf plugins.

### High Redis eviction rate[​](#high-redis-eviction-rate "Direct link to High Redis eviction rate")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
rate(redis_evicted_keys[5m]) / sum without (db) (redis_keyspace_keys) > 0.1
```

Runbook:

1. Use INFO memory to compare used\_memory against maxmemory and confirm whether it has topped out;
2. Use redis-cli --bigkeys to find abnormally large keys and clean up or split them;
3. Confirm maxmemory-policy matches expectations (allkeys-lru for a pure cache; data you cannot afford to lose must not be left evictable);

### High Redis memory usage rate[​](#high-redis-memory-usage-rate "Direct link to High Redis memory usage rate")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
redis_maxmemory > 0 and (redis_used_memory / redis_maxmemory) > 0.85
```

Runbook:

1. Check used\_memory\_rss and the fragmentation ratio mem\_fragmentation\_ratio in INFO memory — enable activedefrag if fragmentation is high;
2. Use redis-cli --bigkeys / --memkeys to find big keys and split them or add TTLs;
3. Check whether keys without an expiry are piling up;
4. Confirm maxmemory-policy, then scale up memory or shard as needed.

### High Redis Ping latency (above 100 milliseconds)[​](#high-redis-ping-latency-above-100-milliseconds "Direct link to High Redis Ping latency (above 100 milliseconds)")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
redis_ping_use_seconds > 0.1
```

Runbook:

1. Use redis-cli --latency and SLOWLOG GET 10 to check whether slow commands (KEYS, HGETALL, big-key operations) are blocking the main thread;
2. Check INFO persistence to see whether an RDB/AOF rewrite fork is causing the stall;
3. Check whether the host CPU is saturated or the machine is swapping;
4. Once you find the slow command, replace it with SCAN or batched operations.

### Low Redis hit rate[​](#low-redis-hit-rate "Direct link to Low Redis hit rate")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
rate(redis_keyspace_hits[5m])

/

(rate(redis_keyspace_misses[5m]) + rate(redis_keyspace_hits[5m]))

< 0.9
```

Runbook:

1. First rule out a cold start after a restart or scale-out (check redis\_uptime\_in\_seconds);
2. Compare the growth of keyspace\_hits and keyspace\_misses in INFO stats to tell unwarmed new keys apart from heavy eviction;
3. If an eviction alert fired at the same time, treat it as insufficient memory (scale up or clean up big keys);
4. Review the cache key design and whether the TTL is too short on the application side.

### Redis connection refused[​](#redis-connection-refused "Direct link to Redis connection refused")

Warning · — · Trigger:

```
(rate(redis_rejected_connections[5m])) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Compare connected\_clients from INFO clients against CONFIG GET maxclients;
2. Use CLIENT LIST grouped by source address to find the application leaking connections;
3. As an emergency measure run CONFIG SET maxclients \<larger value>, confirming the system ulimit -n is high enough;
4. For the root cause, cap the application connection pool and enable connection reuse.

## How to use these rules[​](#how-to-use-these-rules "Direct link to How to use these rules")

# Windows alert rules for Prometheus: 13 rules with runbooks

13 ready-to-use Windows alert rules in PromQL, each with severity, duration and runbook steps. Metrics from windows\_exporter, Categraf. Download as a Prometheus rules file or import into Nightingale.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Windows Server alert rules for high CPU and memory usage, disks that are full or predicted to fill within 4 hours, busy disk IO, inbound and outbound packet loss, an unexpected reboot, and a host whose collector has gone silent. The exporter group uses prometheus-community/windows\_exporter metric names (`windows_*`); the Categraf group covers hosts collected by Categraf on Windows.

## At a glance[​](#at-a-glance "Direct link to At a glance")

* **13 rules**, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a `for` duration and runbook steps
* **Metrics from**: windows\_exporter, Categraf
* **Download**: [`windows.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/windows.yml), a standard Prometheus rules file (`groups:` format), checked with `promtool check rules`
* Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

## Rule list[​](#rule-list "Direct link to Rule list")

| Rule                                                                     | Severity | For |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- | --- |
| High CPU utilization - exporter                                          | Warning  | 1m  |
| High memory usage rate - exporter                                        | Warning  | 1m  |
| machine reboot in the last 15 minutes - exporter                         | Info     | 1m  |
| packet loss issue in the inbound direction - exporter                    | Warning  | 1m  |
| packet loss issue in the outbound direction - exporter                   | Warning  | 1m  |
| The hard disk is almost full - exporter                                  | Critical | 1m  |
| Hard disk - expected to be written full in 4 hours - categraf \[Windows] | Critical | 1m  |
| Hard disk - IO is a bit busy - categraf \[Windows]                       | Warning  | 1m  |
| Machine load - high memory, please pay attention - categraf\[Windows]    | Info     | 1m  |
| packet loss in the inbound direction - categraf\[Windows]                | Info     | 1m  |
| packet loss in the outbound direction - categraf \[Windows]              | Info     | 1m  |
| Disk larger than 200G is running out of space \[Windows]                 | Info     | 1m  |
| Disk smaller than 200G is running out of space \[Windows]                | Info     | 1m  |

## Prometheus exporter (6)[​](#prometheus-exporter-6 "Direct link to Prometheus exporter (6)")

### High CPU utilization - exporter[​](#high-cpu-utilization---exporter "Direct link to High CPU utilization - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
100 * sum by (instance) (rate(windows_cpu_time_total{mode != 'idle'}[5m])) / count by (instance) (windows_cpu_core_frequency_mhz) > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Open Task Manager, or run Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 to find the busiest processes;
2. Use Resource Monitor (resmon) to see whether user or kernel time dominates — high kernel time points at drivers or antivirus;
3. Tell traffic growth apart from a program fault (infinite loop, frequent GC);
4. For growth, scale out or rate limit; for a fault, restart the service and fix it.

### High memory usage rate - exporter[​](#high-memory-usage-rate---exporter "Direct link to High memory usage rate - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
100 * (windows_cs_physical_memory_bytes - windows_os_physical_memory_free_bytes) / windows_cs_physical_memory_bytes  > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-Process | Sort-Object WS -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 to find the largest consumers;
2. Use perfmon to watch Available MBytes and Pages/sec — a sustained high Pages/sec means it is already paging heavily;
3. Determine whether it is growth or a process leak — a leak must be located in the application, a restart only helps temporarily;
4. Confirm the page file is sized sensibly and add memory if needed.

### machine reboot in the last 15 minutes - exporter[​](#machine-reboot-in-the-last-15-minutes---exporter "Direct link to machine reboot in the last 15 minutes - exporter")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
time() - windows_system_system_up_time  < 900
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-EventLog -LogName System -Newest 50, or use Event Viewer to look for Event ID 6008 (unexpected shutdown) and 1074 (planned shutdown and its initiator) to find the cause;
2. If Windows Update triggered it, evaluate adjusting the update window and restart policy;
3. If it was a bugcheck or power loss, check the minidump and hardware logs;
4. Confirm critical services started automatically after the reboot (check startup type with Get-Service).

### packet loss issue in the inbound direction - exporter[​](#packet-loss-issue-in-the-inbound-direction---exporter "Direct link to packet loss issue in the inbound direction - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
100 * rate(windows_net_packets_received_errors[5m]) / (rate(windows_net_packets_received_errors[5m]) + rate(windows_net_packets_received_total[5m])>0)  > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-NetAdapterStatistics to confirm inbound error counters are growing;
2. Use Get-NetAdapter to confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match the peer;
3. Check the cable/optical module, swapping the cable or port to cross-check;
4. Update the NIC driver and ask the network team for the switch port's error counters.

### packet loss issue in the outbound direction - exporter[​](#packet-loss-issue-in-the-outbound-direction---exporter "Direct link to packet loss issue in the outbound direction - exporter")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
100 * rate(windows_net_packets_outbound_errors[5m]) / (rate(windows_net_packets_outbound_errors[5m]) + rate(windows_net_packets_sent_total[5m])>0)  > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-NetAdapterStatistics to confirm outbound error counters are growing;
2. Use Get-NetAdapter to confirm speed and duplex match the peer;
3. Check the cable/optical module and cross-check by swapping;
4. Update the NIC driver and confirm whether the link is saturated and needs more bandwidth.

### The hard disk is almost full - exporter[​](#the-hard-disk-is-almost-full---exporter "Direct link to The hard disk is almost full - exporter")

Critical · 1m · Trigger:

```
100 * (windows_logical_disk_size_bytes - windows_logical_disk_free_bytes) / windows_logical_disk_size_bytes  > 90
```

Runbook:

1. Identify the drive letter with Get-PSDrive or Explorer;
2. Use a tool like TreeSize, or Get-ChildItem -Recurse | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 20, to find the large files;
3. Start with logs, temporary files (cleanmgr) and the Windows Update cache (C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download);
4. Longer term, expand the disk or move the data directory to another volume.

## Categraf (7)[​](#categraf-7 "Direct link to Categraf (7)")

For hosts and instances collected by Categraf; metric names follow Categraf plugins.

### Hard disk - expected to be written full in 4 hours - categraf \[Windows][​](#hard-disk---expected-to-be-written-full-in-4-hours---categraf-windows "Direct link to Hard disk - expected to be written full in 4 hours - categraf \[Windows]")

Critical · 1m · Trigger:

```
predict_linear(disk_free{platform=~"windows"}[1h], 4*3600) < 0
```

Runbook:

1. Identify the drive letter in Explorer or with Get-PSDrive;
2. Run Get-ChildItem \<drive>:\ -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 20 to find the fastest-growing large files;
3. Start with logs, temporary files (run cleanmgr) and the Windows Update cache at C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download;
4. Confirm whether something abnormal is writing (an application looping on logs, backups piling up) — without fixing the root cause, cleanup only buys time.

### Hard disk - IO is a bit busy - categraf \[Windows][​](#hard-disk---io-is-a-bit-busy---categraf-windows "Direct link to Hard disk - IO is a bit busy - categraf \[Windows]")

Warning · 1m · Trigger:

```
rate(diskio_io_time{platform=~"windows"}[1m])/10 > 99
```

Runbook:

1. Open Resource Monitor (resmon), go to the Disk tab and sort by response time to see which disk and which file;
2. Run Get-Counter '\PhysicalDisk(\*)\Avg. Disk sec/Transfer' to check average response time;
3. Use Resource Monitor to find the process doing the most IO — usually a database, a backup job or an antivirus full scan;
4. Move deferrable work off peak; if the load is sustained, consider SSDs or spreading the data.

### Machine load - high memory, please pay attention - categraf\[Windows][​](#machine-load---high-memory-please-pay-attention---categrafwindows "Direct link to Machine load - high memory, please pay attention - categraf\[Windows]")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
mem_available_percent{platform=~"windows"} < 25



mem_available_percent{platform=~"windows"} < 15



mem_available_percent{platform=~"windows"} < 5
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-Process | Sort-Object WS -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 to find the largest consumers;
2. Use perfmon to watch Available MBytes and Pages/sec — a sustained high Pages/sec means it is already paging heavily;
3. Determine whether it is growth or a process leak — a leak must be located in the application, a restart only helps temporarily;
4. Confirm the page file is sized sensibly and add memory if needed.

### packet loss in the inbound direction - categraf\[Windows][​](#packet-loss-in-the-inbound-direction---categrafwindows "Direct link to packet loss in the inbound direction - categraf\[Windows]")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
increase(net_drop_in{platform=~"windows"}[1m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-NetAdapterStatistics to confirm inbound discard and error counters are growing;
2. Use Get-NetAdapterAdvancedProperty to check the Receive Buffers setting and raise it if it is small;
3. Use Get-NetAdapter to confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match the peer;
4. Update the NIC driver and ask the network team for the switch port's drop counters.

### packet loss in the outbound direction - categraf \[Windows][​](#packet-loss-in-the-outbound-direction---categraf-windows "Direct link to packet loss in the outbound direction - categraf \[Windows]")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
increase(net_drop_out{platform=~"windows"}[1m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-NetAdapterStatistics to confirm outbound discard and error counters are growing;
2. Use Get-NetAdapterAdvancedProperty to check the Transmit Buffers setting;
3. Check whether the link is saturated (Resource Monitor's Network tab) — if so throttle or add bandwidth;
4. Update the NIC driver and check the peer switch port state.

### Disk larger than 200G is running out of space \[Windows][​](#disk-larger-than-200g-is-running-out-of-space-windows "Direct link to Disk larger than 200G is running out of space \[Windows]")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
disk_free{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 < 20 and disk_total{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 >= 200



disk_free{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 < 10 and disk_total{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 >= 200



disk_free{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 < 2 and disk_total{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 >= 200
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-PSDrive to confirm the drive letter and free space;
2. Use a tool like TreeSize, or Get-ChildItem \<drive>:\ -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 20, to find the largest files and directories;
3. Clean up logs and expired data, and tier cold data off data disks per the business archiving policy;
4. Evaluate whether to expand the disk or move the data directory to another volume.

### Disk smaller than 200G is running out of space \[Windows][​](#disk-smaller-than-200g-is-running-out-of-space-windows "Direct link to Disk smaller than 200G is running out of space \[Windows]")

Info · 1m · Trigger:

```
disk_used_percent{platform=~"windows"} > 90 and disk_total{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 < 200



disk_used_percent{platform=~"windows"} > 95 and disk_total{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 < 200



disk_used_percent{platform=~"windows"} > 99 and disk_total{platform=~"windows"}/1024/1024/1024 < 200
```

Runbook:

1. Run Get-PSDrive to confirm the drive letter and free space;
2. On a system disk the usual consumers are the Windows Update cache (C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download), the hibernation file hiberfil.sys and the page file;
3. Run cleanmgr /sdclean for disk cleanup, and powercfg /h off to disable hibernation and reclaim space if appropriate;
4. Longer term, expand the disk or move large data directories to another volume.

## How to use these rules[​](#how-to-use-these-rules "Direct link to How to use these rules")

* **With Prometheus or vmalert**: download [`windows.yml`](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/windows.yml), add it to `rule_files` (or `-rule` for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a `severity` label (critical / warning / info), and `runbook_url` points back to this page.
* **With Nightingale**: the same rules ship in the [Windows](https://n9e.github.io/integrations/windows.md) integration template. Open the integration center, [import the rules into a business group](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md), and enable them one by one. Nightingale keeps the runbook with each alert and can evaluate the rules against Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and other data sources.

## Sources and license[​](#sources-and-license "Direct link to Sources and license")

The runbook steps and the remaining rules come from Nightingale's integration templates ([Windows](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/tree/main/integrations/Windows), Apache-2.0). Corrections are welcome as pull requests there.

# Connect Datadog Agent

Send Datadog Agent v1 metric series to Nightingale, with the API-version and authentication boundaries made explicit.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

This page lets hosts with Datadog Agent keep their collectors and send **compatible metric series** to Nightingale.

Compatibility

Nightingale v9 registers `/datadog/api/v1/series`. It is not a complete Datadog backend and does not provide a v2 series receiver. The settings below are checked against **Datadog Agent 7.70.0**. Verify that other versions still support v1 before using them.

## Configure[​](#configure "Direct link to Configure")

Edit `/etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml` on Linux:

```
api_key: "replace-with-agent-key"

dd_url: "http://127.0.0.1:17000/datadog"

use_v2_api:

  series: false
```

Replace the URL and key. End `dd_url` at `/datadog`; the Agent appends the API path itself.

Changing `dd_url` alone is insufficient: [Agent 7.70.0 enables v2 series by default](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/blob/7.70.0/pkg/config/setup/config.go). Setting `use_v2_api.series: false` selects the v1 JSON format Nightingale receives.

Enable `[HTTP.APIForAgent].Enable` on the server. If `[HTTP.APIForAgent.BasicAuth]` is configured, Nightingale matches the request's `api_key` against its configured **password values**. A web-login token is not interchangeable with that key.

Without server authentication, Nightingale does not check this value, although the Agent still requires a valid nonempty configuration.

## Restart and verify[​](#verify "Direct link to Restart and verify")

```
sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent

sudo datadog-agent status

sudo journalctl -u datadog-agent -n 100 --no-pager
```

**Expected result**: the Agent starts and sends series to `/datadog/api/v1/series` without authentication or routing errors. In Nightingale's explorer, select the actual destination store and confirm that collected metrics appear and keep receiving new samples.

Nightingale replaces dots and hyphens in metric names with underscores: `system.cpu.user` becomes `system_cpu_user`. Inspect both Agent and Nightingale logs; a running service alone does not prove delivery.

Success on auxiliary compatibility endpoints does not prove that logs, APM, events or all service checks were stored. This guide covers the v1 metric-series path only. If your Agent cannot use it, choose [Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md) or a verified Prometheus collection path.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Data ingestion protocols](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/write-protocols.md)
* [Connected datasource with no data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md)

Implementation: [Pushgw routes](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/blob/01a8e22eb21d81f5cbe5c34e5a1511ff63e39983/pushgw/router/router.go) and [series parsing and authentication](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/blob/01a8e22eb21d81f5cbe5c34e5a1511ff63e39983/pushgw/router/router_datadog.go).

# Connect Telegraf

Send Telegraf metrics to Nightingale with HTTP output and Prometheus Remote Write, then verify the stored data.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, your existing Telegraf will write metrics to the store used by Nightingale. The example targets **Telegraf 1.36.3 and Nightingale v9**. Nightingale writes received metrics to its embedded TSDB or a configured external store.

## Telegraf or Categraf?[​](#telegraf-vs-categraf "Direct link to Telegraf or Categraf?")

Both are MIT-licensed agents written in Go, and Nightingale accepts metrics from either. The differences that matter in practice:

|                               | Telegraf                                                                       | Categraf                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Plugins                       | 300+ inputs, plus processors and many outputs                                  | 90+ inputs covering operating systems, databases, middleware, network gear and Kubernetes                                                    |
| How it sends to Nightingale   | `outputs.http` with `data_format = "prometheusremotewrite"` (configured below) | Prometheus Remote Write by default                                                                                                           |
| Hosts list in Nightingale     | Does not send Nightingale's heartbeat                                          | Sends a [heartbeat](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/targets.md) every 10 s with host metadata that fills **Infrastructure → Hosts** |
| Built-in dashboards and rules | A few templates include Telegraf rule groups (Linux, for example)              | Many [integration templates](https://n9e.github.io/integrations.md) ship a Categraf rule group and Categraf dashboards                       |
| Metric names                  | Telegraf plugin naming, for example `cpu_usage_active`                         | Several host plugins use the same names, so some rules work for both                                                                         |

**Keep Telegraf** if it is already deployed or you rely on plugins Categraf does not have; nothing about alerting in Nightingale requires switching. **Choose Categraf** for new hosts when you want the host list and the bundled dashboards and [alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules.md) to work without rewriting metric names. The two can run side by side during a migration.

## Before you start[​](#before-you-start "Direct link to Before you start")

* Nightingale is running and reachable from the Telegraf host on port 17000.
* `[HTTP.APIForAgent].Enable` is `true`.
* Choose the [embedded TSDB](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/embedded-tsdb.md) or configure an [external writer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/external-tsdb.md).

Keep your existing Telegraf installation. For a new installation, use the [official instructions](https://docs.influxdata.com/telegraf/v1/install/) rather than the old 1.20.4 download script.

## Configure the output[​](#configure-output "Direct link to Configure the output")

Merge this into `telegraf.conf` and replace the URL. `outputs.http` is the output plugin; `prometheusremotewrite` is its serialization format.

```
[agent]

interval = "15s"

flush_interval = "15s"



[[outputs.http]]

url = "http://127.0.0.1:17000/prometheus/v1/write"

method = "POST"

data_format = "prometheusremotewrite"

[outputs.http.headers]

Content-Type = "application/x-protobuf"

Content-Encoding = "snappy"

X-Prometheus-Remote-Write-Version = "0.1.0"



[[inputs.cpu]]

percpu = false

totalcpu = true

collect_cpu_time = false

report_active = true



[[inputs.mem]]
```

If Nightingale configures `[HTTP.APIForAgent.BasicAuth]`, add matching `username` and `password` inside `[[outputs.http]]`, **before** its headers table. Leave them out when authentication is disabled.

Review any default InfluxDB output already enabled in the file; an unrelated failing output can obscure the result. OpenTSDB remains a compatibility protocol, but its metric names differ. Check existing dashboards when switching formats.

## Verify collection and delivery[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify collection and delivery")

```
telegraf --config /etc/telegraf/telegraf.conf --test

telegraf --config /etc/telegraf/telegraf.conf --once
```

**Expected result**: `--test` shows CPU and memory samples; `--once` performs collection and delivery without authentication, routing or connection errors. `--test` alone does not test delivery.

In Nightingale's metrics explorer, select the destination store and query `cpu_usage_active`. You should see series with Telegraf tags. Then restart the existing service. An installation with the official systemd unit can use `sudo systemctl restart telegraf`.

Telegraf does not send Categraf heartbeat metadata. Receiving metrics does not grant the same target-registration or self-healing capabilities. See the [1.36.3 format documentation](https://github.com/influxdata/telegraf/blob/v1.36.3/plugins/serializers/prometheusremotewrite/README.md) for Histogram and Summary batching limitations.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Data ingestion protocols](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/write-protocols.md)
* [Create your first alert](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/first-rule.md)

# A2A endpoint

The A2A endpoint exposes Nightingale as an agent that other agent platforms can discover and call; the agent card declares the address and supported methods.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: a Nightingale agent that a third-party agent platform can discover and call on its own, plus one verified `message:send` request.

## Not the same thing as MCP[​](#not-the-same-thing-as-mcp "Direct link to Not the same thing as MCP")

|                          | `/mcp`                                                  | `/a2a`                                       |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| What the caller gets     | 74 fine-grained tools to orchestrate themselves         | One agent that talks                         |
| Interaction              | JSON-RPC tool calls                                     | Natural language in, natural language out    |
| Needs an LLM configured? | **No** — tools hit Nightingale's API directly           | **Yes** — it drives the built-in assistant   |
| Suits                    | Clients that bring their own model: Claude Code, Cursor | Somebody else's agent orchestration platform |

Both endpoints are on by default and share one auth path. **A question the assistant cannot answer in the UI, it cannot answer over A2A either** — get a conversation working first, see [Nightingale AI overview](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/nightingale-ai.md).

## The agent card is the only address a third party needs[​](#the-agent-card-is-the-only-address-a-third-party-needs "Direct link to The agent card is the only address a third party needs")

```
curl -s https://n9e.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json
```

This address needs **no authentication** (the spec requires it to be discoverable). `/.well-known/agent.json` is an alias for older clients.

What the card declares:

| Field                                      | Value                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`                                     | `Nightingale Agent`                                                                    |
| `supportedInterfaces`                      | One HTTP+JSON interface at `<BaseURL>/a2a`                                             |
| `capabilities.streaming`                   | `true`                                                                                 |
| `defaultInputModes` / `defaultOutputModes` | Both `text`                                                                            |
| `securitySchemes`                          | `x-user-token` (apiKey, in a header); an extra `oidc` scheme appears when RSAuth is on |
| `skills`                                   | Every built-in skill, with its name, description and example prompts                   |

`skills` is generated from the built-in skills' frontmatter, so the caller sees what Nightingale is actually good at — diagnosing why a rule did not fire, analyzing a dashboard, generating PromQL — rather than one generic blurb.

An empty `BaseURL` is inferred from request headers. **Set it explicitly behind a reverse proxy**, or the third party may end up with an internal address:

```
[HTTP.A2A]

BaseURL = "https://n9e.example.com"
```

## Send a message[​](#send-a-message "Direct link to Send a message")

The REST binding path is `/a2a/message:send` (**no** `/v1` prefix). `messageId`, `role` and `parts` are all required, and the enum value for `role` is `ROLE_USER`:

```
curl -s -X POST https://n9e.example.com/a2a/message:send \

  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \

  -H 'X-User-Token: YOUR_TOKEN' \

  -d '{

    "message": {

      "messageId": "req-0001",

      "role": "ROLE_USER",

      "parts": [{ "text": "Which alerts are firing right now?" }]

    },

    "metadata": { "lang": "en_US" }

  }'
```

Expected result: a `task` object carrying `id`, `contextId`, `status.state`, and `n9e.chat_id` / `n9e.seq_id` under `metadata`. A `status.state` of `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` means the turn finished; the answer is in `artifacts`. This step can take tens of seconds while the model thinks and calls tools — that is normal.

For multi-turn, put `"contextId": "<the contextId you got back>"` inside `message`. `contextId` maps one-to-one onto Nightingale's `chat_id`, which means an A2A conversation is the same conversation you see in the Nightingale AI conversation list.

## Which methods are supported[​](#which-methods-are-supported "Direct link to Which methods are supported")

| Method                      | Path                             |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Send a message (unary)      | `POST /a2a/message:send`         |
| Send a message (SSE stream) | `POST /a2a/message:stream`       |
| Get a task                  | `GET /a2a/tasks/{id}`            |
| Cancel a task               | `POST /a2a/tasks/{id}:cancel`    |
| Resubscribe                 | `POST /a2a/tasks/{id}:subscribe` |

`tasks/list` is **deliberately not implemented** and returns `UnsupportedOperation` per the spec — enumerating tasks across users is meaningless for a built-in assistant and would leak other people's activity.

A bare GET on `/a2a` returns a short JSON hint listing the paths above. That exists so a client still using the legacy JSON-RPC style (`tasks/send`) gets a sentence it can read, rather than being redirected into the frontend SPA.

Task state lives in Redis with a 24-hour TTL, shared across instances. After it expires `tasks/get` returns task-not-found, but the conversation itself is still in the database.

## Reverse proxy and timeouts[​](#reverse-proxy-and-timeouts "Direct link to Reverse proxy and timeouts")

A2A sits at the root path and holds long connections:

```
location /.well-known/ {

    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:17000;

}



location /a2a/ {

    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:17000;

    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;



    proxy_buffering off;        # without this, streaming answers never emit anything

    proxy_read_timeout 3600s;   # the default 60s cuts answers in half

    proxy_send_timeout 3600s;

}
```

The server sends an empty "working" status heartbeat every 30 seconds precisely to survive gateway idle timeouts — but the gateway's own read timeout still has to be raised.

## The command-line client[​](#the-command-line-client "Direct link to The command-line client")

The repository ships a test client built on the official SDK:

```
go run ./cmd/a2a-cli --server http://127.0.0.1:17000 --token YOUR_TOKEN \

    --message "Show the alert events currently firing"



# Continue the same conversation

go run ./cmd/a2a-cli --server http://127.0.0.1:17000 --token YOUR_TOKEN \

    --context-id CHAT_ID --message "Analyze the first one in more detail"
```

It streams by default; `--get` calls `tasks/get` afterwards to prove the task really was stored.

## Turning it off[​](#turning-it-off "Direct link to Turning it off")

```
[HTTP.A2A]

Disable = true   # closes /a2a, /mcp and the agent card together
```

To close MCP only and keep A2A, use `DisableMCP = true`.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Get the assistant answering first: [Nightingale AI overview](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/nightingale-ai.md)
* Let callers use their own accounts: [OAuth 2.1 and external identity providers](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/oauth.md)
* The fine-grained-tools path: [Enable the MCP endpoint](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/mcp-endpoint.md)
