# ElasticSearch / OpenSearch

Connect an ES or OpenSearch cluster, choose index patterns and the timestamp field, and run a log query.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: a connected ES cluster, one reusable index pattern, and a query that returns real log lines in the Log explorer.

One difference up front, because it changes how you will use this: **in the open-source edition ElasticSearch works in the Log explorer and on dashboards, while OpenSearch is only usable for alert rules.** Both register as data sources and both drive log alert rules, but the OpenSearch explorer and dashboards are not available. If you want to search logs, use the ElasticSearch type.

## Before you start[​](#before-you-start "Direct link to Before you start")

* The HTTP endpoint of your cluster, e.g. `http://10.0.0.21:9200`;
* Network access to it from the machine running Nightingale Center;
* Credentials — ES 8.x enables X-Pack security by default;
* A date-typed field in the index (usually `@timestamp`); Nightingale filters the time range on it.

## 1. Register the cluster[​](#1-register-the-cluster "Direct link to 1. Register the cluster")

**Integrations → Data sources → Add → Elasticsearch**.

The **HTTP** section is a list you can extend: click the `+` next to the heading to add more node addresses, and Nightingale rotates between them.

| Field                         | Notes                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name                          | Required; rules and queries pick the source by this name                                                                      |
| HTTP                          | Node address in the form `http://localhost:9200`. At least one                                                                |
| Timeout(ms)                   | Defaults to 10000                                                                                                             |
| User / Password               | Fill these if auth is on. ES 8.x requires them by default                                                                     |
| Version                       | **Leave it blank** — Nightingale detects it on save. To pin one, use `x.y.z`, e.g. `7.10.2`                                   |
| Max concurrent shard requests | Defaults to 5. Lower it on a cluster with very many shards so one query cannot saturate ES                                    |
| Min time interval (s)         | Defaults to 10. The lower bound for automatic time bucketing; set it to your write frequency — 60 if data lands once a minute |

The **Enable write** switch is unused in the open-source edition; leave it off.

![The Elasticsearch data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-elasticsearch.webp)![The Elasticsearch data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-elasticsearch.dark.webp)

Click **Save & test**. For ES, that step fetches the version number: on success the version is stored with the config, and on failure the record is **still saved** with the reason shown in the result panel — so when you see "Saved, connectivity not verified", read the reason before moving on.

## 2. Define an index pattern[​](#2-define-an-index-pattern "Direct link to 2. Define an index pattern")

There are two ways to say which data a query covers:

* **Indices** — type an index name directly; wildcards work, e.g. `log-*`. Good for a one-off look;
* **Index patterns** — a stored definition that binds an index name to its time field, which queries and alert rules then select by name.

Index patterns are managed at **`/log/index-patterns`** (the gear icon next to the index-pattern box in the ES query editor links there). Click **Create index pattern**; each one holds:

| Field       | What to put in it                         |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Data source | Which ES data source it belongs to        |
| Name        | Index name or wildcard, e.g. `log-prod-*` |
| Time field  | The date field, such as `@timestamp`      |

Those three plus an operations column are exactly what the list shows. An index pattern referenced by an alert rule cannot be deleted; the attempt is refused.

**Why bother** — the time field is answered once. From then on no query and no rule has to answer "which field is the timestamp" again.

## 3. Run a log query[​](#3-run-a-log-query "Direct link to 3. Run a log query")

**Explorer → Logs**, then select the source you just created. On the left, in order:

1. **Mode**: `Indices` or `Index patterns`;
2. **Index** / **Index pattern**;
3. **Date field** (only needed separately in Indices mode);
4. **Syntax**: KQL or Lucene;
5. **Query**, e.g. `status:500 AND method:GET`.

Log lines appearing means the path works. If nothing comes back, check the time range first — the picker in the top right defaults to a recent window, and older logs need it widened.

## 4. Alert on the result[​](#4-alert-on-the-result "Direct link to 4. Alert on the result")

A log rule differs from a metric rule only in what it queries: a metric rule writes PromQL, a log rule runs a query that produces a number, and the threshold expression judges that number.

Under **Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules → Add**, pick Elasticsearch (or OpenSearch) as the data source type. Besides index, time field and query, there are two extra groups:

* **Value field** — which number takes part in the judgement. Beyond count, sum, avg, min and max, percentile functions such as p90 / p95 / p99 are available;
* **Group By** — split by a field. Each group becomes its own series, judged independently, and produces its own event carrying the group value as a label.

Three shapes you can copy directly:

* **More than two 4xx lines in ten minutes, per host**: filter to 4xx in the query, value field count, group by `host.hostname`, threshold `> 2`;
* **p95 request latency above 1700 ms**: value field p95 over `request_time`, group by `remote_addr`;
* **More than ten slow requests**: query `request_time > 1900`, value field count, group by `request_uri`.

Click **Preview** before setting the threshold, to confirm the query really returns the number you expect.

## What is different for OpenSearch[​](#what-is-different-for-opensearch "Direct link to What is different for OpenSearch")

OpenSearch is a fork of ES 7.10 and the form is nearly identical (the timeout defaults to 100000 rather than 10000). In the open-source edition, though:

* you **can** register the data source and **can** write log alert rules against it;
* you **cannot** search it in the Log explorer or chart it on a dashboard — neither supports it, and OpenSearch sources do not appear in those data source pickers.

So if your workflow is "look at the logs, then decide what to alert on", register the cluster under the ElasticSearch type.

## When it doesn't work[​](#when-it-doesnt-work "Direct link to When it doesn't work")

**The version fetch fails on save.** From the Nightingale Center host, run `curl http://<es>:9200/_cluster/health`. No 200 means network or auth. ES 8.x ships a self-signed certificate, so turn on **Skip SSL verify**.

**Indices are listed but no data comes back.** Check three things in order: the date field is the right one, the wildcard actually matches a real index, and the time range genuinely contains data.

**Several clusters.** One data source per cluster. To span indices within one cluster, use a wildcard (`log-prod-*`).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Write log rules properly: [Log alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/log-rules.md)
* Search technique and index patterns in depth: [Log explorer and index patterns](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/log-explorer.md)
* A different log store: [Loki / VictoriaLogs](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/loki-victorialogs.md)

# Auto-registered Embedded TSDB datasource

A fresh install auto-registers a Prometheus-type source named embedded-tsdb; Pushgw writes into it by default, and it is queried like any external Prometheus source.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Open **Integrations → Data sources** on a fresh install and there is already a Prometheus-type source named `embedded-tsdb`, carrying a default badge. This page explains who created it, what writes into it, and how it actually differs from an external Prometheus source you add yourself.

![The data source list, with embedded-tsdb at the top](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/datasource-list.webp)![The data source list, with embedded-tsdb at the top](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/datasource-list.dark.webp)

## Who creates it[​](#who-creates-it "Direct link to Who creates it")

At startup, as long as `[EmbeddedTSDB] Enable = true` (the default), the Center process inserts one row into the data source table:

| Field                     | Value                               |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Name                      | `embedded-tsdb`                     |
| Type                      | Prometheus                          |
| URL                       | `http://127.0.0.1:17000/prometheus` |
| Time series database type | Prometheus                          |
| Created by                | `system`                            |
| Default data source       | yes                                 |

The action is idempotent: on every restart, if the URL, the auth or the time series database type have drifted from the current config, they are written back. **Editing this record's URL therefore achieves nothing** — the next restart undoes it. It recognises itself through an internal identifier (`n9e-embedded-tsdb`), so renaming it is safe.

The default badge is set by the server (`is_default`). The open-source form has no checkbox for it; you neither need to nor can toggle it by hand.

## What writes into it[​](#what-writes-into-it "Direct link to What writes into it")

Categraf pushes metrics to Nightingale's `/prometheus/v1/write`, and the forwarding layer then writes those samples to this instance's own `/prometheus/api/v1/write` as if it were any other remote write backend. In other words, **the embedded store is fed through the `Pushgw.Writers` path** — the writer entry is just injected at startup, so you never see it in the config file.

The consequence is that every forwarding behaviour an external store gets, the embedded one gets too: server-side timestamps, target label rewriting (`Pushgw.LabelRewrite`), write statistics.

## How it differs from an external Prometheus source[​](#how-it-differs-from-an-external-prometheus-source "Direct link to How it differs from an external Prometheus source")

At the query interface, it doesn't. Nightingale serves a Prometheus-compatible HTTP API in front of it — `/api/v1/query`, `/api/v1/query_range`, `/api/v1/series`, `/api/v1/labels` — so rules, dashboards and the Metrics explorer behave identically.

Three things are genuinely different:

1. **It only accepts local requests by default.** With no `BasicAuthUser` configured, `/prometheus/api/v1/*` admits requests from this machine only, which is why the auto-registered URL is `127.0.0.1`. To let `n9e-edge`, Grafana or an agent talk to it directly, configure basic auth — the auto-registered URL then switches to the detected host IP. `DatasourceUrl` lets you pin a VIP or domain instead, and setting it also lifts the local-only restriction;
2. **The data lives on the local disk of one Center process.** With several replicas each holds a fragment, so high availability means turning it off;
3. **Administrative endpoints such as delete-series are not registered at all** by default. Set `EnableAdminAPI = true` to get them, and configure basic auth first.

## When it is not created[​](#when-it-is-not-created "Direct link to When it is not created")

If Center finds an **enabled Prometheus-type data source already exists** at startup, it skips the auto-registration and says so in the log. That keeps a deployment that already points at an external store from sprouting an extra data source.

Note that samples are **still written to the local store** in that case — there is simply nothing pointing at it. To query them, create a Prometheus data source aimed at `http://127.0.0.1:17000/prometheus`; if you don't want the local store at all, set `[EmbeddedTSDB] Enable = false`.

## Retention and capacity[​](#retention-and-capacity "Direct link to Retention and capacity")

```
[EmbeddedTSDB]

Enable = true

Dir = "data/tsdb"

RetentionDuration = "15d"

MaxBytes = "10GiB"

OutOfOrderTimeWindow = "10m"

QueryTimeout = "1m"

QueryMaxSamples = 50000000
```

Exceeding `MaxBytes` deletes the oldest blocks first. `OutOfOrderTimeWindow` is the tolerance for out-of-order samples — it absorbs agent clock skew and resends.

**Only the Center process reads this section.** `n9e-edge`, `n9e-alert` and `n9e-pushgw` read the same `etc` directory, ignore it, and print a warning at startup if it is enabled.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Where it stops being enough: [Embedded TSDB single-Center limits](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/embedded-tsdb-limits.md)
* Moving to an external store: [External TSDB and dual-write migration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/external-tsdb.md)
* Nothing in it: [No data in the embedded TSDB](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/embedded-tsdb-data.md)
* How the two kinds of storage divide up: [Embedded TSDB and external storage](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/storage.md)

# Install collector configuration

Copy a template's collector config into Categraf and start collecting the component's metrics.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: the target host has a new `conf/input.<plugin>/<plugin>.toml`, Categraf is collecting that component's metrics, and you have confirmed they reached Nightingale.

This assumes Categraf is **already installed** on the host — if not, start at [Install and register](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md). Nightingale collects nothing itself; it only tells you what to put into Categraf.

## Two paths[​](#two-paths "Direct link to Two paths")

The open-source edition offers two; pick one:

|                          | Collection wizard                              | Instructions in the template center                             |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Entry point              | **Infrastructure → Hosts → Set up collection** | **Integrations → Components → pick a component → Instructions** |
| Coverage                 | 55 common components                           | 83<!-- --> components                                           |
| How it lands on the host | Generates a command you run there              | You create the file, paste, restart                             |
| Best for                 | Common components, repeated across many hosts  | Components the wizard doesn't cover, or heavy customisation     |

## Path 1: the collection wizard[​](#path-1-the-collection-wizard "Direct link to Path 1: the collection wizard")

**Infrastructure → Hosts**, then **Set up collection** at the top right. Four steps:

**1. Pick component.** Filter by category (All / Databases / Middleware / Web services / Network probes / Host & processes / Other) or just search. Taking MySQL as the example, click its card.

**2. Configure.** Two modes:

* **Form mode**: field by field. MySQL asks for **Address** (required), username, password, whether to collect extra status metrics, and an **Instance label** — that last one matters: it is attached to every metric of this instance as the `instance` label, the built-in dashboards depend on it, and it must be **globally unique**;
* **Edit toml**: edit the generated config directly. Switching back to form mode discards those manual edits.

Leave **Collect interval (seconds)** empty to use the global default of 15s. For several instances of the same component (three MySQL servers, say), click **Add instance** rather than writing three configs.

The **Generated config preview** on the right always shows exactly what will be written.

**3. Run command.** The wizard hands you a command of this shape:

```
curl -sSfL 'http://<nightingale>/api/n9e/agents/categraf/collect.sh' \

  | sudo bash -s -- --input 'mysql' --conf-b64 '<base64-encoded config>'
```

**Run it on the target host as root.** The same command can be run on any number of hosts.

If piping straight into bash makes you uncomfortable, the wizard also offers the stepwise version: `curl -o collect-config.sh`, read it with `less`, then `sudo bash collect-config.sh --input ... --conf-b64 ...`.

The command embeds the whole config base64-encoded. **It may contain passwords — do not share it over untrusted channels.**

**4. Verify data.** The wizard watches for a sentinel metric, polling every 5 seconds; it normally appears within a minute of the command succeeding. See [Verify incoming data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md).

## Path 2: the Instructions tab in the template center[​](#path-2-the-instructions-tab-in-the-template-center "Direct link to Path 2: the Instructions tab in the template center")

**Integrations → Components**, click a component card, and the first tab is **Instructions**.

It is a Markdown document explaining how that component is collected: which Categraf file to edit, what each setting means, what prerequisites exist. For MySQL it tells you to write `conf/input.mysql/mysql.toml` and gives you a config you can copy wholesale:

```
[[instances]]

address = "127.0.0.1:3306"

username = "root"

password = "1234"



# turn on for the full set of global status metrics

extra_status_metrics = true

# replication state matters, so it is collected by default

gather_slave_status = true



# a globally unique identifier attached to every metric of this instance

labels = { instance="n9e-10.2.3.4:3306" }
```

Three steps to apply it:

1. Create `conf/input.mysql/mysql.toml` under the Categraf directory, paste the config, and change the address and credentials to yours;
2. Test-run it once to check both the config and the connection:
   <!-- -->
   ```
   ./categraf --test --inputs mysql
   ```
3. Restart Categraf to pick it up.

The Instructions tab is **documentation for a human, not a config pushed to the agent** — the open-source edition does not deliver it to your hosts, so that last mile is yours (or the wizard's).

The **Edit** button on that tab has no effect on the <!-- -->83<!-- --> bundled components: their content comes from the `integrations` directory Nightingale ships with, and edits are not persisted.

## What the command does[​](#what-the-command-does "Direct link to What the command does")

The wizard's command is not a black box. It does three things:

1. Writes `conf/input.<plugin>/<plugin>.toml`, **backing up any existing file**;
2. Test-runs the plugin with `categraf --test`, and stops there if it fails;
3. Restarts Categraf once the test passes.

So a broken config stops at step 2 rather than leaving you with an agent that won't start.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Install this component's dashboards and rules too: [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)
* Confirm the metrics really arrived: [Verify incoming data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md)
* Writing plugin configs by hand: [Input plugins](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/plugins.md)
* Nothing showed up: [Categraf troubleshooting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/troubleshooting.md)

# Import dashboards and rules

Import the bundled dashboards and alert rules into a business group, and adjust thresholds before enabling.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: a business group that now has this component's dashboards, plus a batch of alert rules sitting **disabled**, waiting for you to adjust thresholds and enable them one by one.

Nightingale ships templates for <!-- -->83<!-- --> components. Once metrics are arriving there is no need to draw panels or write rules from scratch — import the templates into a business group and tune them.

## What a component ships with[​](#what-a-component-ships-with "Direct link to What a component ships with")

**Integrations → Components**, click any component card, and the drawer has four tabs:

| Tab          | Contents                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Instructions | How this component is collected — see [Install collector configuration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/collector-config.md) |
| Metrics      | Which metrics it produces and what each one means                                                                                         |
| Dashboards   | Ready-made dashboard templates                                                                                                            |
| Alert rules  | Ready-made alert rule templates                                                                                                           |

Not every component has all four. Of the <!-- -->83<!-- -->, <!-- -->63<!-- --> ship alert rules, <!-- -->51<!-- --> ship dashboards, and <!-- -->21<!-- --> ship metric descriptions.

## Importing dashboards[​](#importing-dashboards "Direct link to Importing dashboards")

On the component drawer's **Dashboards** tab the columns are Name / Tags / Note / Updated by / Operations. Bundled entries show **System** in the Updated by column.

Tick the rows you want and click **Import to business group**. The dialog has two fields:

| Field          | Notes                                                                               |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Business group | Where it lands. It **must be a leaf group**; intermediate levels are not selectable |
| Content        | Pre-filled with the JSON of the templates you ticked; normally leave it alone       |

Click **Clone** to finish. The dashboards then appear under **Explorer → Dashboards** with that business group selected.

The import is a **one-time copy**: when Nightingale is upgraded and a template changes, dashboards you already imported do not follow. Re-import to pick up the new version.

**Panel data sources are not chosen at import time**, they are chosen when the dashboard is opened — so one imported copy can be pointed at different sources.

## Importing alert rules[​](#importing-alert-rules "Direct link to Importing alert rules")

On the **Alert rules** tab, tick the rules and click **Import to business group**. This dialog has more fields than the dashboard one:

| Field             | Notes                                                                                          |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Business group    | As above, must be a leaf group                                                                 |
| Enabled           | **Off by default.** Leave it off until the thresholds are right                                |
| Source type       | Read-only, derived from the templates themselves. Bundled rules are almost always `prometheus` |
| Data source       | Which source(s) these rules run against. A **Data source preview** sits next to it             |
| Notification rule | Where events go; you can pick an existing one or create one inline                             |
| Content           | The rules' JSON, pre-filled                                                                    |

Click **Import** to finish.

One import covers **one data source type**. Mixing types produces *"Cannot import alert rules of different data source types"* and disables the submit button — import them in two passes.

## The other direction: from the dashboard and rule lists[​](#the-other-direction-from-the-dashboard-and-rule-lists "Direct link to The other direction: from the dashboard and rule lists")

If you would rather not start in the template center, the reverse path works too:

* **Explorer → Dashboards → pick a business group → Import**, and the first tab is **Import built-in dashboard**: choose a **Component**, then tick rows in the **Templates** table. That table has an extra **Variable** column so you can set dashboard variables before importing;
* **Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules → pick a business group → Import**, first tab **Import built-in alert rules**, which adds a **Category** dropdown (a component often ships two rule sets — `xxx_by_categraf` and `xxx_by_exporter` — split by how the data was collected).

Both entry points read the same templates through the same API; use whichever page you are already on.

Those **Import** buttons only appear once a **leaf business group** is selected.

## A third entry point: one-click import after saving a data source[​](#a-third-entry-point-one-click-import-after-saving-a-data-source "Direct link to A third entry point: one-click import after saving a data source")

When a Prometheus-type data source is saved successfully, the result panel runs a template match: it merges the sentinel metrics of the bundled templates into a single query against your source, and **whichever sentinels have recent samples tell it which components' data is already there**. Those components are then listed as cards:

> Found data from 3 components in this datasource. Click a card to import templates

Clicking a card opens the import dialog with dashboards and alert rules on separate tabs, each showing its count. This path works for **Prometheus-family sources only**, and it judges "has recent data", not "has ever had data".

## Adjust thresholds before enabling[​](#adjust-thresholds-before-enabling "Direct link to Adjust thresholds before enabling")

The thresholds in bundled rules are **generic defaults**, not calibrated for your environment. After importing, go through at least these three:

1. **The threshold.** "CPU above 90%" is normal on a load generator and an incident on a database primary;
2. **The for-duration.** A rule that fires on every blip gets ignored fast; look at how much the metric normally moves first;
3. **Notification rule and severity.** S1 should wake someone up; S3 should not.

Then turn **Enabled** on. Enabling all of them at once is the classic way to lose the team's trust — switch on the five that matter, watch for a week, then do the next batch.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Confirm the data is really there before trusting the rules: [Verify incoming data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md)
* Tuning rules: [Alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/overview.md)
* Editing dashboards: [Build a dashboard](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/dashboards.md)
* Nothing collecting yet: [Install collector configuration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/collector-config.md)

# Verify incoming data

A quiet imported rule may just mean no data arrived; query the metric name the template lists in the Metrics explorer to confirm the component's metrics are in.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

An imported alert rule that stays quiet means one of two things: everything is fine, or **the data never arrived**. Those look identical from the outside, so spend two minutes confirming the metrics are really there before you trust the rules.

This page gives three checkpoints, from the host outwards, and what you should see at each one.

## 1. Which metric to look for[​](#1-which-metric-to-look-for "Direct link to 1. Which metric to look for")

Start by knowing what to search for. A component drawer's **Metrics** tab lists exactly what that component produces: **Integrations → Components → open a component → Metrics**, with metric name, unit and PromQL in the table.

The same data is browsable across components under **Explorer → Metrics → Built-in metrics**, where the columns are Component type / Category / Name / Unit / PromQL / Operations.

Only <!-- -->21<!-- --> of the <!-- -->83<!-- --> components ship metric descriptions. Without one, guess from the plugin name: Categraf plugins almost always prefix their metrics with the plugin name — `mysql` produces `mysql_*`, `redis` produces `redis_*`, `nginx` produces `nginx_*`.

## 2. On the host: is the plugin collecting[​](#2-on-the-host-is-the-plugin-collecting "Direct link to 2. On the host: is the plugin collecting")

The checkpoint closest to the source, on the machine running Categraf:

```
cd /path/to/categraf

./categraf --configs /path/to/categraf/conf --test --inputs mysql
```

`--test` prints collected metrics to stdout and **sends nothing to Nightingale**. The output looks like this:

```
1788432166 18:42:46 mysql_global_status_threads_connected agent_hostname=n9e-web-01 instance=n9e-10.2.3.4:3306 5
```

Metric lines mean the plugin config is right. **Two caveats**: the process does not exit on its own, so Ctrl-C once you have seen output; and `--test` **does not disable the heartbeat** — it still reports to Nightingale, so don't run it casually in production.

Not a single line? See [Troubleshooting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/troubleshooting.md).

## 3. In Nightingale: did the metrics arrive[​](#3-in-nightingale-did-the-metrics-arrive "Direct link to 3. In Nightingale: did the metrics arrive")

**Explorer → Metrics**, pick the source that holds host metrics (on a default install that is `embedded-tsdb`), and query one of the names you just saw:

```
mysql_global_status_threads_connected
```

**What you should see**: one or more lines, each carrying an `agent_hostname` label, with values in the same range you saw on the host.

If nothing comes back, widen the net to tell "this metric is missing" from "this host is missing":

```
# no metrics from this component at all?

{__name__=~"mysql_.*"}



# is this host reporting anything?

{agent_hostname="n9e-web-01"}
```

If the second one is empty too, the problem is not the plugin but the write path — back to [Categraf troubleshooting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/troubleshooting.md).

## 4. The wizard's automatic check[​](#4-the-wizards-automatic-check "Direct link to 4. The wizard's automatic check")

If you came through **Infrastructure → Hosts → Set up collection**, its fourth step, **Verify data**, does all of the above for you.

It polls a sentinel metric every 5 seconds; it usually appears within a minute of the command succeeding. Two optional inputs:

* **Data source**: defaults to the Prometheus source the server matched from the write config. If nothing shows up there, switch to the one that actually stores your host metrics;
* **Target hosts** (optional): pick the hosts you ran the command on to confirm each individually; leave it empty to watch for any newly reporting host.

What the outcomes mean:

| Message                                           | Meaning                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Waiting for xxx metrics, checking every 5 seconds | Still waiting; normal                                                                                                           |
| N new host(s) reporting xxx metrics               | Done                                                                                                                            |
| N host(s) already reporting these metrics         | Those were reporting before the check started                                                                                   |
| The check fell back to the xxx prefix             | The exact sentinel kept returning nothing, so it matched on the prefix; existing reporters cannot be distinguished in this mode |
| This component has no fixed metric names          | For `exec`, `mtail` and friends the names come from your own script, so nothing can be checked automatically                    |
| Timed out                                         | See the next section                                                                                                            |

**If you only changed the config on an existing host, nothing counts as "new" here** — continuously reported metrics mean it took effect.

## 5. Still nothing[​](#5-still-nothing "Direct link to 5. Still nothing")

Work through the three leads the timeout message gives, in order:

1. **Did the command actually succeed?** The wizard's command test-runs the plugin with `categraf --test` first and stops there if it fails;
2. **Is categraf still running on the host?**
   ```
   journalctl -u categraf -n 50
   ```
3. **Search differently**: look for the `mysql_` prefix in the Metrics explorer, in case the metric name is not what you assumed.

One level up, confirm the host has a heartbeat at all: **Infrastructure → Hosts** shows Alive / Dead in the left-hand overview, and the **Updated at** column carries the last heartbeat. No heartbeat means Categraf is not running, or cannot reach Nightingale.

One more case worth calling out on its own: **the wrong data source**. Metrics went into A and you are querying B. Host metrics land in the embedded store (`embedded-tsdb`) by default; if you configured `Pushgw.Writers` to forward to an external store, query that source instead.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Data is in, now tune the thresholds: [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)
* Data is not in: [Categraf troubleshooting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/troubleshooting.md)
* The data source itself is the problem: [Why does a data source connect but return no data?](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md)

# Loki / VictoriaLogs

Register a log store, write a LogQL or LogsQL query, and alert on counts or matches.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: a connected Loki or VictoriaLogs, a query that returns log lines in the Log explorer, and a rule that fires when a keyword appears more than N times in five minutes.

Both play the same role in Nightingale — a log store you search under **Explorer → Logs** and write log alert rules against. Only the query language and the URL shape differ.

One shared limitation up front: **neither type can back a dashboard panel.** They do not appear in the dashboard data source picker. To chart something, turn the count into a metric, or use a different store.

## Loki: the URL must end in `/loki`[​](#loki-the-url-must-end-in-loki "Direct link to loki-the-url-must-end-in-loki")

**Integrations → Data sources → Add → Loki**.

| Field               | What to put in it                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name                | Required                                                                                                                          |
| URL                 | **Must carry the `/loki` suffix**, e.g. `http://loki:3100/loki`. The form's placeholder is literally `http://localhost:3100/loki` |
| Timeout(ms)         | Defaults to 10000                                                                                                                 |
| User / Password     | Fill these when an auth gateway sits in front of Loki                                                                             |
| Custom HTTP headers | In multi-tenant mode, add `X-Scope-OrgID` here with the tenant ID as its value                                                    |

![The Loki data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-loki.webp)![The Loki data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-loki.dark.webp)

A URL missing `/loki` is the single most common mistake. **Save & test** requests `<URL>/api/v1/labels`; on a 404 with no `/loki` in the URL, Nightingale hands you the corrected address directly: `/loki suffix is miss, please add /loki to the url: ...`.

To find out whether you need a tenant ID, query Loki once without the header. `no org id` back means multi-tenancy is on and `X-Scope-OrgID` is required.

## VictoriaLogs: address and row cap[​](#victorialogs-address-and-row-cap "Direct link to VictoriaLogs: address and row cap")

**Integrations → Data sources → Add → VictoriaLogs**.

| Field                                  | What to put in it                                                                |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name                                   | Required                                                                         |
| HTTP                                   | The service address, `http://localhost:9428/`. **No** extra path suffix          |
| Timeout(ms)                            | Defaults to 10000                                                                |
| Maximum number of returned log entries | Defaults to 500. The per-query row cap; raise it too far and the browser suffers |
| User / Password                        | Fill these if auth is enabled                                                    |
| Custom HTTP headers                    | For a gateway that needs extra headers                                           |

![The VictoriaLogs data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-victorialogs.webp)![The VictoriaLogs data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-victorialogs.dark.webp)

## Querying: LogQL and LogsQL[​](#querying-logql-and-logsql "Direct link to Querying: LogQL and LogsQL")

**Explorer → Logs**, pick the source. The two query editors differ.

**Loki speaks LogQL.** You can type the query directly or fill in the builder field by field — labels, line filter, parser, parsed-field filter, limit, range aggregation. Typed by hand:

```
# every 401 line from one container

{container="checkout"} | json | status="401"



# how many 401s in the last five minutes

count_over_time({container="checkout"} |= "401" [5m])
```

The LogQL selector `{label="value"}` is mandatory — an empty query is rejected. The line filter has four operators: `|=` contains, `!=` does not contain, `|~` regex match, `!~` regex non-match. Use `| json`, `| logfmt` or `| pattern` to parse fields out of the line before aggregating.

**VictoriaLogs speaks LogsQL.** Write the query in the box, cap the returned rows on the right, and read the result as a group, a table or JSON. To render it as a time series you also pick a **value field** (the numeric columns to plot, several allowed) and a **label field** (what separates one line from another).

```
_stream:{app="checkout"} AND status:401
```

If nothing comes back, check the time range first, then check whether the writer side (Promtail, Vector, vlogscli) is actually shipping.

## Alerting on counts and matches[​](#alerting-on-counts-and-matches "Direct link to Alerting on counts and matches")

**Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules → Add**, data source type Loki or VictoriaLogs.

A log rule does not judge log lines directly — it judges **a number the query produced**. The common shape is one sentence: *more than N lines matched this condition in the last N minutes*.

In Loki you put the aggregation in the query itself:

```
count_over_time({container="checkout"} |= "ERROR" [5m])
```

with the threshold `$A > 0` — "alert if ERROR appeared at all in the last five minutes". Swap the keyword for a business error code or a stack-trace fingerprint and the rule shape carries over unchanged.

In VictoriaLogs you run the query, pick the numeric column with the value field, and write the threshold against it.

Hit **Preview** before you set the threshold, to confirm the query returns the number you expect.

## When it doesn't work[​](#when-it-doesnt-work "Direct link to When it doesn't work")

**A 404 on save.** The Loki URL is missing `/loki`.

**It saved but returns no logs.** In this order:

1. Multi-tenant Loki without `X-Scope-OrgID`;
2. LogQL with no label selector — `{}` must contain at least one matcher;
3. Too narrow a time range;
4. Nothing is being written at all. Confirm with `logcli` (Loki) or by curling the VictoriaLogs query endpoint directly.

**The rule never fires.** Run the same query in the Log explorer first and confirm it returns a non-zero result; then check that the data source is associated with an alerting engine cluster.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Writing log rules properly: [Log alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/log-rules.md)
* Search technique: [Log explorer and index patterns](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/log-explorer.md)
* Using ES instead: [ElasticSearch / OpenSearch](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/elasticsearch.md)

# Connect your data

Nightingale queries your stores where they are. Twelve source types share one rule model; Categraf covers what nothing collects yet.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Register what you already run; Nightingale queries it in place. Metrics, logs and SQL-queried stores share one rule model, so there is nothing new to learn per source type. Nothing is migrated: a data source is a connection, not a copy.

Nightingale does not collect anything itself. [Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/categraf.md) is the recommended companion — one agent, 100+ plugins, writing over Prometheus Remote Write. Telegraf, the Datadog Agent and standard exporters write in the same way, and an existing Prometheus that already scrapes your targets can stay exactly as it is.

## [Auto-registered Embedded TSDB datasource](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/embedded-tsdb.md)

[A fresh install auto-registers a Prometheus-type source named embedded-tsdb; Pushgw writes into it by default, and it is queried like any external Prometheus source.](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/embedded-tsdb.md)

## [Prometheus](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md)

[Register a Prometheus or Thanos endpoint, set auth and timeouts, and verify with a query.](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md)

## [VictoriaMetrics](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/victoriametrics.md)

[There is no separate VictoriaMetrics type: register it as Prometheus and set the TSDB type to VictoriaMetrics; single-node and cluster endpoints differ.](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/victoriametrics.md)

## [ElasticSearch / OpenSearch](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/elasticsearch.md)

[Connect an ES or OpenSearch cluster, choose index patterns and the timestamp field, and run a log query.](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/elasticsearch.md)

## [ClickHouse / Doris / IoTDB](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/clickhouse-doris-iotdb.md)

[ClickHouse, Doris and IoTDB are one family in Nightingale: queried with SQL, one numeric column of the result becomes the series value and the rest become labels.](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/clickhouse-doris-iotdb.md)

## [Loki / VictoriaLogs](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/loki-victorialogs.md)

[Register a log store, write a LogQL or LogsQL query, and alert on counts or matches.](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/loki-victorialogs.md)

## [MySQL / PostgreSQL / TDengine](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/sql-databases.md)

[Alert on a business database directly: read-only credentials, the SQL a rule runs, and guarding against slow queries.](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/sql-databases.md)

# Prometheus

Register a Prometheus or Thanos endpoint, set auth and timeouts, and verify with a query.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: a registered Prometheus data source whose connection has been tested and which returns a line in the Metrics explorer. Thanos, Mimir, M3 and VictoriaMetrics all implement Prometheus's query API and use this same type (VictoriaMetrics has one extra switch — see [VictoriaMetrics](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/victoriametrics.md)).

Nothing is moved. A data source is a connection: Nightingale queries your store where it is, and your scrape config stays exactly as it is.

## Before you start[​](#before-you-start "Direct link to Before you start")

* The query endpoint of your Prometheus, e.g. `http://10.0.0.11:9090`;
* Network access to it **from the machine running Nightingale Center** — your browser being able to reach it is not the same thing;
* Credentials, if the endpoint is behind auth;
* An Admin account — adding a data source is an admin operation, and the **Add** button is hidden from everyone else.

## 1. Add the data source[​](#1-add-the-data-source "Direct link to 1. Add the data source")

**Integrations → Data sources → Add**, then pick **Prometheus** from the type list.

Only two fields are required:

| Field | What to put in it                                                            |
| ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name  | Something you will recognise. Rules and queries pick the source by this name |
| URL   | The query endpoint, up to the port. Nightingale appends `/api/v1/...` itself |

The form lists the shape for each product:

```
1. Prometheus                      http://localhost:9090/

2. Thanos                          http://localhost:19192/

3. VictoriaMetrics Cluster         http://{vmselect}:8481/select/0/prometheus/

4. VictoriaMetrics Single-Node     http://{vmselect}:8428/

5. M3                              http://localhost:7201/

6. SLS                             https://{project}.{sls-endpoint}/prometheus/{project}/{metricstore}/

7. Mimir                           http://mimir:9009/prometheus
```

**Timeout(ms)** defaults to 10000. Raise it for a large, slow cluster, but not to minutes — the alerting engine evaluates on a schedule, and one stuck query holds up a whole batch of rules.

![The Prometheus data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-prometheus.webp)![The Prometheus data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-prometheus.dark.webp)

## 2. Auth and TLS[​](#2-auth-and-tls "Direct link to 2. Auth and TLS")

* **User / Password**: fill these if Prometheus has basic auth enabled. Use the **plain password**, not the bcrypt hash from `basic_auth_users` in `web-config.yml`;
* **Skip SSL verify**: turn it on for a self-signed certificate;
* **Advanced settings** holds the four mutual-TLS fields — CA certificate, Server name, Client certificate, Client key. Paste the certificate body, starting at `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----`;
* **Custom HTTP headers**: add Header / Value pairs when a gateway in front requires a token.

## 3. Three more fields[​](#3-three-more-fields "Direct link to 3. Three more fields")

None of these are required, but getting them wrong bites you somewhere else:

| Field                                        | When you need it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Remote Write URL                             | Only when you use [recording rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/recording-rules.md). The new series a recording rule computes are written back to this address. For Prometheus that is `http://localhost:9090/api/v1/write`, for single-node VictoriaMetrics `http://localhost:8428/api/v1/write` |
| Internal address of the time series database | Only when the alerting engine is deployed down in an edge data center. When set, `n9e-edge` uses this address to reach the store; when empty it uses the URL above                                                                                                                                     |
| Time series database type                    | Prometheus / Thanos / VictoriaMetrics / M3 / SLS. It changes how dashboard variables are resolved and which endpoint "delete series" calls, so pick the right one for VictoriaMetrics                                                                                                                  |

Leave **Associated alerting engine cluster** at `default` if you run a single engine. If this field is empty, rules against this data source are never evaluated.

## 4. Verify[​](#4-verify "Direct link to 4. Verify")

Click **Save & test**. Nightingale issues one `/api/v1/query?query=1%2B1` against the address; the record is only stored if that succeeds, and a failure is reported verbatim without saving.

If the endpoint genuinely is not reachable yet but you want the config stored, use **Save**.

After a successful save a result panel opens. For Prometheus-type sources it also runs a data health check:

* **N metrics found · latest data X ago** — everything works;
* **Connected, but no metrics found** — the connection is fine but the store is empty, usually because no collector is writing yet;
* **Historical data exists, but nothing recent** — metrics are there but no fresh samples; go check whether your collectors are still running.

Then confirm it yourself: **Explorer → Metrics**, pick the source you just created, and run a query you know returns data:

```
up
```

A line on the chart means this half works. If nothing comes back, stop here — [Why does a data source connect but return no data?](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md).

## When it doesn't connect[​](#when-it-doesnt-connect "Direct link to When it doesn't connect")

**The test returns 404.** The URL includes a path such as `http://host:9090/api/v1/query`. Trim it back to the port.

**The test returns 401 / 403.** Either the basic auth password was entered as a hash, or a gateway in front of Prometheus needs an auth header added under **Custom HTTP headers**.

**Nightingale gets a 404 forwarding samples to Prometheus.** That is the write path, not the data source. Prometheus does not accept remote write by default; start it with `--web.enable-remote-write-receiver` (older versions: `--enable-feature=remote-write-receiver`).

**Saved fine, but rules never evaluate.** Check that **Associated alerting engine cluster** is not empty.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Write the first rule against it: [Your first alert rule](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/first-rule.md)
* Query ad hoc: [Metrics explorer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/metric-explorer.md)
* Moving to VictoriaMetrics: [VictoriaMetrics](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/victoriametrics.md)
* Nothing collecting yet: [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md)

# MySQL / PostgreSQL / TDengine

Alert on a business database directly: read-only credentials, the SQL a rule runs, and guarding against slow queries.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Some numbers never reach a time series database at all: pending orders, payment failure rate, how long ago the last row landed in a table. There is no need to export those as metrics and scrape them — Nightingale can connect to the business database directly, run a SQL statement on a schedule, and judge the result.

Where this page ends: a read-only account, a connected database source, and a SQL alert rule that runs without dragging the database down.

## What each can do in the open-source edition[​](#what-each-can-do-in-the-open-source-edition "Direct link to What each can do in the open-source edition")

Three databases on one page, with different capability boundaries:

|            | Register a source | Alert rules | Metrics explorer | Dashboards |
| ---------- | ----------------- | ----------- | ---------------- | ---------- |
| MySQL      | ✓                 | ✓           | —                | —          |
| PostgreSQL | ✓                 | ✓           | —                | —          |
| TDengine   | ✓                 | ✓           | ✓                | ✓          |

**In the open-source edition MySQL and PostgreSQL land in alert rules only**; the explorer and dashboards cannot select them. To check whether a statement is correct, use the **Preview** button inside the alert rule form — in the open-source edition that is the only surface that executes SQL against a business database. TDengine has no such limit.

## Start with a read-only account[​](#start-with-a-read-only-account "Direct link to Start with a read-only account")

Don't connect as root. Least privilege pays off directly here: a wrong config, a leaked credential or a runaway statement all stop at the account's permissions.

```
-- MySQL

CREATE USER 'n9e_readonly'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '<password>';

GRANT SELECT ON business_db.* TO 'n9e_readonly'@'%';

FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
```

```
-- PostgreSQL

CREATE ROLE n9e_readonly LOGIN PASSWORD '<password>';

GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE business_db TO n9e_readonly;

GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO n9e_readonly;

GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO n9e_readonly;
```

`GRANT SELECT` only, and only on the database you actually query. Pin the source address too — `'n9e_readonly'@'10.0.0.%'` beats `@'%'`.

## Register the data source[​](#register-the-data-source "Direct link to Register the data source")

**Integrations → Data sources → Add**, then pick MySQL, PostgreSQL or TDengine.

MySQL and PostgreSQL share one form; only the default port differs:

| Field                                                              | Notes                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Database address                                                   | Required. `127.0.0.1:3306` (MySQL) / `127.0.0.1:5432` (PostgreSQL), no scheme |
| Username / Password                                                | **Both required.** Use the read-only account from the previous step           |
| Timeout (unit: seconds)                                            | Defaults to 60                                                                |
| Maximum number of rows allowed to be retrieved in a single request | Defaults to 500, required                                                     |
| Max idle / max open connections                                    | Default 10 / 100. Lower them if the database is tight on connections          |
| Maximum connection lifetime (unit: seconds)                        | Defaults to 14400                                                             |

![The MySQL data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-mysql.webp)![The MySQL data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-mysql.dark.webp)

TDengine talks over its REST interface and needs fewer fields: URL `http://localhost:6041`, timeout in milliseconds (10000 by default), user and password as needed. The connectivity test posts `show databases` to `<URL>/rest/sql`.

For all three, make sure **Associated alerting engine cluster** is not empty — rules against a source with no engine are never evaluated.

## The SQL a rule runs[​](#the-sql-a-rule-runs "Direct link to The SQL a rule runs")

**Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules → Add**, data source type MySQL / PostgreSQL / TDengine, then select the source. The query is a SQL statement — it plays the same role PromQL plays in a metric rule.

The statement has to satisfy two things: **a bounded number of rows**, and **at least one numeric column**.

```
-- pending orders piling up

SELECT count(*) AS pending

FROM orders

WHERE status = 'PENDING'

  AND created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL 10 MINUTE
```

```
-- failure rate per channel

SELECT channel,

       sum(CASE WHEN status = 'FAIL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failed,

       count(*) AS total

FROM payments

WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL 5 MINUTE

GROUP BY channel
```

```
-- freshness: how many seconds since the last row

SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, MAX(updated_at), NOW()) AS lag_seconds

FROM sync_state
```

The TDengine editor adds **SQL templates** and a **time field / time format** pair — which column is the time axis and how to parse it.

## Which column is the number[​](#which-column-is-the-number "Direct link to Which column is the number")

SQL returns a table; Nightingale turns it into series with two **auxiliary settings**:

* **Value field** (required): which columns hold numbers for the threshold to judge;
* **Label field** (optional): which columns become labels, normally the `GROUP BY` columns.

In the second example above, pick `failed` and `total` as value fields and `channel` as the label field, and the threshold becomes:

```
$A.failed / $A.total * 100 > 5
```

**Every row the SQL returns is an independent series, judged on its own.** Three channels means at most three events, each carrying its own `channel` label.

Click **Preview** when the statement is written, confirm the column names and row count match what you expect, and only then set a threshold.

## Guarding against slow queries[​](#guarding-against-slow-queries "Direct link to Guarding against slow queries")

This statement runs **against your production database, over and over, at the evaluation frequency**. Think about the cost before you write it:

1. **Bound the time range in `WHERE`**, on an indexed column. `created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL 5 MINUTE` is orders of magnitude cheaper than a full-table count;
2. **Match the frequency to the cost.** A statement that takes three seconds does not belong on a 15-second schedule; start business-database queries at 60 seconds;
3. **Never `SELECT *`.** Return only the columns that take part in the judgement;
4. **Let the row cap do its job.** **Maximum rows retrieved per request** defaults to 500; raising it to tens of thousands defeats the point — it exists to contain "one statement unexpectedly returned a million rows";
5. **Keep the timeout short.** For MySQL and PostgreSQL it is in **seconds**, 60 by default; setting it to several hundred throws that protection away.

If the query really is expensive, the fix is not tuning these fields — it is building a pre-aggregated table (materialized view, scheduled job) in the database and pointing Nightingale at that.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Writing SQL rules properly: [SQL alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/sql-rules.md)
* Getting events to a person: [Notifications](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/overview.md)
* Bulk log and detail stores: [ClickHouse / Doris / IoTDB](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/clickhouse-doris-iotdb.md)

# VictoriaMetrics

There is no separate VictoriaMetrics type: register it as Prometheus and set the TSDB type to VictoriaMetrics; single-node and cluster endpoints differ.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

To save you hunting through the type list: **the open-source edition has no "VictoriaMetrics" data source type.** VictoriaMetrics implements Prometheus's query API, so you register it under the **Prometheus** type and then set **Time series database type** to `VictoriaMetrics` in the same form.

This page covers three things: which URL to use for single-node versus cluster, what that **Time series database type** setting actually changes, and how to configure the write path when Nightingale is pushing samples into VictoriaMetrics itself.

## Single-node and cluster endpoints differ[​](#single-node-and-cluster-endpoints-differ "Direct link to Single-node and cluster endpoints differ")

Cluster VictoriaMetrics splits reads and writes across two components with completely different addresses. Getting this wrong produces the classic "it connects but returns nothing".

| Purpose                               | Single-node                     | Cluster                                                   |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Data source **URL** (query, vmselect) | `http://{vm}:8428/`             | `http://{vmselect}:8481/select/0/prometheus/`             |
| Write endpoint (vminsert)             | `http://{vm}:8428/api/v1/write` | `http://{vminsert}:8480/insert/0/prometheus/api/v1/write` |

The `0` in the cluster path is the tenant ID (`accountID`). In a multi-tenant setup, register one data source per tenant with its own ID in the path.

Every other field behaves exactly as described in [Prometheus](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md): name, timeout, user and password, skip SSL verify, custom HTTP headers.

## Set the time series database type[​](#set-the-time-series-database-type "Direct link to Set the time series database type")

The **Time series database type** dropdown at the bottom of the form should be set to `VictoriaMetrics`. It does not change the query itself, but it changes two behaviours:

* **Dashboard variables.** For a `label_values(metric, label)` variable over a window shorter than a day, values are resolved through a different series endpoint. VictoriaMetrics makes samples visible slightly later than Prometheus does, and without this the dropdown is frequently empty for short ranges;
* **Delete series.** Nightingale issues the request in VictoriaMetrics's shape; for a cluster URL containing `/select/<tenant>/prometheus` it rewrites the path to `/delete/<tenant>/prometheus/...` automatically.

Leaving it on `Prometheus` is not an error — those two things simply happen the Prometheus way.

## When Nightingale also writes to it[​](#when-nightingale-also-writes-to-it "Direct link to When Nightingale also writes to it")

Everything above is the **read** path. If Categraf pushes metrics to Nightingale and Nightingale forwards them to VictoriaMetrics, there is a **write** path too, and it lives in the config file, not in the data source form:

```
[Pushgw]

# use target labels stored in the database instead of those on the series

LabelRewrite = true

ForceUseServerTS = true



[[Pushgw.Writers]]

# single-node

Url = "http://victoriametrics:8428/api/v1/write"

# cluster

# Url = "http://vminsert:8480/insert/0/prometheus/api/v1/write"

# BasicAuthUser = ""

# BasicAuthPass = ""

# Timeout = 10000
```

Two settings are easy to confuse, so remember this: **the data source URL points at vmselect, `Pushgw.Writers` points at vminsert.** The **Remote Write URL** field in the data source form is a third, unrelated thing — it is only where [recording rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/recording-rules.md) write their results back, and has nothing to do with the Categraf data flow.

`[[Pushgw.Writers]]` can run at the same time as [`[EmbeddedTSDB]`](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/embedded-tsdb.md), writing to both. That overlap is the migration window from the embedded store to VictoriaMetrics — see [External TSDB and dual-write migration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/external-tsdb.md).

## Verify[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify")

1. Click **Save & test**. Nightingale issues one `<URL>/api/v1/query?query=1%2B1`, and only stores the record if it succeeds. A 404 on a cluster almost always means the URL is missing the `/select/0/prometheus/` segment;
2. **Explorer → Metrics**, select this source, and run `up` or any metric you know exists. A line on the chart is what you are after;
3. If Nightingale is doing the writing: wait one collection interval (Categraf defaults to 15s), then query `cpu_usage_active`. Getting data back means the write path works too.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Write the first rule against it: [Your first alert rule](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/first-rule.md)
* Migrating off the embedded store: [External TSDB and dual-write migration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/external-tsdb.md)
* Field-by-field walkthrough of the form: [Prometheus](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md)

# Active and historical events

Active events hold alerts that have not recovered; on recovery they move to history. Both lists are searchable by label, severity and business group, in bulk.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: you know which of the two tables an alert is in and why, and how to pull the handful you care about out of several hundred while on call.

Entry point: **Alerts & Notifications → Events**, with two tabs at the top — **Active alerts** and **Historical alerts**.

## How the two lists differ[​](#how-the-two-lists-differ "Direct link to How the two lists differ")

|                      | Active `/alert-cur-events`                  | Historical `/alert-his-events`                |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Holds                | Events still firing, not yet recovered      | Every event ever produced, recovered included |
| How long a row stays | Disappears the moment it recovers           | Kept until you clean it up                    |
| Default time filter  | Unlimited (including one burning for weeks) | Last 6 hours                                  |
| What you can do      | Mute, delete, share                         | Search, export, clean up                      |

When an event recovers, the row in Active disappears and a `Recovered` row shows up in Historical — **the row is not moved**; the two tables have always been separate stores.

## An event's identity is rule + label set[​](#an-events-identity-is-rule--label-set "Direct link to An event's identity is rule + label set")

One rule running against 5 hosts produces **5 independent events**, because their label sets differ (`ident` is not the same). Each fires, recovers and notifies on its own. Seeing the same rule name on 5 rows is normal, not duplication.

An event's business group comes from **the rule's business group**, not the host's. If "My business groups / All business groups" does not surface an event you expect, check which business group owns the rule.

## Finding the one you want[​](#finding-the-one-you-want "Direct link to Finding the one you want")

![Active alerts](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/events/active-events.webp)![Active alerts](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/events/active-events.dark.webp)

The top row:

* **My business groups / All business groups** plus the group dropdown next to it — two levels of narrowing;
* **Fuzzy search** covers rule names and labels at once. **Several keywords separated by spaces are AND-ed**: `disk n9e-web-01` matches events whose rule name contains disk *and* whose labels contain n9e-web-01;
* **Tag display**: All / Compact / Off. Compact saves the most room on a wall display;
* **Auto refresh**: Off by default, 5s through 5min available.

The left panel has three multi-select groups: **Type** (Metric / Host / Log), **Severity** (S1 Critical / S2 Warning / S3 Info) and **Data source**. The three groups are AND-ed.

Each row has a coloured bar on the left for severity, and the bar under **Duration** shifts green to red with age, so the longest-burning event is visible at a glance.

When there are still too many rows, fold them into cards with the **Aggregate rule** selector above the table — see [Event aggregation and deduplication](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/aggregation.md).

## What to look at inside one event[​](#what-to-look-at-inside-one-event "Direct link to What to look at inside one event")

Clicking the event title (the blue line) slides a detail panel in from the right. Beyond rule name, severity, labels, first trigger time and trigger value, three things are worth going to directly:

* **The query**: the PromQL / SQL the rule actually ran, with a button next to it to re-run it. This is how you tell "the data really is abnormal" from "the threshold is wrong";
* **Notification records**: which media types this event was pushed to, whether they succeeded, and what a failure returned. Start here when nothing arrives, then follow [Why is there an alert event but no notification?](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-notification.md);
* **Hash**: the event fingerprint, computed from rule plus labels. Copy and compare it when working out why two rows are treated as the same event.

Three buttons at the bottom:

* **Mute**: pre-fills a mute rule with this event's labels and jumps to the new-mute form. This is the most-used way to stop the noise — see [Mute rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/mute-rules.md);
* **Delete**: physically removes the event. **Only when you are sure the metric will never be reported again** (host decommissioned, label renamed) — such events can never recover. In every other case let it recover by itself;
* **Sharing link**: issues a read-only link that needs no login, 7 days by default, for a colleague to look at. Same mechanism as [Anonymous time-limited sharing](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/sharing.md), applied to one event.

## Handling several at once[​](#handling-several-at-once "Direct link to Handling several at once")

Tick multiple rows and a batch bar appears above the list. The open-source edition can batch **delete**.

Deleting is not muting: the rule is still enabled, so if the condition still holds on the next evaluation a fresh event is produced (possibly with the same hash). To stop the noise for longer, use [Mute rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/mute-rules.md) or disable the rule.

## Historical events: export and cleanup[​](#historical-events-export-and-cleanup "Direct link to Historical events: export and cleanup")

![Historical alerts](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/events/historical-events.webp)![Historical alerts](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/events/historical-events.dark.webp)

The historical columns differ from the active ones: **First triggered** (when it entered the alerting state) and **Last evaluated** (when evaluation last confirmed it was still firing, or recovered) are separate columns. Those two are what you reconstruct a timeline from.

Two buttons at the top right:

* **Export**: dumps the events matching the current filters, for a monthly review;
* **Event cleanup**: bulk delete by severity plus "older than 1 month / 3 months / 6 months / 1 year". Deleted rows are gone for good, so confirm the match with the filters first.

Historical events never expire on their own; leaving them unattended grows the table. Put a periodic cleanup on your operations checklist.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Silence a class of event during a window: [Mute rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/mute-rules.md)
* Let another team receive them too: [Alert subscriptions](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/subscriptions.md)
* What else happens between event and person: [Noise reduction and routing model](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/noise-routing.md)
* An event that never recovers: [Alerts fire and recover repeatedly](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/alert-flapping.md)

# Event aggregation and deduplication

One rule plus one label set is one event, so repeated evaluations never create a second; the aggregation view folds hundreds of active events into a few cards.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: you know why one incident does not produce a message every evaluation cycle, and how to fold a screenful of hundreds of active events into a handful of cards.

## Deduplication is built in: an event is rule + label set[​](#deduplication-is-built-in-an-event-is-rule--label-set "Direct link to Deduplication is built in: an event is rule + label set")

An event's identity is its **rule together with its label set** — that is the Hash you see in the detail panel.

* The same rule with the same labels has **exactly one active event**. The rule keeps evaluating and the condition keeps holding, which updates that event's trigger time and trigger value — **it does not create a new event each cycle**;
* The same rule across 5 hosts is 5 events (different `ident`), each firing and recovering on its own;
* Only a fresh trigger after recovery counts as a new one.

So "duplicate alerts" in Nightingale is usually not one event sent many times; it is **too fine a label dimension** — a rule that expands over `device` into a dozen series produces a dozen independent events. To get fewer, first see whether the rule can aggregate the dimension away (`sum by (...)` in PromQL) — see [Metric rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/metric-rules.md).

Repeat notifications for one event are governed by two fields on the alert rule: **notify repeat interval (minutes)**, how long to wait before reminding while it is still unrecovered, and **max send count**, where 0 means unlimited. Those two are the most direct "one incident should not send a hundred messages" controls.

## Folding hundreds of active events into cards[​](#folding-hundreds-of-active-events-into-cards "Direct link to Folding hundreds of active events into cards")

**Alerts & Notifications → Events → Active alerts** has an **Aggregate rule** selector above the list. Pick one and events are grouped by the string the rule computes; a row of cards appears above the table, one per group. Clicking a card filters the table to that group.

Next to the selector it shows "N aggregate results", so you can see at a glance that a screenful is really only a few kinds of problem.

## Aggregation expressions worth having[​](#aggregation-expressions-worth-having "Direct link to Aggregation expressions worth having")

Click **Add rule** in the dropdown and fill in two fields: **Rule name** (what shows in the dropdown) and **Aggregate rule** (a Go template whose output becomes the card title). An administrator can also make it public for everyone; otherwise only you see it.

| Group by                  | Expression                                    |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Alert rule                | `{{.RuleName}}`                               |
| Business group + severity | `Group:{{.GroupName}} Severity:{{.Severity}}` |
| Host                      | `{{.TagsMap.ident}}`                          |
| Instance label            | `{{.TagsMap.instance}}`                       |
| Service                   | `{{.TagsMap.service}}`                        |

Available fields include `.RuleName`, `.GroupName`, `.Severity` and `.TagsMap.<label>`.

On call, the two that earn their keep are `{{.RuleName}}` and `{{.TagsMap.ident}}`: the first answers "which rule is flooding the screen", the second answers "is it all just one host".

An aggregate rule only changes **how this page displays**; it does not touch the events or affect notifications.

## Three ways to cut the number of messages[​](#three-ways-to-cut-the-number-of-messages "Direct link to Three ways to cut the number of messages")

Once the cards have shown you a class that does not need to be sent one by one:

1. **Raise the repeat interval and max send count on the rule** — for "the same event keeps ringing";
2. **A mute rule** — for "keep this class quiet for a while", see [Mute rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/mute-rules.md);
3. **The event drop processor in a workflow** — for "this class should never be sent", see [Event pipelines](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/pipelines.md).

The order they act in is in [Noise reduction and routing model](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/noise-routing.md); worked scenarios are in [Noise reduction patterns](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/noise-patterns.md).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Using the two event lists: [Active and historical events](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/active-historical.md)
* Splitting by condition instead of cutting everything: [Conditional routing](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/routing.md)
* Firing and recovering over and over: [Alerts fire and recover repeatedly](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/alert-flapping.md)
