# I already have Prometheus / VictoriaMetrics

Register the store as a data source, keep scraping exactly as before, and get the first rule evaluating against it — no data moves.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this path ends: one alert rule evaluating against the time-series database you **already run**, with your scrape config untouched and not one byte of data moved. About 10 minutes.

## Before you start[​](#before-you-start "Direct link to Before you start")

* Nightingale is running (if not, start at [Quick start](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md));
* the query endpoint of your Prometheus / VictoriaMetrics / Thanos / Mimir, and network access to it **from the host running Nightingale**;
* credentials, if the endpoint is behind auth.

## 1. Register the data source[​](#1-register-the-data-source "Direct link to 1. Register the data source")

**Integrations → Data sources → Add → Prometheus**.

Only two fields are required:

| Field | What to put in it                                                 |
| ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name  | Something you will recognise — rules pick the source by this name |
| URL   | The query endpoint. The form lists the shape for each product     |

The endpoint shapes (the same list the form shows):

```
Prometheus                    http://localhost:9090/

Thanos Querier                http://localhost:19192/

VictoriaMetrics single-node   http://{vmselect}:8428/

VictoriaMetrics cluster       http://{vmselect}:8481/select/0/prometheus/

Mimir query frontend          http://mimir:9009/prometheus

M3                            http://localhost:7201/
```

VictoriaMetrics, Thanos and Mimir all implement the PromQL HTTP API, so all three register as **Prometheus Like** — there is no separate VictoriaMetrics type. For VictoriaMetrics, set **Time series database type** at the bottom of the form to `VictoriaMetrics`; that only tunes how dashboards query it.

If the endpoint uses basic auth, fill **User** and **Password** under **Auth** — the **plain password**, not the bcrypt hash from Prometheus's `web-config.yml`. Turn on **Skip SSL verify** for a self-signed certificate.

Click **Save & test**. A failed test is not saved, and the error names the step that failed.

![The Prometheus data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-prometheus.webp)![The Prometheus data source form](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/data/form-prometheus.dark.webp)

## 2. Saving opens a guided dialog[​](#2-saving-opens-a-guided-dialog "Direct link to 2. Saving opens a guided dialog")

Saving does not drop you back on the list. A dialog opens and answers, right there, whether the source you just registered actually works — and offers the few things worth doing next.

![The guided dialog that opens after saving a data source](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/get-started/ds-next-step.webp)![The guided dialog that opens after saving a data source](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/get-started/ds-next-step.dark.webp)

### Health check[​](#health-check "Direct link to Health check")

The dialog runs a real query against the source as it opens. There are four verdicts:

| Verdict                                    | What it means                                                                  | What to do                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Data is flowing                            | Also reports metric count, latest data time, query latency and a sample metric | Move on                                                     |
| Connected, but no metrics found            | The endpoint answers, the store is empty                                       | Usually nothing is writing yet — not a misconfigured source |
| Historical data exists, but nothing recent | Metrics are there, no recent samples                                           | Check whether the collector is still running                |
| Cannot reach the datasource                | URL, credentials or network                                                    | Use **Back to edit config** in the dialog                   |

The health check only runs for Prometheus-family sources. Other types say it is not available — run a query in the [Metrics explorer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/metric-explorer.md) instead.

### The three "Next steps" buttons[​](#the-three-next-steps-buttons "Direct link to The three \"Next steps\" buttons")

All three open in a new tab, so the dialog and its verdict stay put:

* **Explore this data** opens the Metrics explorer carrying the sample metric the health check found, so there is a chart on arrival and no first query to invent;
* **Create a dashboard** / **Create an alert rule** land on the matching list page, which shows a "Datasource *name* is ready" banner telling you to pick a business group first — both Add buttons need that context.

### Component template matching[​](#component-template-matching "Direct link to Component template matching")

If the source holds data for components Nightingale knows, the dialog lists them at the bottom, each with how many dashboards and rules it carries.

The matching runs on sentinel metrics: every built-in template picks one to three representative metrics from its own queries, they go to your source as a single query, and any that returned a sample in the last five minutes marks its component as present. So the list is what you are **actually collecting**, not a catalogue of everything on offer.

Click a card to open the import dialog:

![Importing component templates from the data source dialog](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/get-started/ds-template-import.webp)![Importing component templates from the data source dialog](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/get-started/ds-template-import.dark.webp)

Pick a business group, tick the dashboards or alert rules to bring in, and the import binds them to the source you just saved. The other two import entry points, and the templates themselves, are covered in [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md).

### Reopening it later[​](#reopening-it-later "Direct link to Reopening it later")

**Integrations → Data sources**, then **Data status** on that row: same dialog, health check runs again. A disabled source is not probed, and the dialog says so rather than reporting it as broken.

## 3. Confirm you can actually query it[​](#3-confirm-you-can-actually-query-it "Direct link to 3. Confirm you can actually query it")

**Explore this data** in the dialog lands here. Coming in by hand: **Explorer → Metrics**, pick the source you just created, and run a PromQL query you know returns data:

```
up
```

A line on the chart means this half works. If nothing comes back, stop here — [Why does a data source connect but return no data?](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md).

## 4. Write the first rule[​](#4-write-the-first-rule "Direct link to 4. Write the first rule")

**Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules → Add**, select your data source, and write a query that will fire. Start with an expression that **must** be true, so you are testing the chain and not your threshold:

```
up == 1
```

Evaluation every 15s, for-duration 60s, severity S2. Save.

A minute later, **Alerts & Notifications → Events** should show events. That means data source → query → evaluation → event works end to end.

**Then change that rule to a real threshold, or delete it** — as written it never stops firing.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Get events to a person: [Notifications](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/overview.md)
* Write rules properly: [Alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/overview.md)
* Also monitor the hosts themselves: [Start with Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/choose-your-path/categraf.md)

# I want to enable Nightingale AI

Configure an LLM provider, turn on the built-in assistant and the MCP endpoint, and connect a client such as Claude Code.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this path ends: you can ask "which S1 alerts are firing right now" inside Nightingale in plain language, and an MCP client such as Claude Code can ask the same thing. About 10 minutes.

## Before you start[​](#before-you-start "Direct link to Before you start")

* Nightingale is running;
* an API key for a model provider, or an Ollama running locally.

## 1. Configure a model[​](#1-configure-a-model "Direct link to 1. Configure a model")

The entry point lives inside **Nightingale AI** (the top-level item in the sidebar); its own secondary navigation has **LLM configs**. There is no top-level menu for it — visiting `/ai-config/llm-configs` redirects here.

Click **Add LLM config** and fill in:

| Field          | Notes                                                                                                          |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name           | Your own                                                                                                       |
| Provider type  | The form offers three: **OpenAI compatible**, **Anthropic Claude**, **Google Gemini**                          |
| API URL        | OpenAI-compatible services (vLLM, Azure OpenAI, Ollama, Kimi…) all use **OpenAI compatible** with your own URL |
| API key        |                                                                                                                |
| Model          | The model name, e.g. `gpt-4o`, `claude-sonnet-4-5`                                                             |
| Context length |                                                                                                                |

Save it and mark it **default**: anything that has no model of its own falls back to this one.

## 2. Ask it something[​](#2-ask-it-something "Direct link to 2. Ask it something")

Back in **Nightingale AI**, start a chat and ask:

> Which S1 alerts are firing right now?

The assistant queries your event data before answering. A useful answer means both halves — model and data — are wired up.

## 3. The MCP endpoint is already on[​](#3-the-mcp-endpoint-is-already-on "Direct link to 3. The MCP endpoint is already on")

`/mcp` and `/a2a` are **enabled by default**; no config change needed. They reuse `HTTP.TokenAuth`, so a client authenticates with `X-User-Token`. They also accept `Authorization: Bearer` when the built-in authorization server or external-IdP auth is enabled.

**The important part: an MCP client has exactly the permissions of the token's owner, and no more.** Create a dedicated least-privilege account for AI access rather than handing over root's token.

Only **read** tools are registered by default. Write tools (create / update / delete) are an explicit opt-in:

```
[HTTP.A2A]

MCPEnableWriteTools = true
```

You can also expose a subset of toolsets:

```
# empty = all default toolsets

MCPToolsets = ["alerts", "dashboards"]
```

There are 13 toolsets: `alerts`, `targets`, `datasource`, `mutes`, `busi_groups`, `notify_rules`, `alert_subscribes`, `event_pipelines`, `users`, `metrics`, `logs`, `dashboards`, `roles`. Unknown names are ignored — the list never widens by accident.

## 4. Connect a client[​](#4-connect-a-client "Direct link to 4. Connect a client")

Create a token first: avatar menu → personal settings → generate a token. Then point the client at Nightingale's `/mcp` endpoint with that token.

Verify with something read-only, such as "list all alert rules".

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* What the assistant can see and do: [AI and MCP](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/overview.md)
* Turning on write access safely: [Enable write tools safely](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/write-tools.md)
* The tool list: [MCP tool reference](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/mcp-tools.md)

# What Nightingale (n9e) is

Nightingale (n9e, 夜莺) is an open-source alerting engine for existing data sources, with an embedded TSDB for small, single-Center deployments.

Last reviewed 2026-10-15

Nightingale (夜莺, also known as **n9e**) is an open-source alerting engine, hosted by the China Computer Federation's open-source committee (CCF ODTC) and developed on [GitHub](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale) under Apache-2.0. It queries your existing Prometheus, log stores and databases to evaluate alert rules, reduce noise and deliver notifications. You can keep your data and collectors in place.

Without an external time series store, small, single-Center deployments can use the embedded TSDB. Multi-Center or larger deployments should use an external TSDB. See [Embedded TSDB and external storage](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/storage.md) for the limits and migration path.

## What it owns[​](#what-it-owns "Direct link to What it owns")

| Layer                                     | Nightingale                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Storage                                   | Reuse Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Elasticsearch or ClickHouse; an embedded TSDB supports small, single-Center deployments |
| Collection                                | ❌ — Categraf, Telegraf, Datadog Agent and exporters all write in                                                          |
| **Alert rules, noise reduction, routing** | ✅ **this is the layer it owns**                                                                                           |
| Dashboards                                | ✅ built in, but Grafana stays a first-class option                                                                        |

## Where it fits[​](#where-it-fits "Direct link to Where it fits")

Register a data source, write one rule against it, and the resulting event flows through mute rules, subscriptions and event pipelines before reaching a notification channel. Since v9 the same process is also an MCP server, so an AI client can drive all of it in plain language.

* **10+<!-- --> data source types** — metrics, logs and SQL-queried stores alike
* **20<!-- --> built-in message templates** covering DingTalk, Feishu, WeCom, phone, SMS, Slack, PagerDuty and more — six media types ship configured, the rest you point at your own endpoint
* **83<!-- --> built-in integrations** bundling collector config, dashboards and rules
* **74<!-- --> MCP tools** across
  <!-- -->
  13
  <!-- -->
  toolsets

Apache-2.0, fully featured.

Next: [Quick start](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md).

# Guided live demo

Sign in to the public demo and walk the path from data source to delivered alert, in the same order as the quick start — no install needed.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

After this page you will have seen, on a running instance, every stop an alert makes in Nightingale: the data source it reads, the rule that evaluates it, the event it produces and the rule that delivers it.

## Sign in[​](#sign-in "Direct link to Sign in")

Open **[the live demo](https://play.n9e.io/api/n9e/auth/demo-login)**. The link signs you in as the shared demo account, so there is no username or password to type.

Expected result: you land on **Home**, with a **Getting started** checklist at the top. The demo is the open-source edition, so every menu you see here is one you get from the [quick start](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md).

The environment is shared with every other visitor. Do not type real passwords, webhook URLs, phone numbers or API keys into it.

## The tour[​](#the-tour "Direct link to The tour")

Follow the left-hand menu in this order. Each stop is one step of the quick start.

1. **Integrations → Data sources.** The sources Nightingale queries in place: nothing is copied in. Open one to see the address and the timeout it uses. Expected result: a list of data sources, each with a type icon such as Prometheus.
2. **Explorer → Metrics.** Pick a data source and run a query such as `up`. This is the same query language an alert rule uses, so a query that returns data here will also work in a rule. Expected result: a chart and a table of series.
3. **Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules.** Choose a business group on the left, then open a rule. Look at three things: the query, the threshold for each severity (S1 / S2 / S3), and the for-duration that filters out spikes.
4. **Alerts & Notifications → Events.** **Active alerts** are still firing; **Historical alerts** keeps every event, recovered ones included. Open an event to see its labels, the value that triggered it and which notifications it set off ([more on the two lists](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/active-historical.md)).
5. **Alerts & Notifications → Notification rules.** This is where an event is matched to people and media types. **Media types** and **Message templates** in the same menu define how a message is sent and what it looks like.
6. **Explorer → Dashboards.** Charts built on the same data sources. If you already use Grafana you can keep it; dashboards here are optional.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

Run your own instance with the [quick start](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md), or go straight to [your first alert rule](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/first-rule.md).

# Production readiness checklist

What to change before real traffic: default credentials, external database, TSDB choice, HA, backups and self-monitoring.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Getting a single instance running is easy, but those defaults are **not for production**. This is the list to walk before you go live.

## Must do[​](#must-do "Direct link to Must do")

### Change the default password[​](#change-the-default-password "Direct link to Change the default password")

A fresh install has `root` / `root.2020`, and **that is public knowledge**. Change it on first login, or create a new admin account and disable root.

The same goes for the sample credentials under `[HTTP.APIForService.BasicAuth]` in `etc/config.toml` (`user001` / `ccc26da7b9aba533cbb263a36c07dcc5`) — public, so replace them if you turn that API on.

### Replace SQLite and the in-process Redis[​](#replace-sqlite-and-the-in-process-redis "Direct link to Replace SQLite and the in-process Redis")

The defaults are a SQLite file and miniredis, an in-process stand-in. They exist so a single process can run with nothing else installed: there is no second copy of the data if the process dies, and no way for several instances to share state.

```
[DB]

DBType = "mysql"

DSN = "n9e:<password>@tcp(mysql:3306)/n9e_v6?charset=utf8mb4&parseTime=True&loc=Local"



[Redis]

RedisType = "standalone"

Address = "redis:6379"
```

PostgreSQL works too, with `DBType = "postgres"`.

### Decide on the time-series database[​](#decide-on-the-time-series-database "Direct link to Decide on the time-series database")

The embedded TSDB is on by default and keeps data on the local disk of **one Center process**. Two consequences:

* with several replicas each holds a fragment, so **high availability means turning it off**;
* it does not carry large volumes (roughly past 100k active series).

Production usually means an external store:

```
[EmbeddedTSDB]

Enable = false



[[Pushgw.Writers]]

Url = "http://victoriametrics:8428/api/v1/write"
```

Both can be on at once as a dual write while you migrate, then turn the embedded one off once the new store has enough history.

## Strongly recommended[​](#strongly-recommended "Direct link to Strongly recommended")

### Run more than one instance[​](#run-more-than-one-instance "Direct link to Run more than one instance")

Run `n9e` on several hosts with identical config, sharing one MySQL and one Redis. Alert rules are distributed across instances automatically — a rule runs on exactly one instance, so no duplicate alerts — and another instance takes over the rules of one that dies.

### Back up[​](#back-up "Direct link to Back up")

The metadata database is the thing that matters: users, business groups, alert rules, dashboards and notification config all live there. Keep `etc/` in version control too. Whether to back up the embedded TSDB depends on whether you still depend on it.

Rehearse the restore. A backup nobody has restored is not a backup.

### Monitor Nightingale itself[​](#monitor-nightingale-itself "Direct link to Monitor Nightingale itself")

An alerting system that is down will not alert you about being down. Every process exposes its own metrics on `/metrics`; point Nightingale at itself and watch at least process liveness, whether rule evaluation is still running on schedule, and notification delivery failures.

See [Monitor Nightingale itself](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/self-monitoring.md).

### Decide whether anonymous access stays on[​](#decide-whether-anonymous-access-stays-on "Direct link to Decide whether anonymous access stays on")

Both switches under `[Center.AnonymousAccess]` **default to `true`**:

```
[Center.AnonymousAccess]

PromQuerier = true

AlertDetail = true
```

While they are on, **the query and proxy endpoints need no login**. Measured on a default install: an unauthenticated `GET /api/n9e/datasource/brief` returns every data source's name, type and connection address (passwords are redacted), and `GET /api/n9e/proxy/<datasource id>/api/v1/query?query=<PromQL>` returns query results.

The default exists so anonymous dashboard share links work. Turn it off if you do not need them — and if you do need them, **this port must not face the internet directly**.

### Close down the network[​](#close-down-the-network "Direct link to Close down the network")

The write endpoints (`/prometheus/v1/write`, `/v1/n9e/heartbeat`) and the admin UI should not face the internet directly. Put them behind a gateway with TLS if outside access is needed. See [Network and TLS hardening](https://n9e.github.io/docs/security/network-tls.md).

### Get credentials out of the config file[​](#get-credentials-out-of-the-config-file "Direct link to Get credentials out of the config file")

Database passwords, channel tokens and LLM API keys do not belong hard-coded in `config.toml`. See [Secret management](https://n9e.github.io/docs/security/secrets.md).

## After you are live[​](#after-you-are-live "Direct link to After you are live")

* **Actually verify the notification chain once**, rule to phone. Do not discover a misconfigured channel during a real incident;
* add at least one "collector went quiet" rule, or you will not notice when data stops arriving;
* walk the upgrade and rollback procedures before you need them: [Upgrade](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/upgrade.md), [Rollback](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/rollback.md).

# Bring up Nightingale in five minutes

One docker compose up -d brings up Nightingale with its dependencies; sign in on port 17000 as root, then register a data source, write a rule and add a channel.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

The compose bundle starts Nightingale together with the database and time-series store it needs, so there is nothing to prepare beforehand.

```
git clone https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale.git

cd nightingale/docker/compose-bridge

docker compose up -d
```

Open **`http://localhost:17000`** and sign in as `root` / `root.2020`.

## What to do first[​](#what-to-do-first "Direct link to What to do first")

1. **Register a data source** — Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, ElasticSearch, ClickHouse, Loki and more are all supported. Nightingale queries them where they are; nothing is migrated.
2. **Write one alert rule** against that source, scoped to a business group and graded S1 / S2 / S3.
3. **Add a notification channel** so the event reaches somebody.

Nothing collecting yet? [Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/categraf.md) covers operating systems, middleware, databases, network gear and Kubernetes with a single agent.

Next: [Installation](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/overview.md) for production deployments.

# Where it fits in the observability stack

Of the six observability layers, Nightingale owns the middle three — rules, noise reduction, routing and delivery; collectors, storage and Grafana stay as they are.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

After this page you can place Nightingale in the stack you already run, and say which pieces stay.

## Six layers, Nightingale owns the middle three[​](#six-layers-nightingale-owns-the-middle-three "Direct link to Six layers, Nightingale owns the middle three")

Layers 1 and 2 stay yours: your collectors keep running, your stores keep storing. At layer 6 Nightingale sends the message but does not run rotas or escalation policies — that is what on-call platforms are for, and Nightingale can hand events to them.

## What you do not have to replace[​](#what-you-do-not-have-to-replace "Direct link to What you do not have to replace")

| What you run today                               | After Nightingale                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Prometheus / VictoriaMetrics / Thanos / Mimir    | Register as a data source, scrape config untouched                                                      |
| ElasticSearch / OpenSearch / Loki / VictoriaLogs | Register as a data source, same rule model as metrics                                                   |
| MySQL / PostgreSQL / ClickHouse / TDengine       | Register as a data source, rules run SQL directly                                                       |
| Grafana                                          | Keep it. Nightingale ships dashboards but does not ask you to migrate                                   |
| node\_exporter and friends                       | Keep being scraped by Prometheus; Nightingale queries Prometheus                                        |
| Alertmanager                                     | This is the layer that gets replaced — rules, silences, routes and receivers become Nightingale objects |

Alertmanager and the alerting built into your TSDB are the only real overlap. That overlap is the point.

## One exception: the embedded TSDB[​](#one-exception-the-embedded-tsdb "Direct link to One exception: the embedded TSDB")

Nightingale ships with a time-series database, on by default, so the whole flow works before you install anything else. It exists for onboarding, not as another TSDB to run: data lives on the local disk of **one Center process**, so with several replicas each one holds a fragment.

It is fine at small scale (roughly under 100k active series). Past that, turn it off and point `Pushgw.Writers` at an external store. Both can run at once as a dual write during migration.

## Three common shapes[​](#three-common-shapes "Direct link to Three common shapes")

* **Data does not flow through Nightingale.** You handle collection and storage; Nightingale only queries. The host list stays empty and self-healing is unavailable, but alert rules work fully.
* **Data flows through Nightingale.** Categraf remote-writes to Nightingale, which keeps it in the embedded TSDB by default and can forward it to one or more TSDBs per `Pushgw.Writers`. Host list and self-healing work.
* **Edge deployment.** Where a site's link to the centre is unreliable, run `n9e-edge` there so evaluation happens locally and alerting survives a partition. See [Edge data centers](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/edge.md).

Next: [Choose your path](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/choose-your-path/existing-metrics.md).

# Deprecations and EOL policy

Features, fields and UI items marked deprecated, with their replacements; the project publishes no removal schedule, and GitHub releases are the version record.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

This page lists what Nightingale marks as deprecated and what replaced it. It does not list removal dates, because **the project does not publish any** — see the first section before reading the rest.

## There is no published maintenance policy[​](#there-is-no-published-maintenance-policy "Direct link to There is no published maintenance policy")

The project publishes no support matrix, no LTS designation, no stated maintenance window per minor version, and no announced removal schedule for anything on this page. [Compatibility matrix](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/compatibility.md) says the same thing about platform versions, for the same reason.

In practice the head of the release line is what receives fixes: v9.1.1 is a patch on top of v9.1.0, and that is where a bug fix appears. Beyond that, the authoritative record is GitHub:

| What you want to know                            | Where                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Which versions exist, and when each was released | [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/releases)                                           |
| Whether a fix has landed                         | The `fix:` entries in each release — see [Release notes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/help/release-notes.md) |
| Whether a field is still read by the engine      | The source. Nothing else is binding                                                                        |

**Everything marked deprecated below still exists and still works in v9.1.1.** Nothing has been removed. Read "deprecated" as "the replacement is where new work should go", not as "this stops working next release" — nobody has said when, and you should not infer a date from this page.

## The install date decides what you still see[​](#the-install-date-decides-what-you-still-see "Direct link to The install date decides what you still see")

The interface hides deprecated menu entries based on **when the installation was created, not which version it runs**. The cutoff is 2025-06-20, the v8 beta 14 release:

* an installation created **after** that date never shows the deprecated notification pages, and never shows the notification-version switch on the alert rule form;
* an installation created **before** it still shows them, with a deprecation marker beside them in the sidebar.

So two systems both running v9.1.1 can have different menus, and neither is broken. If a colleague's install has entries yours does not, theirs predates the cutoff.

## Deprecated in the interface[​](#deprecated-in-the-interface "Direct link to Deprecated in the interface")

| What                                         | Where it was           | Replacement                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Notification (`/help/notification-settings`) | Alerts & Notifications | **Notification rules** plus **Media types**                           |
| Templates (`/help/notification-tpls`)        | Alerts & Notifications | **Message templates**                                                 |
| Relabel, on the alert rule form              | The alert rule form    | The **Event label rewrite** processor in an event-processing workflow |

The first two are the entries hidden by the install-date rule above. The third is not hidden — the form carries its own notice saying that existing relabel configuration is better expressed as a workflow processor.

## Deprecated fields on the alert rule[​](#deprecated-fields-on-the-alert-rule "Direct link to Deprecated fields on the alert rule")

These carry a `Deprecated` marker in the alert rule model. All of them are still accepted and still returned by the API:

| Field                                                 | Replacement                                              | Note                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `datasource_ids`, `cluster`                           | `datasource_queries`                                     | `datasource_ids` is back-filled on read for the list page; the engine reads only `datasource_queries`                     |
| `notify_channels`, `notify_groups`, `callbacks`       | `notify_rule_ids`                                        | The three-layer notification model. A rule on `notify_version: 1` does not use them                                       |
| `enable_stime`, `enable_etime`, `enable_days_of_week` | `enable_stimes`, `enable_etimes`, `enable_days_of_weeks` | The singular forms held one effective window; the plural forms hold several                                               |
| `prom_for_duration`                                   | Marked *use cron pattern instead*                        | **Still the only implementation of the for-duration**, and still read at every evaluation. Do not strip it from rule JSON |

Anything that reads or writes alert rule JSON — an exporter, a provisioning script, a sync job — should move to the replacements, and must keep `prom_for_duration` regardless.

## Subscription rule fields cleared by the new notification version[​](#subscription-rule-fields-cleared-by-the-new-notification-version "Direct link to Subscription rule fields cleared by the new notification version")

Saving a subscription rule with `notify_version: 1` clears these fields to empty on the server, with no error and no warning:

* the authorised teams (`user_group_ids`);
* the redefined channels (`redefine_channels`, `new_channels`);
* the redefined webhooks (`redefine_webhooks`, `webhooks`);
* the redefined severity (`redefine_severity`, `new_severity`).

This is intended, not a bug: on the new model those decisions belong to the notification rules the subscription selects, not to the subscription. See [Alert subscriptions](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/subscriptions.md). If you create subscriptions from a script, sending those fields alongside `notify_version: 1` silently drops them.

## Code that is still there but no longer on any path[​](#code-that-is-still-there-but-no-longer-on-any-path "Direct link to Code that is still there but no longer on any path")

Two things you may find by reading the source or watching a network trace. Both still respond; build on neither.

* **`POST /api/n9e/busi-group/alert-rules/notify-tryrun` and `.../enable-tryrun`.** The frontend still defines a wrapper for each, and its only call sites for them are commented out. Their job is done by [test fire](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/test-fire.md), which walks query → threshold → event → notification in one pass instead of two partial checks.
* **The v7-era senders in `alert/sender/`** (DingTalk, WeCom, Feishu, Lark, Telegram, Mattermost, email). They are still compiled in and still wired up, but only the legacy path reaches them: an event from a rule on `notify_version: 0` carrying `notify_channels` and `notify_groups`. Notification rules take an entirely different route, through the media types configured under **Alerts & Notifications → Media types**. Editing a template on the old path does not change what notification rules send.

## Related[​](#related "Direct link to Related")

* [Release notes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/help/release-notes.md) — upgrade impact per version
* [v8 to v9](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/v8-to-v9.md) — where most of these replacements arrived
* [Compatibility matrix](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/compatibility.md) — the other page with no official promise behind it

# Release notes

Curated notes per release with upgrade impact, in addition to the GitHub changelog.

Last reviewed 2026-10-15

This page does not mirror the changelog — the full per-commit list lives on GitHub and is updated faster than this page could be. It answers one question instead: **if I move to this version, what do I have to change?**

Curated through **[v9.2.0 (2026-10-11)](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/releases/tag/v9.2.0)**. For later releases, see the full changes on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/releases).

## Where the authoritative record is[​](#where-the-authoritative-record-is "Direct link to Where the authoritative record is")

| What you want                       | Where                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The full set of changes per release | [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/releases)                                                                                                        |
| Every commit between two versions   | The **Full Changelog** link at the bottom of each release                                                                                                               |
| Schema changes per version          | [`docker/migratesql/migrate.sql`](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/blob/main/docker/migratesql/migrate.sql) in the repository, sectioned by `/* vX.Y.Z */` comments |
| Why a change was made               | The PR number in the release notes — open it and read the discussion                                                                                                    |

## How the product tells you a new version exists[​](#how-the-product-tells-you-a-new-version-exists "Direct link to How the product tells you a new version exists")

On startup Nightingale checks GitHub for the latest tag and compares it with its own. In the **open-source edition** the page header shows the running version; when there is an update it carries a red dot, and hovering says *New version available vX.Y.Z*, linking to GitHub Releases.

**System → About** lists the **frontend version** and the **backend version** separately. They should match; when they do not, usually only half the upgrade landed, or the browser is holding cached frontend assets — hard-refresh once.

## Upgrade impact of the v9 releases[​](#upgrade-impact-of-the-v9-releases "Direct link to Upgrade impact of the v9 releases")

**Only the things you have to act on.** Feature improvements are not here; they are in the GitHub release notes.

| Version    | Date       | What to handle before upgrading                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **v9.2.0** | 2026-10-11 | Replace both the binary and the `integrations` directory; also replace `etc/metrics.yaml` if you need metric descriptions in the added languages. Check database permissions for this release's schema changes. Keeping an old config does not enable the embedded TSDB. See the checklist below                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **v9.1.1** | 2026-08-18 | Nothing. A pure fix release: replace the binary and restart                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **v9.1.0** | 2026-08-06 | 1. **Evaluation records are on by default** — the alerting engine writes to its local `./evallog`, retained 8 days and capped at 20 GB, so leave disk headroom or turn it off under `[Alert.EvalLog]`. 2. **The embedded TSDB is not switched on for you**: `[EmbeddedTSDB]` exists only in the new `etc/config.toml`, so carrying an old config over leaves it off. 3. Two `notification_record` indexes are created online after startup, which takes a while on a large table |
| **v9.0.0** | 2026-07-25 | 1. **Redis 5.0 or later is required** (the AI assistant relies on Redis Streams); 7.0+ is recommended on Cluster. 2. telegraf users must append `ignore_host=false` to the write URL, or those machines stop appearing in the host list. 3. `n9e-edge` and `n9e-pushgw` must be upgraded in the same pass                                                                                                                                                                        |

Headline features per release, one line each — details on GitHub:

* **v9.0.0**: Nightingale AI (assistant, skills marketplace, LLM configs); **test fire** on alert rules; **mute notifications only** on mute rules; a built-in `/mcp` endpoint; navigation, layout and tables redesigned; the alert rule / mute / subscription / notification rule forms rebuilt.
* **v9.1.0**: the embedded TSDB; one-click data source import from Grafana; per-cycle evaluation records; testable media types and previewable message templates; mock events in workflow try runs; a much larger library of built-in alert rule templates.
* **v9.1.1**: list pages keep the current page in the URL; the log viewer renders through a virtual list; a batch of fixes.
* **v9.2.0**: native Jira, Discord, JSM Alert, Slack and Mattermost channels; mixed-datasource dashboard queries, time-limited anonymous sharing and Grafana import reports; reversible account disabling; AI script tasks through ibex; more languages and fixes including multi-instance login loops.

### v9.2.0 upgrade checklist[​](#v920-upgrade-checklist "Direct link to v9.2.0 upgrade checklist")

1. **Back up the metadata database and config, then check schema-change permissions.** This release adds `source_token.note`, the `idx_source_token_token` index on `source_token.token`, and `users.disabled`. Nightingale migrates them at startup when its database account has the required DDL permissions. Otherwise, have a DBA apply the missing changes using the [MySQL or PostgreSQL SQL in the v9.2.0 release notes](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/releases/tag/v9.2.0). Expected result: startup migration reports no permission or schema errors.
2. **Update the files together.** Replace the binary and the `integrations` directory. Also replace `etc/metrics.yaml` if you need metric descriptions in the added languages. Preserve your connection settings and restart; upgrade `n9e-edge` / `n9e-pushgw` in the same pass if you run them. Expected result: the processes start normally and the new integration templates are available.
3. **Choose metric storage for your deployment.** To enable the embedded TSDB, merge the `[EmbeddedTSDB]` section from the [v9.2.0 config](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/blob/v9.2.0/etc/config.toml) into your old config; replacing the binary alone does not enable it. It suits small, single-Center deployments only. Multi-Center deployments should keep an external TSDB. Expected result: existing data source queries, dashboards and alert rules still return data.

When upgrading from v8, also follow [v8 to v9](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/v8-to-v9.md) for Redis requirements, telegraf write parameters, verification and rollback preparation.

## Three sections to read in any release note[​](#three-sections-to-read-in-any-release-note "Direct link to Three sections to read in any release note")

Every GitHub release follows the same shape. Before upgrading, read at least these three:

1. **Upgrade note ⚠️ / Notes** — the only place that says "you must do this first", such as the Redis version requirement or a config section you have to add by hand. **Skipping this section is the number one cause of a bad upgrade.**
2. **Schema changes** — how the tables change. Check that the database account can create and alter tables and add indexes, so Nightingale can migrate at startup. Otherwise, give the DBA the changes for the versions you need; do not rerun the entire cumulative migration file.
3. The `fix:` entries under **What's Changed** — to find out whether the bug you have been living with is gone.

## Reading the version number[​](#reading-the-version-number "Direct link to Reading the version number")

`vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, plus `-beta.N` pre-release tags.

* **PATCH** (v9.1.0 → v9.1.1): bug fixes only; usually replace the binary and restart.
* **MINOR** (v9.0.0 → v9.1.0): new features, possibly with changed defaults — v9.1.0 is exactly that case, so read the upgrade note.
* **MAJOR** (v8 → v9): environment requirements change and the UI is reorganised; follow the [migration page](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/v8-to-v9.md).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* How to upgrade: [v8 to v9](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/v8-to-v9.md)
* What has been deprecated: [Deprecations and EOL policy](https://n9e.github.io/docs/help/deprecations.md)

# Binary packages

Download the Linux amd64 / arm64 tarball from GitHub releases, verify the checksum, point it at your MySQL and Redis, and run n9e under systemd.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

By the end of this page you have an `n9e` process managed by systemd, talking to your own MySQL and Redis, listening on 17000.

## Download and verify[​](#download-and-verify "Direct link to Download and verify")

Releases carry two Linux builds, amd64 and arm64. There is no Windows or macOS package — Nightingale is a server-side program. (If you really need one, the `Makefile` in the repository shows how to build it.)

```
VERSION=9.1.1

curl -LO https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/releases/download/v${VERSION}/n9e-v${VERSION}-linux-amd64.tar.gz

curl -LO https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt

sha256sum -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing
```

**Expected result**: `n9e-v9.1.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz: OK`.

The archive has **no top-level directory**, so create one before extracting or the files scatter into the current directory:

```
mkdir -p /opt/n9e && tar zxf n9e-v${VERSION}-linux-amd64.tar.gz -C /opt/n9e
```

## What is in the package[​](#what-is-in-the-package "Direct link to What is in the package")

| Path               | What it is                                                                   |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `n9e`              | The Center process, the only binary you have to have                         |
| `n9e-edge`         | Local alerting engine for edge data centers                                  |
| `n9e-cli`          | One-shot v5 → v6 data migration tool; not an operations CLI                  |
| `etc/`             | Configuration directory, required by the process                             |
| `integrations/`    | Integration templates (dashboards, alert rules, collector configs), required |
| `agents/categraf/` | Bundled categraf packages, served by the "install collector" page            |
| `docker/`          | Compose bundles and schema SQL                                               |
| `n9e.sql`          | A copy of `docker/initsql/a-n9e.sql`, the MySQL bootstrap script             |

The `n9e` process only needs `etc/` and `integrations/` next to the binary; everything else can go.

`n9e-alert` and `n9e-pushgw` are **not** in the release. The `Makefile` has `build-alert` and `build-pushgw` targets, but they are not part of the release build — splitting those out means building from source.

## Get it running[​](#get-it-running "Direct link to Get it running")

```
cd /opt/n9e && ./n9e
```

The defaults need nothing else installed: SQLite for metadata, an in-process miniredis, and the embedded TSDB for metrics. Open `http://<server>:17000` and sign in as `root` / `root.2020`.

**Expected result**: the log says `http server listening on: 0.0.0.0:17000` and the login works.

Those defaults are **not for production**. Keep going to replace them, or walk the [Production readiness checklist](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/production-checklist.md).

## Point it at an existing MySQL and Redis[​](#point-it-at-an-existing-mysql-and-redis "Direct link to Point it at an existing MySQL and Redis")

Create the database. You do not have to import a schema — `n9e` runs AutoMigrate on every start, so an empty database plus an account that may create and alter tables is enough:

```
CREATE DATABASE n9e_v6 DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8mb4;
```

The database is conventionally called `n9e_v6`; the name has been carried since v6 and the bundled schema scripts still use it.

Then edit `etc/config.toml`:

```
[DB]

DBType = "mysql"

DSN = "n9e:<password>@tcp(mysql:3306)/n9e_v6?charset=utf8mb4&parseTime=True&loc=Local"



[Redis]

RedisType = "standalone"

Address = "redis:6379"
```

**Expected result** after a restart: no `failed to migrate table` in the log, and the login is still `root` / `root.2020` — that row is written into the new database on first start. For the choice itself and the permissions involved, see [Choosing a metadata database](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/databases.md).

## Run it under systemd[​](#run-it-under-systemd "Direct link to Run it under systemd")

```
[Unit]

Description=Nightingale

After=network-online.target

Wants=network-online.target



[Service]

Type=simple

User=n9e

WorkingDirectory=/opt/n9e

ExecStart=/opt/n9e/n9e

Restart=always

RestartSec=5

LimitNOFILE=65536



[Install]

WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Save it as `/etc/systemd/system/n9e.service`. `WorkingDirectory` has to be the directory you extracted into: `etc/`, `integrations/`, `data/tsdb` and `logs/` are all resolved relative to it.

```
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

sudo systemctl enable --now n9e

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:17000/ping
```

**Expected result**: `/ping` returns `pong`.

## Edge data centers[​](#edge-data-centers "Direct link to Edge data centers")

`n9e-edge`, from the same package, runs at an edge site. It must be started with a **config directory**, not a config file:

```
./n9e-edge --configs etc/edge
```

Passing `--configs etc` makes it load the central `config.toml` instead, and it does not complain. See [Edge data centers](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/edge.md).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Choosing a metadata database](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/databases.md) — MySQL or PostgreSQL, and what Redis is for
* [Configuration layout](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/configuration.md) — what each section of `etc/` does
* [High availability](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/high-availability.md) — running more than one instance

# Configuration layout

Configuration is a directory: config.toml is read by n9e, alert and pushgw, etc/edge by n9e-edge; environment variables fill in blanks but never override set keys.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Nightingale is configured by a **directory**, not a file. Knowing how that directory is loaded, and when environment variables actually apply, removes a whole class of "I changed the config and nothing happened".

## Where the config directory is[​](#where-the-config-directory-is "Direct link to Where the config directory is")

By default, `etc/` next to the binary:

```
etc/

├── config.toml        # read by n9e / n9e-alert / n9e-pushgw

├── metrics.yaml       # built-in metric descriptions, pointed at by [Center] MetricsYamlFile

├── edge/

│   └── edge.toml      # read by n9e-edge

└── script/            # example notification scripts
```

Point somewhere else with `--configs`, or the matching environment variable:

```
./n9e --configs /etc/n9e

N9E_CONFIGS=/etc/n9e ./n9e
```

| Process      | Flag default | Environment variable |
| ------------ | ------------ | -------------------- |
| `n9e`        | `etc`        | `N9E_CONFIGS`        |
| `n9e-edge`   | `etc`        | `N9E_EDGE_CONFIGS`   |
| `n9e-alert`  | `etc`        | `N9E_ALERT_CONFIGS`  |
| `n9e-pushgw` | `etc`        | `N9E_PUSHGW_CONFIGS` |

`n9e-edge` also defaults to `etc`, and `etc` holds the **central** `config.toml` — so an edge process must always be started with `--configs etc/edge`. Pointing at the file (`--configs etc/edge/edge.toml`) is equally wrong: the flag takes a directory.

## How the directory is loaded[​](#how-the-directory-is-loaded "Direct link to How the directory is loaded")

The process concatenates **every** `.toml` file in the directory, in filename order, and parses the result as one document; `.json` and `.yaml` files are read too. Two consequences:

* to keep credentials out of the main file, just drop them in `etc/secret.toml` — nothing else needs changing;
* a backup named `config.toml.bak` is harmless (the suffix is not `.toml`), but one named `config.bak.toml` is merged in as real configuration.

`etc/edge/` is a subdirectory and is never picked up by the central process — the scan does not recurse.

## Environment variables fill gaps, they do not override[​](#environment-variables-fill-gaps-they-do-not-override "Direct link to Environment variables fill gaps, they do not override")

Config keys can be supplied through the environment, named `CONFIGTYPE_<SECTION>_<KEY>` in upper case:

```
CONFIGTYPE_HTTP_PORT=17001

CONFIGTYPE_DB_DSN="n9e:<password>@tcp(mysql:3306)/n9e_v6?parseTime=True"

CONFIGTYPE_REDIS_ADDRESS=redis:6379
```

The file wins over the environment

Loading order is defaults → environment → config file, and **each stage overrides the last**. A key present in `config.toml` therefore ignores its environment variable completely. The shipped `config.toml` sets nearly every key explicitly, which means **environment overrides are inert by default** until you comment the corresponding line out.

The quickest way to tell whether a variable took effect is to comment the line out of the file, restart, and read the value back from the log.

Two other groups are unaffected because they never reach the config loader: the `N9E_*_CONFIGS` variables above, and `WAIT_HOSTS` / `WAIT_TIMEOUT`, which make the process wait for dependency ports before starting and are how the compose bundles order themselves.

## What each section covers[​](#what-each-section-covers "Direct link to What each section covers")

| Section                                                    | Covers                                                                           | Read by              |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `[Global]`                                                 | Run mode                                                                         | All                  |
| `[Log]`                                                    | Log directory, level, rotation                                                   | All                  |
| `[HTTP]`                                                   | Listen address and port, TLS, timeouts, `/metrics`                               | All                  |
| `[HTTP.APIForAgent]`                                       | The collector-facing API (heartbeat, writes) and its auth                        | Center, Edge         |
| `[HTTP.APIForService]`                                     | The service-to-service API (edge callbacks, eval-record forwarding) and its auth | Center, Edge         |
| `[HTTP.JWTAuth]` / `[HTTP.ProxyAuth]` / `[HTTP.TokenAuth]` | The three authentication modes                                                   | Center               |
| `[DB]`                                                     | Metadata database                                                                | All                  |
| `[Redis]`                                                  | Redis                                                                            | All                  |
| `[Center]`                                                 | Metric description file, anonymous access, event history retention               | Center               |
| `[Alert]`                                                  | Engine heartbeat, engine cluster name, evaluation records                        | Center, Alert, Edge  |
| `[Pushgw]`                                                 | Ingestion and forwarding; `[[Pushgw.Writers]]` are external TSDB write URLs      | Center, Pushgw, Edge |
| `[EmbeddedTSDB]`                                           | The built-in time-series store                                                   | **Center only**      |
| `[Ibex]`                                                   | RPC listener for self-healing tasks                                              | Center, Edge         |
| `[CenterApi]`                                              | Central address and credentials (only in `edge.toml`)                            | Edge                 |

Defaults and notes for every key are in the [Configuration reference](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/configuration.md).

## Keep passwords out of plain text[​](#keep-passwords-out-of-plain-text "Direct link to Keep passwords out of plain text")

`[DB] DSN`, `[Redis] Password`, the BasicAuth passwords, `[[Pushgw.Writers]] BasicAuthPass` and `[EmbeddedTSDB] BasicAuthPass` all accept ciphertext: write the value as `{{cipher}}<ciphertext>` and supply the key at startup with `--crypto-key`.

```
./n9e --crypto-key '<your-key>'
```

Values without the `{{cipher}}` prefix are treated as plain text, so you can migrate them one at a time. For the full approach see [Secret management](https://n9e.github.io/docs/security/secrets.md).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Configuration reference](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/configuration.md) — every key and its default
* [Choosing a metadata database](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/databases.md)

# MySQL / PostgreSQL / SQLite and Redis

The metadata store is MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQLite (testing only); the process creates the schema on first start, and Redis holds runtime state such as heartbeats.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Nightingale connects to two stores: a **metadata database** (users, business groups, alert rules, dashboards, notification config) and **Redis**. Metrics are not in either — those belong to the [time-series store](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/storage.md).

## Which one[​](#which-one "Direct link to Which one")

|                | Use it when                                             | Cost                                                                                   |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| SQLite         | Trying it alone, writing docs, CI                       | No second copy, no sharing between instances, and two processes on one file corrupt it |
| MySQL 8        | The default choice, and what most of the community runs | You provide the high availability                                                      |
| PostgreSQL 12+ | Your team already runs PG                               | Same, and a few tables use different column types under PG                             |

MySQL and PostgreSQL are both first-class in production; pick the one your team can operate. **SQLite is for testing** — that is its purpose, not a tuning problem.

## MySQL[​](#mysql "Direct link to MySQL")

```
[DB]

DBType = "mysql"

DSN = "n9e:<password>@tcp(mysql:3306)/n9e_v6?charset=utf8mb4&parseTime=True&loc=Local"

MaxOpenConns = 150

MaxIdleConns = 50
```

`parseTime=True` is not optional. Use `utf8mb4`, or emoji in notification templates fail to write.

The database is conventionally called `n9e_v6`; the name has been carried since v6 and the bundled schema scripts still use it. Another name works fine — change the DSN.

## PostgreSQL[​](#postgresql "Direct link to PostgreSQL")

```
[DB]

DBType = "postgres"

DSN = "host=postgres port=5432 user=n9e dbname=n9e_v6 password=<password> sslmode=disable"
```

The DSN is key=value form, not a URL. In production set `sslmode` to `require` or stricter.

## SQLite[​](#sqlite "Direct link to SQLite")

The default, with nothing to configure:

```
[DB]

DBType = "sqlite"

DSN = "n9e.db"
```

The file lands next to the binary. To reset it, delete `n9e.db`, `n9e.db-wal` and `n9e.db-shm` **together** — removing only the main file leaves a fresh database paired with a stale WAL.

## Where the schema comes from[​](#where-the-schema-comes-from "Direct link to Where the schema comes from")

`n9e` **runs AutoMigrate on every start**: it creates missing tables and adds missing columns and indexes. Bootstrapping therefore needs only an empty database and an account that may create and alter tables.

The SQL files in the repository are conveniences for specific situations, and **none of them is a complete schema**:

| File                                            | Purpose                                                                               | Caveat                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `docker/initsql/a-n9e.sql`                      | Creates the MySQL database and tables; run by compose on first start                  | Missing `notify_channel_config`, `ai_llm_config` and others — AutoMigrate fills them in |
| `docker/compose-postgres/initsql_for_postgres/` | The PostgreSQL equivalent                                                             | Same                                                                                    |
| `docker/migratesql/migrate.sql`                 | Cumulative DDL deltas, for people who bootstrapped from SQL and want to align by hand | Not a required upgrade step                                                             |
| `docker/sqlite.sql`                             | An early SQLite schema                                                                | **Stale** — none of the v9 tables are in it; SQLite relies on AutoMigrate               |

A failed migration is logged and does not stop startup, so after an upgrade search the log for `failed to migrate table`. The two large tables, `alert_his_event` and `alert_cur_event`, migrate asynchronously; building indexes on a large one can take tens of minutes.

## What Redis is for[​](#what-redis-is-for "Direct link to What Redis is for")

Redis is not an optional cache layer, it is required:

* **Login sessions** — JWT issuing and revocation, under `[HTTP.JWTAuth] RedisKeyPrefix` (`/jwt/` by default);
* **Host metadata** — CPU, memory and OS reported by heartbeats, written to Redis in batches every second; the host list reads from there;
* **Captchas**, when `[HTTP.ShowCaptcha]` is on;
* **AI conversation state and locks**, plus the pub/sub channel that cancels a conversation across instances.

```
[Redis]

RedisType = "standalone"

Address = "redis:6379"

# Password = ""

# DB = 0
```

`RedisType` accepts `standalone`, `cluster`, `sentinel` and `miniredis`. The default `miniredis` is a **fake Redis running inside the Nightingale process** — its data goes when the process does, so it is for testing only. For `cluster` and `sentinel`, put several comma-separated addresses in `Address`.

**`n9e-edge` cannot reuse the central Redis.** Deploy a separate one at the edge site, otherwise the edge dies with the link it was supposed to survive.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Binary packages](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/binary.md) — starting the process after the config change
* [Configuration layout](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/configuration.md) — keeping passwords out of plain text
* [High availability](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/high-availability.md) — several instances on one MySQL and one Redis

# Docker Compose

Bring up Nightingale with its database and time-series store in one command; what the bundle contains and how to change it.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

The repository ships four ready-made bundles under `docker/`. One `docker compose up -d` gives you Nightingale plus a database, a time-series store and a collector, with nothing to prepare first.

## Four bundles, pick one[​](#four-bundles-pick-one "Direct link to Four bundles, pick one")

```
git clone https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale.git

cd nightingale/docker
```

| Directory                         | Metadata database | Time-series store                             | Networking                          |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `compose-bridge`                  | MySQL 8           | VictoriaMetrics                               | bridge, ports published to the host |
| `compose-postgres`                | PostgreSQL 12     | VictoriaMetrics                               | bridge                              |
| `compose-host-network`            | MySQL 8           | Prometheus                                    | `network_mode: host`                |
| `compose-host-network-metric-log` | MySQL 8           | Prometheus + Kafka / Elasticsearch / Logstash | `network_mode: host`                |

The two host-network bundles are Linux only

`network_mode: host` is a Linux capability. On Docker Desktop (macOS / Windows) containers do not really share the host network stack, and these two will not come up. Use `compose-bridge` to evaluate on a Mac.

When in doubt, use `compose-bridge`.

## Bring it up[​](#bring-it-up "Direct link to Bring it up")

```
cd compose-bridge

docker compose up -d
```

**Expected result**: `docker compose ps` shows five containers running, and `http://localhost:17000` accepts `root` / `root.2020`.

The `nightingale` container carries `WAIT_HOSTS: mysql:3306, redis:6379`, so the process waits for those ports before starting and you do not have to care about container ordering.

## What the bundle contains[​](#what-the-bundle-contains "Direct link to What the bundle contains")

`compose-bridge` runs five containers and publishes four ports:

| Container         | Ports         | What it does                                                         |
| ----------------- | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `mysql`           | 3306          | Metadata database; `docker/initsql/` creates `n9e_v6` on first start |
| `redis`           | 6379          | Sessions and heartbeat caches                                        |
| `victoriametrics` | 8428          | Time-series store                                                    |
| `nightingale`     | 17000 / 20090 | Web, API and write endpoints / ibex RPC for self-healing             |
| `categraf`        | —             | Collects host metrics and writes back to `nightingale:17000`         |

3306 and 6379 are published straight to the host, so they **collide with a MySQL or Redis you already run there**. Change `ports`, or stop the local service.

## Changing the configuration[​](#changing-the-configuration "Direct link to Changing the configuration")

Nightingale's config directory is mounted in, not baked into the image:

```
volumes:

  - ./etc-nightingale:/app/etc
```

Edit `compose-bridge/etc-nightingale/config.toml`, then `docker compose restart nightingale`. This file differs from the binary package's default in a few places, all of them to fit container networking:

```
[DB]

DBType = "mysql"

DSN="root:1234@tcp(mysql:3306)/n9e_v6?charset=utf8mb4&collation=utf8mb4_general_ci&parseTime=True&loc=Local&allowNativePasswords=true"



[Redis]

RedisType = "standalone"

Address = "redis:6379"



[[Pushgw.Writers]]

Url = "http://victoriametrics:8428/api/v1/write"
```

Note there is **no `[EmbeddedTSDB]` section**: the bundle already has a real time-series store, so metrics go straight to VictoriaMetrics. The addresses are compose service names — replace them with real hostnames when you point outside the bundle.

The `root:1234` database credentials sit in both the compose file and the config file. Change them before this becomes production.

## Switching to PostgreSQL[​](#switching-to-postgresql "Direct link to Switching to PostgreSQL")

`compose-postgres` is the same bundle with a different metadata database:

```
[DB]

DBType = "postgres"

DSN="host=postgres port=5432 user=root dbname=n9e_v6 password=1234 sslmode=disable"
```

It publishes 5432 instead of 3306. For the trade-off between the two, see [Choosing a metadata database](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/databases.md).

## Using your own database and TSDB[​](#using-your-own-database-and-tsdb "Direct link to Using your own database and TSDB")

The MySQL, Redis and VictoriaMetrics services exist so that one command produces a working system. If you already run them, delete those services from `docker-compose.yaml` and put the real addresses into `etc-nightingale/config.toml` — the `nightingale` container does not care whether its dependencies are part of the bundle.

Update `WAIT_HOSTS` at the same time, or the process waits forever on a service name that no longer resolves.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Choosing a metadata database](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/databases.md)
* [External TSDB and dual-write migration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/external-tsdb.md)
* [Production readiness checklist](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/production-checklist.md)

# Edge data centers

A local alerting engine for sites whose link to the center is unreliable, and the one flag that silently breaks it.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where the network to the central site is unreliable, run `n9e-edge` as a local alerting engine so alerts keep firing and keep being delivered through a partition:

```
n9e-edge --configs etc/edge
```

Point it at the edge config directory

`--configs` defaults to `etc`, which holds the **central** `config.toml`. The edge process has its own config at `etc/edge/edge.toml` — passing `etc` instead makes it load the wrong file, and the resulting misrouting is silent. Edge also needs its own Redis; it cannot share the one at the center.

# Embedded TSDB for onboarding and small scale

Use the built-in store to get going with zero extra components; retention, capacity and the single-Center constraint.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

The embedded time-series store is **on by default**, so charts and alert rules work straight after install with nothing else configured. This page is about tuning its retention and capacity, and about where it stops being the right answer.

## It is already running[​](#it-is-already-running "Direct link to It is already running")

```
[EmbeddedTSDB]

Enable = true

Dir = "data/tsdb"

RetentionDuration = "15d"

MaxBytes = "10GiB"
```

At startup it does two things: creates `data/tsdb` under the working directory, and **auto-registers a Prometheus-type data source named `embedded-tsdb`**.

Pick that data source under **Explorer → Metrics**, query `up`, and getting points back confirms the write path works. Metrics that Categraf remote-writes land here with no forwarding to configure.

## Retention and capacity[​](#retention-and-capacity "Direct link to Retention and capacity")

```
[EmbeddedTSDB]

RetentionDuration = "30d"   # forms like 12h / 7d / 15d

MaxBytes = "50GiB"          # empty or 0 means unlimited
```

The two limits are an **or**: samples past the retention window are deleted, and so are the oldest blocks once disk usage passes `MaxBytes`. A `MaxBytes` that is too small therefore shortens the effective retention below `RetentionDuration`, silently.

Set `MaxBytes` to something the disk can absorb, then watch how large `data/tsdb` actually grows. That beats trying to compute a series count up front.

Two others you may occasionally touch:

* `OutOfOrderTimeWindow` (`10m`) — tolerance for collector clock skew and resends; samples outside the window are dropped;
* `QueryMaxSamples` and `QueryTimeout` — read-side limits, worth raising only when dashboards span very long ranges.

Restart `n9e` for changes to take effect.

## By default it only accepts local requests[​](#by-default-it-only-accepts-local-requests "Direct link to By default it only accepts local requests")

The `/prometheus/api/v1/*` endpoints — both query and remote write — **only accept requests from the local machine** by default, which is why the auto-registered data source points at `http://127.0.0.1:17000/prometheus`.

To let Grafana, `n9e-edge` or another agent read from or write to it directly, configure credentials:

```
[EmbeddedTSDB]

BasicAuthUser = "n9e"

BasicAuthPass = "<password>"
```

Setting them lifts the local-only restriction, and the auto-registered data source URL switches from `127.0.0.1` to the detected host IP. If there is a VIP or a domain in front, name it with `DatasourceUrl` — setting that lifts the restriction as well.

## When to stop using it[​](#when-to-stop-using-it "Direct link to When to stop using it")

Three hard boundaries; hitting any one of them means moving to an external store:

1. **The data lives on the local disk of one Center process.** With several instances each holds a fragment and query results go silently incomplete — so **high availability means turning it off**.
2. **Only the Center process handles this section.** `n9e-edge`, `n9e-alert` and `n9e-pushgw` read the same `etc` directory but ignore `[EmbeddedTSDB]`, and say so at startup.
3. **It suits roughly 100k active series or fewer.** Past that, query latency and memory use become noticeable.

One more thing that is not a limit but is worth knowing: this data has no replica. If the machine dies it is gone, and whether that matters depends on whether you still rely on that history.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [External TSDB and dual-write migration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/external-tsdb.md) — moving without downtime
* [Auto-registered Embedded TSDB datasource](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/embedded-tsdb.md) — using it from the UI
* [Embedded TSDB and external storage](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/storage.md) — which data lives where
