# Upgrade and database migration

How schema migrations run on startup, and how to upgrade a multi-instance deployment in order.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

The commands for replacing a binary are in [Upgrade](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/upgrade.md). This page is the runtime half: **what the process does to your schema when it boots, and what a multi-instance deployment looks like from the moment the first instance goes down until the last one is back**.

## Migration runs inside the process, at startup[​](#migration-runs-inside-the-process-at-startup "Direct link to Migration runs inside the process, at startup")

There is no migration command and no migration state table. Right after `n9e` connects to the metadata database — before Redis, before the caches, before the HTTP listener — it runs GORM's AutoMigrate over the model list compiled into the binary. Everything the new version needs appears then, or not at all.

Two properties follow from that, and both matter:

* **It is additive.** Missing tables, columns and indexes are created; nothing is ever dropped, and nothing is recorded about what the schema looked like before. That is why there is no reverse migration — see [Rollback](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/rollback.md).
* **The models are the schema, not the SQL files.** `docker/sqlite.sql` and `docker/initsql/a-n9e.sql` are fresh-install artefacts and lag behind: `sqlite.sql` contains no `notify_rule`, `notify_channel_config`, `message_template`, `event_pipeline` or `ai_llm_config` table at all. Those tables exist in a running v9 **only because AutoMigrate created them**. Never diff your live schema against those files to decide whether an upgrade landed.

Startup order, in the order things can fail:

| Step                                                         | If it fails                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| Connect to the metadata database                             | **The process exits**                 |
| Run the schema migration                                     | Logged, and startup continues         |
| Create the root user and the JWT signing key                 | Logged, and startup continues         |
| Connect to Redis                                             | **The process exits**                 |
| Load config into in-memory caches, start the alerting engine | Rules do not evaluate                 |
| Listen on 17000                                              | The port is in use; the process exits |

## Two phases: small tables block startup, big ones do not[​](#two-phases-small-tables-block-startup-big-ones-do-not "Direct link to Two phases: small tables block startup, big ones do not")

| Phase                  | Covers                                                                                | Blocks startup |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| Synchronous            | Every table except the event tables — rules, users, data sources, notification config | Yes            |
| Asynchronous goroutine | `alert_cur_event`, `alert_his_event`, and three indexes                               | No             |

The asynchronous phase also builds three indexes, on the two tables that grow without bound — and they are **not built the same way**:

* the two on `notification_record` are issued deliberately non-blocking: `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` on MySQL, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on PostgreSQL. Where MySQL cannot do it online it fails loudly rather than degrading into a write-blocking DDL;
* `idx_group_last_eval_time` on `alert_his_event` is a **plain `CREATE INDEX`** with no such clause. On PostgreSQL that holds a share lock on the table for the whole build, which blocks inserts into it — and `alert_his_event` is usually the largest table you have. On a big PostgreSQL deployment, expect historical events to stall while it builds.

Which means the process answers `/ping`, serves the UI and evaluates rules **while the largest table in your database is still being altered**. On a multi-gigabyte `alert_his_event` that runs for tens of minutes. Do not restart to unstick it: a restart begins the same work again.

One expected warning: if `notification_record` does not yet have a `notify_rule_id` column, the index that needs it is skipped with *will retry on next start*, and the other one is created anyway. Leave it alone.

## A failed migration does not stop the process[​](#a-failed-migration-does-not-stop-the-process "Direct link to A failed migration does not stop the process")

Every migration error is written to the log and swallowed; a panic inside migration is recovered. The design is deliberate — another instance or the next restart repairs the schema — but the consequence is easy to miss: **an instance can be up, serving traffic and heartbeating while a column it needs is missing.** You will not see a startup failure. You will see one feature failing at runtime with an `Unknown column` error, days later.

So the check after an upgrade is a log grep, not a health check:

```
grep -iE "failed to migrate table|failed to create index" /opt/n9e/logs/*.log
```

**Expected result**: no output. Anything there is almost always a permissions problem — the account in `[DB] DSN` may read and write but not `CREATE` or `ALTER`. Fix the grant and restart, or hand the matching version sections of `docker/migratesql/migrate.sql` to your DBA, as described in [v8 to v9](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/v8-to-v9.md).

## Let one instance migrate, then roll the rest[​](#let-one-instance-migrate-then-roll-the-rest "Direct link to Let one instance migrate, then roll the rest")

The migration code carries explicit guards against two things that only happen when several instances start at once, which tells you they are real:

* two instances issuing `ALTER` on the same table concurrently can make the MySQL driver's column-type lookup dereference a nil type. The panic is recovered, but that migration entry point is abandoned for that start;
* a duplicated `CREATE INDEX` on a large `alert_his_event` blocks on the metadata lock and hangs startup — not for seconds, indefinitely.

Neither corrupts data, and both cost you a start you then have to diagnose. The ordering that avoids both:

1. Stop **one** instance, replace its binary, start it. It owns the migration.
2. Wait for its log to go quiet: no `failed to migrate`, and no index work still running.
3. Only then take the next instance, and one at a time from there.

![The alerting engines page](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/operations/alerting-engines.webp)![The alerting engines page](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/operations/alerting-engines.dark.webp)

[Upgrade](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/upgrade.md) already asks you to roll one at a time so that alerting never stops. The migration race is a **second, independent reason** for the same rule — and the reason the first instance deserves a pause before you touch the second, rather than a fixed interval.

## What the upgrade window actually costs[​](#what-the-upgrade-window-actually-costs "Direct link to What the upgrade window actually costs")

Per instance, from `systemctl stop` to steady state:

| Function                                   | During that instance's restart                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Rule evaluation                            | Its rules move to a surviving instance within 30 seconds, then keep running                                                                        |
| Rule evaluation, on the restarted instance | Nothing for a further 30 seconds after start (`[Alert] EngineDelay`)                                                                               |
| Metric ingestion                           | Whatever writes to that instance's `/prometheus/v1/write` fails; put a load balancer in front, or accept the gap                                   |
| UI and API                                 | Unavailable on that instance only                                                                                                                  |
| Notifications                              | Follow evaluation — the owning instance sends them                                                                                                 |
| Embedded TSDB                              | Its data is unreadable and unwritable for the whole restart, and it must not be on in a cluster anyway                                             |
| Edge sites                                 | `n9e-edge` keeps evaluating and notifying locally — see [Edge network partition behavior](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/edge-partition.md) |

Restarting every instance together turns the first row into "nothing is evaluated for as long as the upgrade takes", which is the whole reason for rolling.

## Related[​](#related "Direct link to Related")

* [Upgrade](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/upgrade.md) — the commands
* [v8 to v9](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/v8-to-v9.md) — the cross-major breaking points
* [High availability and failure domains](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/high-availability.md) — how rules move between instances
* [Rollback and recovery](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/rollback.md) — when it goes wrong
* [Why does an upgrade or database migration fail?](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/upgrade-fails.md) — when the log has something in it

# Custom collector scripts

Run a script with the Categraf exec input, emit Prometheus metrics, and verify permissions, timeouts and service execution.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, a script will emit custom samples that Categraf sends to Nightingale's TSDB. The example uses **Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9**. The executable may be Shell, Python or a compiled program.

## Write the script[​](#script "Direct link to Write the script")

Create `/opt/categraf/scripts/collect_demo.sh`:

```
#!/bin/sh

printf 'custom_check_success{check="demo"} 1\n'
```

```
chmod +x /opt/categraf/scripts/collect_demo.sh

/opt/categraf/scripts/collect_demo.sh
```

**Expected result**: stdout contains only the Prometheus metric line. Send diagnostics to stderr rather than mixing prose with samples. Resolve nonzero process-exit errors before diagnosing delivery.

## Configure the exec input[​](#configure "Direct link to Configure the exec input")

In `conf/input.exec/exec.toml`:

```
[[instances]]

commands = ["/opt/categraf/scripts/collect_demo.sh"]

timeout = 5

data_format = "prometheus"
```

The format must match stdout. The input also supports `influx` and `falcon`, but their formats are not interchangeable. Command paths support globs; check which scripts they match before enabling them. See the [exec input documentation](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/blob/v0.5.17/inputs/exec/README.md).

## Verify[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify")

```
./categraf --test --inputs exec
```

**Expected result**: `custom_check_success` with `check="demo"` and value 1, without parsing or timeout errors. Restart the existing service and query the metric in the destination store to confirm new samples continue arriving.

If foreground execution works but service execution fails, check the service account, permissions, working directory, PATH and environment. Use absolute paths and bounded execution times instead of relying on an interactive shell.

## Design meaningful metrics[​](#metric-design "Direct link to Design meaningful metrics")

The constant value 1 verifies the pipeline only. A real check should report its actual result, such as queue length or last-success time. Emit an explicit failure value. No output and a value of zero require different alert conditions.

Avoid random IDs, timestamps and full error messages as labels; they create unbounded series. Use Counter semantics for cumulative counts and Gauge semantics for current values. See [Prerequisites](https://n9e.github.io/docs/prologue/pre-knowledge.md).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Create your first alert](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/first-rule.md)
* [Connected datasource with no data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md)

# Monitor Java applications

Choose Actuator, Micrometer, JMX Exporter or built-in application metrics, then scrape them with Categraf or Prometheus.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, you will choose a suitable Java metrics endpoint and connect JVM or application metrics to Nightingale. Nightingale v9 does not scrape Java processes itself. Use **Categraf v0.5.17**, Prometheus or vmagent.

## Actuator[​](#actuator "Direct link to Actuator")

For a Spring Boot application, prefer Actuator. This example uses dependency management from **Spring Boot 3.5.x**:

```
<dependency>

  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>

</dependency>

<dependency>

  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>

  <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>

</dependency>
```

Let the application's Spring Boot BOM manage versions instead of mixing Micrometer release lines. Expose the endpoint in `application.properties`:

```
management.server.port=8081

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,prometheus
```

Allow the collector to access the management port. Adjust paths and credentials for Spring Security, proxies and custom application contexts.

```
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8081/actuator/prometheus
```

**Expected result**: Prometheus text with JVM metrics, not a login page, JSON error or 404. See the [Spring Boot 3.5 metrics documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/3.5/reference/actuator/metrics.html).

## Micrometer[​](#micrometer "Direct link to Micrometer")

Without Spring Boot, use `micrometer-registry-prometheus`, register application meters with a shared `PrometheusMeterRegistry`, and serve its `scrape()` output over HTTP.

Package names vary between Micrometer and Prometheus client versions. Follow the [official example](https://docs.micrometer.io/micrometer/reference/implementations/prometheus.html) for your dependencies instead of copying old imports.

A registry without an HTTP endpoint cannot be scraped. Adding a registry dependency without binding JVM meters does not create all JVM metrics automatically.

## JMX[​](#jmx "Direct link to JMX")

For an application you cannot modify but that exposes MBeans, use the JMX Exporter Java Agent. This HTTP-mode example uses **JMX Exporter 1.3.0**. Put the jar and `jmx.yaml` in the working directory:

```
rules:

  - pattern: ".*"
```

```
java -javaagent:./jmx_prometheus_javaagent-1.3.0.jar=9404:./jmx.yaml -jar ./app.jar

curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:9404/metrics
```

**Expected result**: port 9404 returns Prometheus metrics. The broad rule is for initial verification; narrow it to required MBeans and restrict endpoint access for production. Use the [1.3.0 documentation](https://prometheus.github.io/jmx_exporter/1.3.0/java-agent/http-mode/) for the package and options.

## Built-in component metrics[​](#component-metrics "Direct link to Built-in component metrics")

Reuse a component's existing Prometheus endpoint rather than adding a second JMX collection path. Some middleware and service frameworks already expose `/metrics`; verify the format and authentication first. Metric names and labels vary, so choose matching dashboards and rules.

## Connect and verify[​](#verify "Direct link to Connect and verify")

Add the actual endpoint to `conf/input.prometheus/prometheus.toml`. This example matches the Actuator configuration above:

```
[[instances]]

urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:8081/actuator/prometheus"]

url_label_key = "instance"

url_label_value = "{{.Host}}"
```

```
./categraf --test --inputs prometheus
```

**Expected result**: metrics such as `jvm_` without scraping or parsing errors. Restart collection and check that new samples arrive in Nightingale's destination store. If Prometheus or vmagent already scrapes the application, register its store as a datasource without adding another scrape path.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Prometheus datasource](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md)
* [Process monitoring](https://n9e.github.io/docs/practice/proc.md)

# Monitor Linux hosts

Collect Linux metrics with Categraf, distinguish heartbeat metadata from stored samples, and detect missing hosts.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, Linux host metrics will be queryable in Nightingale, and you will know why an online target and a populated dashboard are separate checks. The collector commands target **Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9**.

## Collect and connect[​](#collect "Direct link to Collect and connect")

Configure `writers` and `heartbeat` using [Install and register](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md). Host metrics come from inputs such as `cpu`, `mem`, `disk`, `diskio`, `net` and `system`, configured under `conf/input.<name>/`.

From the collector installation directory:

```
./categraf --test --inputs cpu:mem:disk
```

**Expected result**: the terminal prints the corresponding metrics without permission or configuration errors. This proves local collection only. Select the destination store in Nightingale's explorer and verify that new samples arrive.

## Online target, empty dashboard[​](#no-data "Direct link to Online target, empty dashboard")

Check the two paths separately:

| Path                                      | Purpose                                               |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `heartbeat` → `/v1/n9e/heartbeat`         | Target metadata and liveness                          |
| `writers` → `/prometheus/v1/write` → TSDB | Samples used by queries, dashboards and metric alerts |

Nightingale v9 **can use its embedded TSDB**. The old statement that it always forwards metrics without storing them is no longer generally correct. For external storage, also check the `Pushgw.Writers` destinations and the backend's receiver configuration.

Work through these checks:

1. Does `--test` produce samples? If not, fix collection first.
2. Does `writers` in `conf/config.toml` point to the intended Nightingale or Edge?
3. Do collector logs show authentication, connection or write failures?
4. Is the destination accepting data? Prometheus needs its Remote Write receiver enabled.
5. Is the query using the right source, and are clocks synchronized?
6. Are dashboard variables excluding the business group, `ident` or `instance`?

```
sudo journalctl -u categraf.service -n 100 --no-pager
```

**Expected result**: a direct query against the correct store returns samples. Resolve dashboard filtering after that. See [Connected datasource with no data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md) for detailed troubleshooting.

## Detect missing hosts[​](#missing-host "Direct link to Detect missing hosts")

Prometheus generates `up` when it actively scrapes a Node Exporter endpoint. Categraf pushes with Remote Write and **does not automatically generate that scrape-status metric**.

Use a **Host-type rule** in Nightingale for missing-target detection. Select the intended targets, tags or business groups and configure the missing duration. Stop and restart collection on one test host to verify triggering and recovery before applying the rule broadly.

**Expected result**: the test host produces an event after the configured duration and recovers when its heartbeat resumes. Independent Ping or port probes are also useful, but measure reachability or service response rather than collector health.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Targets and heartbeat](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/targets.md)
* [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)

# Monitor MySQL

Collect MySQL runtime metrics with Categraf and distinguish them from business-SQL alerts and Nightingale metadata storage.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, MySQL runtime metrics will be collected, and you will know how that differs from business-SQL alerting. The configuration targets **Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9**.

## Choose the intended use[​](#choose "Direct link to Choose the intended use")

* **MySQL performance monitoring**: a collector reads server status and writes metrics to a TSDB.
* **Business-SQL alerts**: Nightingale queries the business database directly, for example for failed-order counts. See [SQL datasources](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/sql-databases.md).
* **Nightingale metadata database**: stores users and rules. See [Database deployment](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/databases.md). It does not automatically provide either monitoring path.

## Configure collection[​](#configure "Direct link to Configure collection")

First [install and register Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md). Create a monitoring account reachable from the collector, then edit `conf/input.mysql/mysql.toml`:

```
[[instances]]

address = "127.0.0.1:3306"

username = "monitor"

password = "replace-with-monitor-password"

parameters = "tls=false"

timeout_seconds = 3

gather_table_size = false

gather_slave_status = false

labels = { instance = "mysql-local:3306" }
```

Replace the address, password and unique instance label. Configure TLS for network connections; this example is for local verification. Grant the permissions required by enabled queries. Replication status, process lists and table-size collection have different permissions and costs; do not use root as a shortcut. Enable replication metrics only when needed, and check whether the server supports `SHOW SLAVE STATUS` or `SHOW REPLICA STATUS`.

Use another `[[instances]]` for each target, with a distinct `instance` label. See the [v0.5.17 configuration](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/blob/v0.5.17/conf/input.mysql/mysql.toml) for the full option list.

## Verify[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify")

From the collector installation directory:

```
./categraf --test --inputs mysql
```

**Expected result**: metrics starting with `mysql_`, without authentication or SQL-permission errors. Restart the existing collector service, select the destination store in Nightingale's explorer, and check the metrics and instance labels.

Import the MySQL dashboards and rules from integration templates. Confirm collection before enabling thresholds against absent data.

## Business metrics[​](#business-metrics "Direct link to Business metrics")

Order counts and failed jobs are not MySQL server-status metrics. Use custom SQL queries in the collector when you also need stored trends, or a Nightingale SQL datasource for direct query-based evaluation. Use read-only credentials and bounded queries with timeouts so monitoring does not impair the business workload.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Input plugins](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/plugins.md)
* [SQL alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/sql-rules.md)

# Monitor Oracle

Configure Categraf Oracle instances and SQL collection, map labels and values, and verify database permissions.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, Oracle samples will reach your TSDB, and you will know where shared and per-instance SQL belongs. The example uses the **Categraf v0.5.17** Oracle configuration and the store used by Nightingale v9.

## Configuration files[​](#configuration-files "Direct link to Configuration files")

* `conf/input.oracle/oracle.toml`: connections and `[[instances]]` for one or more targets.
* `conf/input.oracle/metric.toml`: shared collection queries.
* `[[instances.metrics]]`: queries specific to the owning instance.

Reuse the writer configured during [installation and registration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md); Oracle collection does not require another TSDB.

## Configure one instance[​](#configure "Direct link to Configure one instance")

Use a monitoring account permitted to query the required views:

```
interval = 15



[[instances]]

address = "127.0.0.1:1521/ORCLPDB1"

username = "monitor"

password = "replace-with-monitor-password"

is_sys_dba = false

is_sys_oper = false

max_open_connections = 5

labels = { instance = "oracle-local:1521" }



[[instances.metrics]]

mesurement = "sessions"

label_fields = ["status", "type"]

metric_fields = ["value"]

timeout = "3s"

request = '''

SELECT status, type, COUNT(*) AS value

FROM v$session GROUP BY status, type

'''
```

Replace the service name, credentials and instance label. `mesurement` is the plugin's actual key; do not correct it to `measurement`. The `status` and `type` columns become labels; `value` is numeric. Column names must match the mapping.

Avoid SYS. Ask a DBA to grant access for each enabled query. This custom query needs `v$session`; the bundled queries may require additional views. Passing one query is not proof that the account can run the entire collection set.

## Verify[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify")

```
./categraf --test --inputs oracle
```

**Expected result**: Oracle metrics without connection, permission or column-mapping errors. For an ORA error, check the service and credentials, then the views used by the failing SQL.

After local collection succeeds, restart the existing service and check `oracle_` metrics and `instance` labels in the destination store. Give each target distinct labels to prevent collisions.

## Shared queries and cost[​](#shared-queries "Direct link to Shared queries and cost")

Put queries required by every instance in `metric.toml`; keep special queries under the target's `[[instances.metrics]]`. Have a DBA review execution plans and frequency before enabling queries against large tables. See the [Oracle configuration directory](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/tree/v0.5.17/conf/input.oracle) for fields and bundled queries.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Input plugins](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/plugins.md)
* [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)

# Probe ports and HTTP endpoints

Configure Categraf TCP, UDP and HTTP probes, then verify result codes, response content and certificate expiry metrics.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, an independent probe will check service ports and HTTP responses rather than process existence alone. The configuration targets **Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9**.

## TCP and UDP[​](#tcp-udp "Direct link to TCP and UDP")

Edit `conf/input.net_response/net_response.toml`:

```
[[instances]]

targets = ["127.0.0.1:22"]

protocol = "tcp"

timeout = "2s"

labels = { probe = "ssh-local" }
```

Replace the target. A successful TCP connection proves that the port accepts connections, not that the application is healthy. Configure a protocol-appropriate `send` and `expect` pair when response checking is required.

UDP needs a meaningful request and expected reply. Changing `protocol` to `udp` alone does not make a complete probe. See the [net\_response configuration](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/blob/v0.5.17/conf/input.net_response/net_response.toml).

## HTTP[​](#http "Direct link to HTTP")

Edit `conf/input.http_response/http_response.toml`:

```
[[instances]]

targets = ["http://127.0.0.1:8080/health"]

method = "GET"

response_timeout = "5s"

expect_response_status_code = 200

expect_response_substring = "ok"

follow_redirects = false

labels = { probe = "application-health" }
```

Use the application's actual health endpoint and response. Check both status and body. Enable redirect following deliberately so a login redirect does not masquerade as health. HTTPS targets can also produce certificate-expiry metrics.

## Verify and alert[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify and alert")

```
./categraf --test --inputs net_response:http_response
```

**Expected result**: `net_response_result_code` or `http_response_result_code` for the intended target. Zero means the configured check succeeded; nonzero means failure. The plugins use different nonzero codes, so do not share their error-code descriptions.

Restart collection after testing and check labels, result codes and timestamps in the destination store. Start with a `result_code != 0` condition, an appropriate sustained duration and a meaningful severity.

When an HTTPS target produces `http_response_cert_expire_timestamp`, this expression returns seconds until expiry:

```
http_response_cert_expire_timestamp - time()
```

Verify the metric exists before enabling an expiry threshold. DNS, network access and probe permissions also affect results; a failed probe does not necessarily mean a process exited.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Metric alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/metric-rules.md)
* [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)

Full HTTP options: [v0.5.17 configuration](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/blob/v0.5.17/conf/input.http_response/http_response.toml).

# Monitor processes

Distinguish system process counts from a service’s resource usage and verify processes, procstat or application metrics.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, you will distinguish excessive system process counts from a missing service and collect per-service resource metrics. The configuration targets **Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9**.

## Choose the signal[​](#choose "Direct link to Choose the signal")

* `processes` counts system processes by state and helps detect runaway jobs.
* `procstat` matches a service and collects its count, CPU, memory and file descriptors.
* Application Prometheus metrics also describe requests, errors and runtime behavior. See [Java monitoring](https://n9e.github.io/docs/practice/java.md).

An existing process does not prove that a service works; add [port or HTTP probes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/practice/port.md) where needed.

## Configure procstat[​](#configure "Direct link to Configure procstat")

Edit `conf/input.procstat/procstat.toml`:

```
[[instances]]

search_exec_substring = "nginx"

gather_total = true

gather_per_pid = false

gather_more_metrics = ["cpu", "mem", "fd", "uptime"]

labels = { service = "nginx" }
```

Replace the match and confirm that it selects the intended service. Add another `[[instances]]` for another service. Select one suitable matching method per instance. `gather_per_pid = true` adds PID labels and can increase series counts when processes restart frequently.

## Verify and alert[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify and alert")

```
./categraf --test --inputs processes:procstat
```

**Expected result**: system counts and service metrics appear; the matched count agrees with the actual processes. Restart the collector service and query `procstat_lookup_count` in Nightingale.

It is positive when matching processes exist and zero when none match. Verify on a test service before adding a sustained-duration alert to avoid noise from normal restarts. If the host or collector disappears, samples may disappear instead of becoming zero. Add [missing-host detection](https://n9e.github.io/docs/practice/linux.md#missing-host) separately.

## JVM and systemd environment[​](#jvm "Direct link to JVM and systemd environment")

The `jvm` option in `gather_more_metrics` requires `jstat` on the target host. If foreground testing works but systemd fails, check its PATH, the JDK location and permissions to inspect the process. Use `sudo systemctl edit categraf.service` with the actual JDK path:

```
[Service]

Environment="PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-17-openjdk-amd64/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin"
```

Restart and inspect the logs. Replace the example path if that JDK is not installed. Configuration reference: [procstat v0.5.17](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/blob/v0.5.17/conf/input.procstat/procstat.toml).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Java application monitoring](https://n9e.github.io/docs/practice/java.md)
* [Metric alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/metric-rules.md)

# Monitor Redis

Use the Categraf Redis input or scrape an existing Redis Exporter, then verify the stored runtime metrics.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

By the end of this page, Redis runtime metrics will be available in Nightingale. An existing Redis Exporter can remain in place. The examples target **Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9**.

## Collect Redis directly[​](#direct-collection "Direct link to Collect Redis directly")

The input connects to Redis and reads status using commands such as `INFO`. After [installing and registering Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), edit `conf/input.redis/redis.toml`:

```
[[instances]]

address = "127.0.0.1:6379"

username = "monitor"

password = "replace-with-monitor-password"

pool_size = 2

labels = { instance = "redis-local:6379" }
```

Replace the credentials and instance label. Older Redis installations without ACL users may require an empty `username`. Use a monitoring account with permissions for the enabled collection set. Allowing `INFO` alone does not necessarily cover every optional command. Slow-log and custom-command collection need their own permissions. See the [configuration](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/blob/v0.5.17/conf/input.redis/redis.toml).

## Reuse an exporter[​](#exporter "Direct link to Reuse an exporter")

If Prometheus or vmagent already scrapes the exporter, register that [store as a datasource](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/overview.md) without collecting it twice.

Alternatively, add the exporter to `conf/input.prometheus/prometheus.toml`:

```
[[instances]]

urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:9121/metrics"]

url_label_key = "instance"

url_label_value = "{{.Host}}"
```

This is the exporter's HTTP endpoint, not Redis port 6379. Fetching it from the collector host should return Redis metrics in Prometheus text format.

## Verify[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify")

Test the selected path:

```
./categraf --test --inputs redis

# For the exporter path:

./categraf --test --inputs prometheus
```

**Expected result**: Redis metrics without authentication or scraping errors. Restart the collector service. Select the destination store in Nightingale's explorer and check `redis_` metrics, instance labels and new samples.

The native input and Redis Exporter do not use identical metric names. Import dashboards and rules matching the collector you chose.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)
* [Remote Write](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/remote-write.md)

# Prerequisites for using Nightingale

Learn logs, processes, time-series concepts, PromQL and the data path before diagnosing collection, storage, alerting or delivery.

Last reviewed 2026-10-11

After this page, you will know the prerequisites for Nightingale and be able to separate missing data, missing alerts and missing notifications into specific checks.

## Linux and deployment basics[​](#linux "Direct link to Linux and deployment basics")

For binaries, understand working directories, configuration files, stdout / stderr and systemd. For containers, understand port mappings, volumes, logs and where a container's `127.0.0.1` points.

```
sudo journalctl -u n9e.service -n 100 --no-pager

sudo journalctl -u categraf.service -n 100 --no-pager
```

Use the actual service names. **Expected result**: recent logs for the component under investigation. If no such unit exists, use the log entry point for its real deployment.

## Time-series model[​](#time-series "Direct link to Time-series model")

* A **metric name** describes the measurement.
* **Labels** distinguish hosts, services and instances; the name and labels identify a series.
* A **timestamp and value** form a sample. Incorrect clocks place data outside the intended range.
* A **Gauge** is a current value; a **Counter** accumulates and may reset when a process restarts.
* Histograms and summaries require understanding buckets, counts and sums.

Avoid unique request IDs as labels. See the [Prometheus data model](https://prometheus.io/docs/concepts/data_model/).

## PromQL[​](#promql "Direct link to PromQL")

Start with selecting series by labels, using `rate()` on counters and aggregating instances. Build thresholds around the meaning of the data; a cumulative count is not a requests-per-second value.

An instant query evaluates a time; a range query returns a series over an interval. Range and step affect the display. Verify an expression in the [metrics explorer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/metric-explorer.md) before putting it into a [metric rule](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/metric-rules.md). See the [Prometheus query documentation](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/basics/).

## Pull and push[​](#collection-paths "Direct link to Pull and push")

Prometheus and vmagent scrape with Pull. The scraper knows whether a request succeeded and can generate `up`. Categraf sends Remote Write with Push. Its liveness cannot be treated as a Prometheus scrape-status check.

Nightingale v9 can use embedded or external storage. If metrics already exist in Prometheus, register the datasource without moving them. Heartbeat metadata and sample delivery are separate paths; see [Linux monitoring](https://n9e.github.io/docs/practice/linux.md).

## Troubleshooting and asking for help[​](#troubleshooting "Direct link to Troubleshooting and asking for help")

Find the failing stage first:

1. Does the collector produce samples locally?
2. Do they reach the correct store?
3. Does Nightingale query that datasource?
4. Does rule evaluation produce an event?
5. Is the event muted, filtered or processed?
6. Is notification delivery successful?

Include versions, deployment method, expected and actual behavior, the incident time range, minimal configuration and relevant logs. Remove credentials and personal information first. Keep enough context to make the failure diagnosable.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Quick start](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md)
* [System architecture](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/architecture.md)
* [Connected datasource with no data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md)

# Built-in metric views

Pre-built views for hosts, containers and common middleware, and how to add your own.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: charts from clicking metric names instead of writing PromQL, and your team's own queries added to the same catalogue so colleagues who do not write PromQL can use them too.

## What this page is for[​](#what-this-page-is-for "Direct link to What this page is for")

You have just connected a component, data is arriving, and you have no idea **which metrics are worth looking at**. Built-in metrics is that catalogue: organised by component type and category, each entry carrying a metric name, a unit, the PromQL and a plain-language description, and charting on one click.

A fresh install ships with more than 1300 entries covering Linux, MySQL, Redis, Nginx, Kafka, ClickHouse, Kubernetes and other common components.

Compared with the [Metrics explorer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/metric-explorer.md): that one is for people writing PromQL during an incident; this one is for routine checks and for finding out what a newly connected component even exposes.

**Explorer → Metrics → Built-in metrics** (`/metrics-built-in`).

## 1. Set a filter before clicking a metric[​](#1-set-a-filter-before-clicking-a-metric "Direct link to 1. Set a filter before clicking a metric")

![Built-in metrics](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/query/metrics-built-in.webp)![Built-in metrics](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/query/metrics-built-in.dark.webp)

The left column is **Filters**, and its job is to **attach a set of label conditions to the query whenever you click a metric**.

In the product's own words: with `{ident="n9e01"}` configured and selected, clicking `cpu_usage_idle` actually issues `cpu_usage_idle{ident="n9e01"}`.

**Set one up before you start clicking.** Without it, a metric like `cpu_usage_idle` returns every series in the environment — thousands of lines, and a stalled browser.

Click **+** at the top of the left column:

| Field             | What to put in it                                                       |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name              | Something recognisable, e.g. "Trading production"                       |
| Data source       | Which source this filter applies to                                     |
| Filter conditions | The label conditions, e.g. `ident="n9e01"`                              |
| Authorized teams  | Which teams may use it, and whether **read and write** or **read only** |

## 2. Find the metric you want[​](#2-find-the-metric-you-want "Direct link to 2. Find the metric you want")

Four filters across the top: **Component type** (Linux, MySQL, Kubernetes…), **Category** (the second level, e.g. cpu / mem / disk under Linux), **Unit**, and a keyword search that matches the name, the PromQL and the description.

The table shows five columns by default: component type, category, name, unit, PromQL. **Display columns** at the top right adds expression type, metric type, custom fields, description and updated-by.

The **Name** column actually renders the metric's **description**, and it is a link; the real expression is in the PromQL column. Clicking it opens a query drawer that charts it straight away, and **Add panel** in that drawer stacks several metrics for comparison.

With rows selected, **More** offers export (JSON), import and delete.

## 3. Add one of your own[​](#3-add-one-of-your-own "Direct link to 3. Add one of your own")

Click **Add metric**:

| Field              | What to put in it                                                                   |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Component type     | Pick an existing one or create a new one                                            |
| Category           | The second level                                                                    |
| Expression type    | **Metric name** (just a name) or **PromQL** (a full expression with functions)      |
| Metric type        | Gauge / Counter / Histogram                                                         |
| PromQL             | The query itself                                                                    |
| Unit               | Used for display conversion                                                         |
| Custom fields      | Name plus value, for whatever context you want to carry                             |
| Metric description | Per language: **Name** (required) and **Description** — this is what the list shows |

Note: **there is no top-level name field**. The name lives inside the per-language description block, so a metric filled in only in Chinese will not show a name in the English UI.

Creating, editing and deleting are gated by the `/builtin-metrics/add`, `/put` and `/del` permission points.

## Where the catalogue comes from[​](#where-the-catalogue-comes-from "Direct link to Where the catalogue comes from")

This decides where you go to change something:

* The 1300-odd built-in entries come from `integrations/<Component>/metrics/*.json` in the backend and are **loaded when n9e-center starts**. No UI action triggers it, and there is nothing for you to "import";
* Metrics you create here are stored in the database. **For the same PromQL, the database row wins over the file** — so when a built-in entry cannot be edited, the workaround is to create a new one with the same PromQL;
* Integrations → Components has a **Metrics** tab under each component. That is another view onto the same data; editing either side is equivalent.

Two other places consume this catalogue: the **Built-in metrics** button beside the PromQL input in the Metrics explorer, and the [one-click drawer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/object-view.md) on the host list.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Write the PromQL yourself: [Metrics explorer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/metric-explorer.md)
* Look at things host by host: [Object quick view](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/object-view.md)
* What else a component template carries: [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)

# Build a dashboard

A dashboard belongs to a business group; build it from an integration template or from scratch with twelve panel types, and export it whole to hand to someone else.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: a dashboard owned by a business group, with at least one panel drawing real data, saved and exportable to hand to someone else.

## First decide: import a template or start empty[​](#first-decide-import-a-template-or-start-empty "Direct link to First decide: import a template or start empty")

* Monitoring a common component (Linux, MySQL, Redis, Nginx…): a usable board almost certainly already ships with the template, and **importing then adjusting** beats drawing from scratch;
* Monitoring your own business metrics: start empty.

Either way, note one thing first: **the Add / Import / More buttons only appear once a specific business group is selected on the left.** While the sidebar sits on the preset filters "My business group dashboards" or "Public dashboards", the buttons are hidden — that is not a permission problem, click a real group and they come back.

## 1. Import from an integration template[​](#1-import-from-an-integration-template "Direct link to 1. Import from an integration template")

**Explorer → Dashboards** (`/dashboards`), pick a business group on the left, then **Import**.

![Dashboard list](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/query/dashboard-list.webp)![Dashboard list](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/query/dashboard-list.dark.webp)

The dialog has four tabs:

| Tab                                            | When to use it                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Import built-in dashboard** (default)        | Pick a component (MySQL, Redis…), then tick the dashboards shipped with it. This is the usual path                                                                 |
| **Import Grafana dashboard URL** (recommended) | Converts nothing; creates an iframe-mode dashboard that embeds your Grafana page                                                                                   |
| **Import Nightingale dashboard JSON**          | Paste JSON exported from another Nightingale                                                                                                                       |
| **Import Grafana dashboard (not recommended)** | Beta, converts Grafana dashboard JSON into Nightingale's model. Plenty of limits — see [Use Grafana with Nightingale](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/grafana.md) |

Expected result: the boards appear in the list and open with charts on them. **If the charts are empty, do not start editing the board** — the component's metrics probably are not arriving yet; go back to [Verify incoming data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md).

The templates themselves live under **Integrations → Components**, which offers the same set of dashboards. Importing collector config and alert rules alongside them is covered in [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md).

## 2. Start empty and add the first panel[​](#2-start-empty-and-add-the-first-panel "Direct link to 2. Start empty and add the first panel")

Click **Add**, give the dashboard a name (ident, tags and note are optional). Saving takes you straight to the detail page.

Click **Add panel**. Besides the 12 visualization types, the dropdown offers **Row** (a collapsible horizontal divider) and **Paste panel** (panel config JSON copied elsewhere).

Pick a type to open the panel editor. It is a full-screen modal with **two columns, not tabs**:

* **Left**: the variable bar on top, a live preview in the middle, the query editor below. That query editor is the same one the [Metrics explorer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/metric-explorer.md) uses, so the preview updates as you type. Text and Iframe panels have no query editor.
* **Right**: a stack of collapsible sections, of which a type-specific subset appears — **Panel options** (name, description, links, repeat by variable), **Graph styles**, Legend, Tooltip, **Value mappings**, **Standard options**, **Thresholds**, **Colors**, **Links**, Override.

The modal header also carries the visualization-type selector and a time range picker. **Change the chart type there** rather than deleting the panel and adding a new one.

Click **Save** to return to the dashboard, then drag a panel's edge to resize it and its title to move it.

## 3. The twelve panel types[​](#3-the-twelve-panel-types "Direct link to 3. The twelve panel types")

| Type            | What it is for                                            |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Time series     | The default. One or more lines over time                  |
| Bar chart       | Comparing categories, or counts bucketed by time          |
| Stat            | One big number, coloured by threshold                     |
| Table NG (Beta) | The newer table with more features; use it for new panels |
| Table           | The older table, still used by existing panels            |
| Pie chart       | Proportions                                               |
| Hexmap          | Many instances on one screen, spot the outlier by colour  |
| Bar gauge       | Top N as horizontal bars                                  |
| Text            | Prose and links; queries nothing                          |
| Gauge           | A single value against a range                            |
| Heatmap         | How a distribution changes over time                      |
| Iframe          | Embeds an external page                                   |

Switching Table to Table NG raises a confirmation offering **Auto upgrade** (carry the old options over where possible) or **Switch type only** (start the options fresh).

## 4. Rows, time range and links[​](#4-rows-time-range-and-links "Direct link to 4. Rows, time range and links")

* **Rows**: `Add panel → Row` inserts a collapsible divider. Deleting one asks whether to **delete the row and its panels** or **delete the row only**.
* **Time range and auto refresh**: top right. The selected range goes into the URL (`__from` / `__to` / `__refresh`) and is remembered per dashboard in the browser. Refresh intervals are 5s / 10s / 20s / 30s / 1m / 2m / 3m / 5m / 10m. **A refresh interval shorter than the query step buys nothing**, and the UI says so.
* **Links**: the link icon in the title bar configures jump targets (name, URL, open in a new tab), which is how you chain related boards together.
* **Dashboard settings** (the gear): name, ident, tags, note, plus two behaviour switches — **Graph tooltip** (Default / Shared crosshair / Shared tooltip) and **Graph zoom** (Default / Update time range).
* **Variables**: the entry point sits at the end of the variable bar, showing "Add variable" while there are none. See [Variables and filters](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/variables.md).

## Save, export, move a panel elsewhere[​](#save-export-move-a-panel-elsewhere "Direct link to Save, export, move a panel elsewhere")

**Changes are not saved automatically.** After adding panels and adjusting the layout, click **Save dashboard** in the title bar; leaving with unsaved changes prompts first.

* **A whole board**: **Export** on the list row gives you JSON, with **Download JSON** and **Copy JSON to clipboard**. Paste it back elsewhere through "Import Nightingale dashboard JSON". **The JSON in that box can be selected and copied, but editing it writes nothing back** — there is no edit-JSON feature.
* **Into another business group**: use **Clone**. The copy is independent; the two are maintained separately from then on.
* **A single panel**: the panel's own menu has **Copy**, which puts that panel's config JSON on the clipboard; on the target dashboard use `Add panel → Paste panel`. The same menu also holds Refresh / Edit / Clone / Share / Inspect / Delete, and table panels add **Export (CSV)**.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Make one board serve many hosts: [Variables and filters](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/variables.md)
* Show it to someone without an account: [Anonymous time-limited sharing](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/sharing.md)
* Import the template's rules too: [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)

# Share, embed and integrate external systems

Embed Nightingale into an existing portal, hide menus selectively, and pass identity through.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: extra entries in the Nightingale side menu that open your other systems, and a way to embed Nightingale pages into your own portal without asking people to log in a second time.

## Two directions, don't mix them[​](#two-directions-dont-mix-them "Direct link to Two directions, don't mix them")

* **Others come in.** *Embedded products* hangs an external page into the Nightingale side menu as an iframe. It has a configuration page under Integrations.
* **Nightingale goes out.** Embedding Nightingale pages into another portal is done with URL parameters plus proxy authentication. There is **no configuration page** — you edit the config file and the link.

## Embed an external system into Nightingale[​](#embed-an-external-system-into-nightingale "Direct link to Embed an external system into Nightingale")

**Integrations → Embedded products** (`/embedded-products`), then **Add**.

![Embedded products](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/query/embedded-products.webp)![Embedded products](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/query/embedded-products.dark.webp)

| Field      | What to put in it                                                                      |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name       | The menu label in the side bar; keep it short                                          |
| URL        | The full URL to embed, e.g. `https://cmdb.example.com/hosts`                           |
| Visibility | **Visible to logged-in users**, or **Visible to specific teams** (then pick the teams) |

Save. Expected result: a new entry at the bottom of the side menu that loads the page in the main area (a browser refresh is sometimes needed).

Each row in the list carries two more controls: **Show in menu** keeps the configuration but hides the entry — handy for taking something down temporarily; and the handle at the start of the row reorders the entries in the side menu.

The usual candidates are a CMDB, a ticketing system, or the team's runbook wiki, so that acting on an alert does not mean switching browser tabs.

## A blank frame almost always means the other side refuses[​](#a-blank-frame-almost-always-means-the-other-side-refuses "Direct link to A blank frame almost always means the other side refuses")

Nightingale is only the iframe container here; whether embedding works is decided entirely by the other side's response headers:

| Their response header                             | Result                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `X-Frame-Options: DENY` or `SAMEORIGIN`           | The browser refuses, the iframe is blank |
| `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'` | Same                                     |
| Neither header, or your domain explicitly allowed | It embeds                                |

The browser console spells it out: `Refused to display ... in a frame because it set 'X-Frame-Options'`, or `Refused to frame ... because an ancestor violates ... frame-ancestors`.

Two fixes: have them add `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors https://<your-nightingale>`, or put an nginx reverse proxy in front of their site that rewrites the headers and point the entry at the proxy.

Cookies are the second layer. If their session cookie is `SameSite=Lax/Strict` it is not sent inside a cross-site iframe, so the user just sees a login page. Either they switch to `SameSite=None; Secure`, or both sides move behind the same SSO.

## Embed Nightingale in another portal: hide the chrome first[​](#embed-nightingale-in-another-portal-hide-the-chrome-first "Direct link to Embed Nightingale in another portal: hide the chrome first")

Nightingale honours three URL parameters, on any page:

| Parameter                   | Effect                                                                |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `?menu=hide`                | Hides the side menu; the page body renders normally                   |
| `?viewMode=fullscreen`      | Dashboard detail only: hides the page header too, leaving just panels |
| `&themeMode=dark` / `light` | Pins light or dark instead of following the browser                   |

For example, a dashboard embedded as a bare canvas:

```
<iframe src="https://n9e.example.com/dashboards/12?viewMode=fullscreen&themeMode=dark"

        width="100%" height="800" frameborder="0"></iframe>
```

There is no way out of `viewMode=fullscreen` from inside an iframe — the exit shortcut is blocked by iframe security, so the parameter has to be removed from the URL by hand. The product says as much in its own hint.

If all you want is to expose one dashboard to someone outside, do not use this route. Use [anonymous time-limited sharing](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/sharing.md) instead: `/dashboards/share/<id>?__token=` already renders without the menu, and it expires on its own.

## Pass identity through[​](#pass-identity-through "Direct link to Pass identity through")

When the portal already has its own login, use proxy authentication so nobody signs in twice:

```
[HTTP.ProxyAuth]

Enable = true

# which request header carries the username

HeaderUserNameKey = "X-User-Name"

# roles given to a user auto-created from a username Nightingale has not seen

DefaultRoles = ["Standard"]
```

The portal or gateway adds `X-User-Name: <username>` when forwarding to Nightingale. Nightingale looks the user up by that header, and creates the account with `DefaultRoles` if it does not exist yet.

Three things you must get right, or this becomes an open impersonation endpoint:

1. **Only a proxy you control may set that header**, and it must **unconditionally strip** an incoming header of the same name at the edge — otherwise anyone can become anyone by adding a header;
2. **Bind Nightingale to an internal address** reachable only from the gateway, never straight to the internet;
3. Enabling `ProxyAuth` **disables JWT login**: Nightingale's own login page stops working and the logout endpoint returns an error. It is a one-way switch, so decide before you flip it.

## What this does not cover[​](#what-this-does-not-cover "Direct link to What this does not cover")

* Visibility only controls who sees the entry in the side menu. It is **not a security boundary for the embedded system** — Nightingale has no say once a user hits that URL directly, so the embedded system must authenticate on its own.
* There is no URL parameter that hides a named subset of menus. `menu=hide` is all or nothing; to tailor menus per person, use roles and permission points — see [Roles and permissions](https://n9e.github.io/docs/security/roles.md).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Expose a single board: [Anonymous time-limited sharing](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/sharing.md)
* Already running Grafana: [Use Grafana with Nightingale](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/grafana.md)
* Who sees what: [Users and teams](https://n9e.github.io/docs/security/users-teams.md)

# Use Grafana with Nightingale

Keep Grafana for visualisation: point it at the same stores, and hand alerting to Nightingale.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: your Grafana dashboards untouched, and Nightingale alerting on the same stores. No data is migrated and no panel is rebuilt.

## Splitting the work[​](#splitting-the-work "Direct link to Splitting the work")

| This                                   | Goes to     | Why                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Charting and ad-hoc exploration        | Grafana     | You already have dozens of panels; rebuilding them buys nothing                                      |
| Alert evaluation                       | Nightingale | Rules carry business-group ownership, muting and subscriptions, and every evaluation leaves a record |
| Notification routing and noise control | Nightingale | Notification rules, media types, templates and workflows are one coherent set                        |
| Closing the loop on events             | Nightingale | Active events, history and self-healing live in one place                                            |

The split rests on one condition: **both sides look at the same data**. Sections 1 and 2 below are the two directions — pick the one that matches where your metrics live.

## 1. Point both sides at the same stores[​](#1-point-both-sides-at-the-same-stores "Direct link to 1. Point both sides at the same stores")

If metrics are already in Prometheus / VictoriaMetrics / Thanos, this is the least work: register the same query endpoint your Grafana data source uses in Nightingale too.

**Integrations → Data sources → Add → Prometheus**, same URL. Field by field, see [Prometheus](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md).

Two things to watch:

* The two sides **do not need matching names**. Nightingale's alert rules pick the source by its Nightingale name.
* If the Grafana data source uses Server (proxy) access, that URL is reached from the Grafana host. **The Nightingale host must be able to reach it too**, or the data source test fails.

## 2. The other direction: let Grafana query Nightingale's embedded TSDB[​](#2-the-other-direction-let-grafana-query-nightingales-embedded-tsdb "Direct link to 2. The other direction: let Grafana query Nightingale's embedded TSDB")

If your metrics only live in Nightingale's embedded TSDB (Categraf pushes straight to Nightingale), Grafana can query it — the embedded store exposes a standard Prometheus query API at `http://<nightingale>:17000/prometheus`.

But **that endpoint only accepts requests from the local machine by default**. To let Grafana reach it from another host, configure basic auth first:

```
[EmbeddedTSDB]

Enable = true

BasicAuthUser = "grafana"

BasicAuthPass = "<pick your own>"
```

Setting these lifts the local-only restriction, and the auto-registered `embedded-tsdb` data source switches from `127.0.0.1` to the detected host IP with the same credentials attached. Restart Nightingale to apply.

Then add a **Prometheus** data source in Grafana:

```
URL        http://<nightingale IP>:17000/prometheus

Auth       Basic auth, with the user and password above
```

Save and test; a result for `up` means it works.

This route suits small deployments only. The embedded store is a single-instance local-disk option, good to roughly 100k active series — see [Embedded TSDB and external storage](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/storage.md) for the limits. Once you outgrow it and move to an external store, go back to section 1 and point both sides there.

## 3. Move alerting to Nightingale[​](#3-move-alerting-to-nightingale "Direct link to 3. Move alerting to Nightingale")

PromQL in a Nightingale rule is the same PromQL you write in a Grafana panel; the only difference is that the threshold goes into the expression itself (`... > 1`).

* Start from scratch: [Create the first rule](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/first-rule.md)
* Bring existing Grafana alert rules across: [Migrate from Grafana alerting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-grafana-alerting.md)
* Run both in parallel before cutting over: [Coexisting with what you already run](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/coexistence.md)

## Bring Grafana dashboards into Nightingale[​](#bring-grafana-dashboards-into-nightingale "Direct link to Bring Grafana dashboards into Nightingale")

The **Import** dialog on the dashboard list has four tabs; two of them concern Grafana:

| Tab                                            | What it does                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Import Grafana dashboard URL** (recommended) | Converts nothing. It creates an iframe-mode dashboard that embeds your Grafana page. You supply a name, ident, tags and the Grafana dashboard URL |
| **Import Grafana dashboard (not recommended)** | Beta. Converts Grafana dashboard JSON into Nightingale's own model                                                                                |

The limits of the second one are stated in the dialog itself: **only dashboards using Prometheus data sources, and only the chart types and features Nightingale supports**. JSON older than v7 is rejected outright; v7 to v8 warns first and lets you continue. Anything non-trivial needs manual cleanup afterwards — "not recommended" is not politeness.

A third option is to hang all of Grafana off the side menu; see [Share, embed and integrate external systems](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/embedding.md).

## Let Grafana be embedded[​](#let-grafana-be-embedded "Direct link to Let Grafana be embedded")

Both of the last two options need an iframe, and Grafana refuses to be framed by default. Edit `grafana.ini`:

```
[security]

allow_embedding = true
```

That is enough when both run on the same domain. **Across domains** you also have to let Grafana's session cookie travel in a third-party context:

```
[security]

allow_embedding = true

cookie_secure = true      ; requires HTTPS

cookie_samesite = none    ; allow the cookie on cross-site requests
```

`cookie_secure = true` means Grafana must be served over HTTPS; if it is plain HTTP today, put a reverse proxy with a certificate in front of it. The classic symptom of missing these two lines is that you are logged into Nightingale on the outside while the framed Grafana keeps showing its login page.

If you would rather viewers did not log into Grafana at all, turn on anonymous read-only access:

```
[auth.anonymous]

enabled = true

org_name = Main Org.

org_role = Viewer
```

Restart Grafana to apply.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Every field on the data source form: [Prometheus](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md)
* Build boards in Nightingale itself: [Build a dashboard](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/dashboards.md)
* Hang external systems off the side menu: [Share, embed and integrate external systems](https://n9e.github.io/docs/query/embedding.md)

# Log explorer and index patterns

Search ElasticSearch, Loki and VictoriaLogs sources, define index patterns, and pivot from a log line to a rule.

Last reviewed 2026-10-10

Where this page ends: one search running against your log store, narrowed to the lines you care about using the field sidebar, and "which indices, which time field" saved as an index pattern so you never type it again.

## Before you start: which sources this page accepts[​](#before-you-start-which-sources-this-page-accepts "Direct link to Before you start: which sources this page accepts")

The open-source Log explorer supports **three categories only**: **Elasticsearch**, **Loki** and **VictoriaLogs**.

OpenSearch, ClickHouse and Doris can be registered as data sources, but **cannot be selected on this page**. With none available, the page says "No available data source type" and points at data source management.

Registering the source itself is covered in [ElasticSearch / OpenSearch](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/elasticsearch.md) and [Loki / VictoriaLogs](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/loki-victorialogs.md).

## 1. Pick a source and run the first search[​](#1-pick-a-source-and-run-the-first-search "Direct link to 1. Pick a source and run the first search")

**Explorer → Logs** (`/log/explorer`).

![Log explorer](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/query/log-explorer.webp)![Log explorer](https://n9e.github.io/img/docs/query/log-explorer.dark.webp)

The left column, top to bottom (this is the Elasticsearch shape):

| Control     | What to put in it                                                                        |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Data source | One of the three categories above                                                        |
| Mode        | **Indices** (type the index directly) or **Index patterns** (use a saved pattern)        |
| Index       | An index name or wildcard such as `app-log-*`. The gear beside it manages index patterns |
| Date field  | Which field is the time axis, usually `@timestamp`                                       |

The top row holds the syntax switch (**KQL** / **Lucene**), **Query conditions**, the time range (last 1 hour by default) and **Query**. Click **Query**.

Expected result: a histogram appears in the middle, the log table below it, and the duration and match count at the top right.

The two syntaxes:

```
Lucene    status:active                  field equals

          title:(quick OR brown)         field contains either term

          author:"John Smith"            exact phrase

          bro*                           wildcard; ? matches one character

          quikc~                         fuzzy

          count:[1 TO 5]  age:>10        ranges

          quick AND brown  NOT fox       boolean



KQL       method: GET

          level: error*

          response_time >= 1 and response_time <= 5

          method: POST and status_code: (500 or 502)

          user:{ first: "Alice" and last: "White" }     nested fields
```

The row above the table: **Original / Table / Time series / Clustering** switch the display form; **Line break**, **Lines** and **Log time** toggle columns; the gear opens field column settings.

## 2. Narrow the results from the field sidebar[​](#2-narrow-the-results-from-the-field-sidebar "Direct link to 2. Narrow the results from the field sidebar")

**Available fields** at the bottom left lists every field seen in this batch. Hover one and three actions appear:

* **Add to current query** — adds `field: value` as a condition;
* **Exclude from current query** — adds the negation;
* **Filter documents with this field**.

Clicking a field name also shows its **top N values** with their share — the fastest way to answer "which service is producing most of these errors".

**Filters → Add** above the table builds explicit conditions as field / operator / value. **Filters are combined with AND**, and each one can be disabled instead of deleted, which makes trying combinations cheap.

To put a colleague in front of the same screen, use **⋮ → Share link** at the top right: it serialises the current query into the URL and copies it. That is for someone **already logged in**, not an anonymous link.

## 3. Index patterns: save "which indices" once[​](#3-index-patterns-save-which-indices-once "Direct link to 3. Index patterns: save \"which indices\" once")

Typing `app-log-*` and `@timestamp` every time gets old. Save them as an index pattern.

The entry point is not in the side menu: switch **Mode** to **Index patterns**, and the **gear** next to the index box opens the manager (`/log/index-patterns`). Click **Create index pattern**:

| Field                                  | What to put in it                                                                     |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Data source                            | Required, Elasticsearch-type only                                                     |
| Cross cluster                          | Turn on for cross-cluster search                                                      |
| Name                                   | An index wildcard such as `app-log-*`. A `*` is appended automatically if you omit it |
| Time field                             | Picked from the `date`-typed fields of that index, `@timestamp` by default            |
| Match any index, including hidden ones | Whether indices starting with `.` count too                                           |
| Note                                   |                                                                                       |

The right half of the drawer previews which indices match, and says "No matching indexes" when none do — check the wildcard there rather than saving and wondering later.

The page is gated by the `/log/index-patterns` permission point; without it, the gear is not even rendered.

## How Loki and VictoriaLogs differ[​](#how-loki-and-victorialogs-differ "Direct link to How Loki and VictoriaLogs differ")

Neither has the concept of an index or a date field, so those two boxes do not appear.

* **Loki**: the box takes **LogQL**, e.g. `{job="varlogs"} |= "error"`. A builder drawer next to it assembles labels, line filters, parsers and range aggregations step by step, with a **Preview QL** before you run it; a log line can also open a context viewer showing what happened around it.
* **VictoriaLogs**: the box takes **LogsQL**, defaulting to `*` (match everything). It adds **Limit entries** and **Total hits**, and the display forms are Group / Table / JSON.

## From a log line to a rule[​](#from-a-log-line-to-a-rule "Direct link to From a log line to a rule")

**There is no "create alert rule" button on this page** — do not go looking for it. The way to turn a working search into an alert is:

1. write down four things: data source, index (or index pattern), date field, query conditions;
2. go to **Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules → Add** and pick a log rule type;
3. fill those four in as they are, then decide how many matches count as a problem.

Field semantics and picking the threshold are covered in [Log rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/log-rules.md).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* Write the log rule: [Log rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/log-rules.md)
* Connect an ES / OpenSearch cluster: [ElasticSearch / OpenSearch](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/elasticsearch.md)
* Connect Loki / VictoriaLogs: [Loki / VictoriaLogs](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/loki-victorialogs.md)
