2. For MongoDB watch the WiredTiger cache share; for MySQL watch the buffer pool and per-connection memory (sort/join buffers);
3. Look for large result set queries or an excessive connection count consuming memory;
4. If it is still short after tuning, upgrade in the console.

### AliYun RDS MySQL / total connections alert[​](#aliyun-rds-mysql--total-connections-alert "Direct link to AliYun RDS MySQL / total connections alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
AliyunRds_MySQL_ThreadsConnected{} > 1200
```

Runbook:

1. Check the connection count curve against the specification ceiling in the console;
2. Group connections by source with SHOW PROCESSLIST (MySQL family) or db.currentOp() (MongoDB) to find the abnormal application;
3. Tell business growth apart from a connection pool leak (many idle connections piling up);
4. Upgrade as an emergency measure, and cap the application pool and shorten idle timeouts for the root cause.

### AliYun RDS MySQL / slow query ratio above 1 alert[​](#aliyun-rds-mysql--slow-query-ratio-above-1-alert "Direct link to AliYun RDS MySQL / slow query ratio above 1 alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
100 * max(AliyunRds_MySQL_SlowQueries) by (instanceId, instanceName, regionId) / max(AliyunRds_MySQL_QPS) by (instanceId, instanceName, regionId) > 1
```

Runbook:

1. Sort the console slow log page by execution time to find the top slow SQL;
2. Use EXPLAIN to inspect the plan and eliminate full table scans;
3. Add indexes or rewrite the SQL and retest;
4. Check whether it relates to a recently released feature and roll back that query first if so.

### AliYun RDS MySQL / slow query alert[​](#aliyun-rds-mysql--slow-query-alert "Direct link to AliYun RDS MySQL / slow query alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
AliyunRds_MySQL_SlowQueries{} > 100
```

Runbook:

1. Sort the console slow log page by execution time to find the top slow SQL;
2. Use EXPLAIN to inspect the plan and eliminate full table scans;
3. Add indexes or rewrite the SQL and retest;
4. Check whether it relates to a recently released feature and roll back that query first if so.

### AliYun RDS MySQL / disk space usage alert[​](#aliyun-rds-mysql--disk-space-usage-alert "Direct link to AliYun RDS MySQL / disk space usage alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
AliyunRds_DiskUsage{engine="MySQL"} > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Use the console's space analysis to see whether data, logs or temporary files dominate;
2. If binlog/redo dominates, shorten the log retention;
3. If data itself is large, archive historical data — after deleting you still need OPTIMIZE TABLE or to wait for space reclamation;
4. Expand the disk in the console as soon as possible; cloud disk expansion is usually online.

### AliYun RDS MySQL / instance state abnormal alert[​](#aliyun-rds-mysql--instance-state-abnormal-alert "Direct link to AliYun RDS MySQL / instance state abnormal alert")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
{__name__=~"AliyunRds_MySQL_(SlaveIO|SlaveSQL)Running"} != 1
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the replication state and lag on the read-only instance page in the Alibaba Cloud console;
2. The console usually offers a repair-replication entry — use it first;
3. If it was caused by the primary's binlog being purged, the read-only instance must be rebuilt;
4. Move read traffic off that read-only instance before you start.

### AliYun RDS MySQL / connection usage alert[​](#aliyun-rds-mysql--connection-usage-alert "Direct link to AliYun RDS MySQL / connection usage alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
AliyunRds_ConnectionUsage{engine="MySQL"} > 80
```

Runbook:

2. Group connections by source with SHOW PROCESSLIST (MySQL family) or db.currentOp() (MongoDB) to find the abnormal application;
3. Tell business growth apart from a connection pool leak (many idle connections piling up);
4. Upgrade as an emergency measure, and cap the application pool and shorten idle timeouts for the root cause.

### RabbitMQ connections exceed 1000[​](#rabbitmq-connections-exceed-1000 "Direct link to RabbitMQ connections exceed 1000")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
aliyun_acs_amqp_instance_connections_value > 1000
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the connection count curve against the specification ceiling in the console;
2. Check whether clients open a new connection for every send/receive — the correct pattern is a reused long-lived connection with one channel per thread;
3. Confirm no client is reconnecting abnormally;
4. If you genuinely need more connections, upgrade the instance specification.

### RabbitMQ consumer count is 0[​](#rabbitmq-consumer-count-is-0 "Direct link to RabbitMQ consumer count is 0")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
aliyun_acs_amqp_instance_consumers_value < 1
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm in the console which vhost/queue has no consumers;
2. On the consumer side, confirm the application process is alive and not reporting connection or auth errors;
3. If the consumer is healthy but not connected, verify the vhost, queue name and credentials;
4. Once consumption resumes, watch the backlog start to drain.

### RabbitMQ message backlog exceeds 1000[​](#rabbitmq-message-backlog-exceeds-1000 "Direct link to RabbitMQ message backlog exceeds 1000")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
aliyun_acs_amqp_instance_vhost_queue_message_accum_maximum > 1000
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm in the console which queue has the largest backlog and how fast it is growing;
2. Check whether the consumer count is zero or clearly insufficient — start or scale out consumers first;
3. If consumers exist but are slow, check the consumer log for abnormal retries or downstream timeouts;
4. For a huge backlog, consider temporarily increasing consumer concurrency.

### AliYun Redis CPU usage alert[​](#aliyun-redis-cpu-usage-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis CPU usage alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|ShardingProxy|Splitrw|SplitrwProxy)CpuUsage"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)CpuUsage") > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Check the CPU curve under console performance monitoring and use real-time key analysis to find hot keys;
2. Use the slow log to find O(N) commands (KEYS, HGETALL, wide ZRANGE) and rework them;
3. Splitting large keys is the single most effective optimisation;
4. If it stays high, upgrade the specification or move to the cluster edition to spread the load.

### AliYun Redis QPS usage alert[​](#aliyun-redis-qps-usage-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis QPS usage alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)QPSUsage"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)QPSUsage") > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the QPS curve against the specification ceiling in the console;
2. Determine whether it is business growth or cache breakdown letting requests through;
3. Adding a local cache and batching requests on the application side reduces QPS significantly;
4. If you genuinely need more capacity, upgrade or move to the cluster edition.

### AliYun Redis memory usage alert[​](#aliyun-redis-memory-usage-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis memory usage alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)MemoryUsage"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)MemoryUsage") > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Use the console's cache analysis to find the key prefixes consuming the most memory;
2. Split large keys and add TTLs to keys that have none;
3. Confirm maxmemory-policy matches expectations;
4. If capacity is genuinely short, upgrade the specification in the console.

### AliYun Redis hit ratio alert[​](#aliyun-redis-hit-ratio-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis hit ratio alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)HitRate"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)HitRate") < 30
```

Runbook:

1. First rule out a cold start after a restart or resize;
2. In the console, check whether it comes with heavy key eviction — if so treat it as insufficient memory;
3. Review the cache key design and whether the TTL is too short;
4. Confirm there is no flood of lookups for non-existent keys (cache penetration) — add null caching or a bloom filter if needed.

### AliYun Redis failure count alert[​](#aliyun-redis-failure-count-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis failure count alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_StandardFailedCount"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)FailedCount") > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Use the console audit log or the application log to identify the failing command type and error;
2. Common causes are writes rejected for lack of memory, exceeding the connection limit, or a disabled command;
3. Handle each accordingly (upgrade, reduce connections, use a supported command);
4. Confirm the application has retry and fallback logic.

### AliYun Redis average response time alert[​](#aliyun-redis-average-response-time-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis average response time alert")

Unit: milliseconds

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|ShardingProxy|Splitrw|SplitrwProxy)AvgRt"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)AvgRt") > 100000
```

Runbook:

1. Use the console slow log to find the slowest commands;
2. Focus on O(N) commands and big-key operations, switching to SCAN or batching;
3. Check whether throttling was triggered (bandwidth/QPS over specification);
4. Once those are ruled out, upgrade the specification in the console.

### AliYun Redis data sync latency alert[​](#aliyun-redis-data-sync-latency-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis data sync latency alert")

Unit: milliseconds

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)SyncDelayTime"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)SyncDelayTime") > 5
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the lag curve and the instance architecture in the console;
2. A spike in primary writes amplifies lag — check for bulk write jobs;
3. Syncing large keys causes obvious latency spikes — use cache analysis to find and split them;
4. If lag persists, move read traffic back to the primary.

### AliYun Redis max response time alert[​](#aliyun-redis-max-response-time-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis max response time alert")

Unit: milliseconds

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|ShardingProxy|Splitrw|SplitrwProxy)MaxRt"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)MaxRt") > 100000
```

Runbook:

1. Use the console slow log to find the single slowest command;
2. Tail latency usually comes from big-key operations or blocking commands — split large keys first;
3. Check whether an RDB/AOF persistence fork is causing periodic stalls;
4. If it persists after tuning, upgrade the specification in the console.

### AliYun Redis inbound bandwidth usage alert[​](#aliyun-redis-inbound-bandwidth-usage-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis inbound bandwidth usage alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)IntranetInRatio"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)IntranetInRatio") > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the bandwidth curve against the specification ceiling in the console;
2. Use cache analysis to find large keys — writing large keys is the main cause of saturated bandwidth;
3. Split large keys and reduce one-shot bulk writes;
4. If you genuinely need more bandwidth, upgrade the specification.

### AliYun Redis outbound bandwidth usage alert[​](#aliyun-redis-outbound-bandwidth-usage-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis outbound bandwidth usage alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)IntranetOutRatio"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)IntranetOutRatio") > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the bandwidth curve against the specification ceiling in the console;
2. Use cache analysis to find large keys — reading large keys is the main source of outbound bandwidth;
3. Split large keys and avoid one-shot HGETALL/SMEMBERS full reads;
4. If you genuinely need more bandwidth, upgrade the specification.

### AliYun Redis connection usage alert[​](#aliyun-redis-connection-usage-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis connection usage alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|ShardingProxy|Splitrw|SplitrwProxy)ConnectionUsage"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)ConnectionUsage")
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the connection count curve against the specification ceiling in the console;
2. Check whether clients fail to reuse connections or the pool is oversized;
3. As an emergency measure upgrade in the console to raise the connection limit;
4. For the root cause, cap the application pool and enable connection reuse.

### AliYun Redis cached key count alert[​](#aliyun-redis-cached-key-count-alert "Direct link to AliYun Redis cached key count alert")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)Keys"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)Keys") > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Use the console's cache analysis to count keys by prefix and find the fastest-growing prefix;
2. Confirm whether those keys should have a TTL — cache keys without expiry are a classic memory leak;
3. Add sensible expiry times and clean up the existing keys;
4. Confirm the application is not using Redis as persistent storage.

### AliYun-SLB - L7 instance Upstream 5xx (Count/Second) above 10[​](#aliyun-slb---l7-instance-upstream-5xx-countsecond-above-10 "Direct link to AliYun-SLB - L7 instance Upstream 5xx (Count/Second) above 10")

4. If it lines up with a recent release, roll back first.

# Monitor AMD ROCm SMI with Nightingale

Runs rocm-smi to collect AMD GPU utilization, memory, temperature, power and clocks; rules cover overheating and full memory.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

The AMD ROCm SMI input is ported from Telegraf. It runs the `rocm-smi` binary that ships with ROCm and parses the output into per-GPU utilization, memory usage, temperature, power draw, fan speed and clock frequencies.

ROCm must be installed on the host; the default binary path is `/opt/rocm/bin/rocm-smi`, adjustable via `bin_path`. The rules fire on high temperature, exhausted memory and power close to the cap.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **4 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.amd_rocm_smi`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.amd_rocm_smi/rocm.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.amd_rocm_smi started` once the plugin is loaded.

   ```
   # Query statistics from AMD Graphics cards using rocm-smi binary

   # bin_path = "/opt/rocm/bin/rocm-smi"



   ## Optional: timeout for GPU polling

   # timeout = "5s"
   ```

2. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find AMD ROCm SMI, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.

3. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

4 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### AMD GPU memory usage too high[​](#amd-gpu-memory-usage-too-high "Direct link to AMD GPU memory usage too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
amd_rocm_smi_memory_used / (amd_rocm_smi_memory_total > 0) * 100 > 90
```

Runbook:

1. Take gpu\_id and name from the alert labels and run rocm-smi --showmemuse --showpids to see which processes hold the memory;
2. If a zombie process has exited without releasing memory, confirm nobody is using it and kill it to free the memory;
3. If the training job genuinely needs that much memory, reduce the batch size or enable gradient accumulation and mixed precision;
4. When several jobs share one card, switch to memory isolation or queued scheduling so they do not squeeze each other into failure.

### AMD GPU junction temperature too high[​](#amd-gpu-junction-temperature-too-high "Direct link to AMD GPU junction temperature too high")

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
amd_rocm_smi_temperature_sensor_junction > 95
```

Runbook:

1. Take gpu\_id from the alert labels and run rocm-smi --showtemp --showfan --showpower to check temperature, fan speed, and power draw;
2. If the fan speed is low, check whether the fan has failed or is clogged with dust and clean it during a maintenance window if needed;
3. If the fan is already at full speed and it is still hot, check the chassis airflow and data centre intake temperature, and whether neighbouring slots are too densely populated;
4. In the short term you can limit heat with rocm-smi --setpoweroverdrive to cap power, but the cooling problem must be fixed promptly.

### AMD GPU edge temperature too high[​](#amd-gpu-edge-temperature-too-high "Direct link to AMD GPU edge temperature too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
amd_rocm_smi_temperature_sensor_edge > 85
```

Runbook:

1. Take gpu\_id from the alert labels and run rocm-smi --showtemp --showclocks to compare temperature with the current clocks and confirm whether it is already throttling;
2. Check the temperature of the other GPUs on the same machine; if they are all high it is a chassis- or room-level cooling problem;
3. If only one card is hot, check that card's fan, thermal paste, and mounting position;
4. While fixing cooling, evaluate whether to reduce job concurrency on that card so it does not run throttled for long periods.

### AMD GPU memory temperature too high[​](#amd-gpu-memory-temperature-too-high "Direct link to AMD GPU memory temperature too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
amd_rocm_smi_temperature_sensor_memory > 95
```

Runbook:

1. Take gpu\_id from the alert labels and run rocm-smi --showtemp to compare the memory temperature with the junction temperature;
2. A memory temperature well above the junction temperature usually means poor contact on the memory heatsink and requires a maintenance window to inspect;
3. Check whether long-running high memory bandwidth workloads (such as large model inference) are involved and reduce concurrency to relieve it;
4. Also run rocm-smi --showretiredpages to check for bad pages; growing bad pages mean the memory is degrading and the card should be scheduled for replacement.

## Related[​](#related "Direct link to Related")

* [AMD ROCm SMI template source](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/tree/main/integrations/AMD_ROCm_SMI): the raw JSON for dashboards, rules and collector config. Pull requests welcome.
* [Categraf `amd_rocm_smi` plugin docs](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/tree/main/inputs/amd_rocm_smi): every config option and the full metric list.
* [Import dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)
* [Verify that metrics are stored](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md)
* [All integrations](https://n9e.github.io/integrations.md)

# Monitor Apache with Nightingale

Reads the server-status?auto output of mod\_status for request rate, busy and idle workers, CPU and traffic; rules watch worker exhaustion and unreachable servers.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

With `mod_status` enabled, Apache httpd serves a machine-readable status page at `/server-status?auto`. The input scrapes it for total accesses and traffic, requests per second, busy and idle workers, CPU load, uptime and the distribution of worker states.

The rules cover idle workers running out, requests queuing, httpd being unreachable and restarts. Remember to restrict who can reach the status page.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **5 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.apache`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.apache/apache.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.apache started` once the plugin is loaded.

   ```
   [[instances]]



   # https://statuslist.app/apache/apache-status-page-simple-setup-guide/

   # scrape_uri = "http://localhost/server-status/?auto"

   # host_override = ""

   # insecure = false

   # custom_headers = {}

   # log_level = "info"
   ```

2. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Apache, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.

3. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### Apache instance unreachable[​](#apache-instance-unreachable "Direct link to Apache instance unreachable")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
apache_up == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Log in to the host and run systemctl status httpd (or apache2) to confirm whether the master process is alive;
2. If the process is alive, run curl -s '<http://127.0.0.1/server-status?auto>' to verify by hand whether the status page is blocked by a Require directive or a firewall;
3. If the process is gone, run httpd -t to validate the configuration before starting it, and check the tail of error\_log for the cause (port already in use, expired certificate, module load failure are common);
4. Confirm the upstream load balancer has removed this node so traffic stops being sent to it.

### Apache idle workers exhausted[​](#apache-idle-workers-exhausted "Direct link to Apache idle workers exhausted")

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
apache_workers{state="idle"} == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run curl -s '<http://127.0.0.1/server-status?auto>' and read the Scoreboard to see which state workers are stuck in (W = sending reply, meaning a slow backend; R = reading request, meaning slow clients);
2. If they are stuck in W, first check whether the backend (PHP-FPM, database, upstream API) has slowed down, and use tail -f access\_log to find the slow URLs from the response-time column;
3. As a stopgap, raise MaxRequestWorkers and ServerLimit and reload gracefully, but re-check memory first (per-worker memory x concurrency must not exceed physical memory);
4. If slow clients are holding workers, enable mod\_reqtimeout and lower KeepAliveTimeout.

### Apache worker utilization too high[​](#apache-worker-utilization-too-high "Direct link to Apache worker utilization too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
sum without (state) (apache_workers{state="busy"}) / sum without (state) (apache_scoreboard) * 100 > 85
```

Runbook:

1. Run curl -s '<http://127.0.0.1/server-status?auto>' and compare BusyWorkers against the open\_slot headroom in the Scoreboard;
2. Use tail -n 10000 access\_log | awk to rank URLs by count and latency, and decide whether this is genuine traffic growth or one slow endpoint holding workers;
3. For traffic growth, scale out instances or raise MaxRequestWorkers (recalculating ServerLimit against memory);
4. For a slow endpoint, fix the backend first and apply mod\_reqtimeout or rate limiting to that URL so a single endpoint cannot drain the whole process pool.

### Apache average request duration too long[​](#apache-average-request-duration-too-long "Direct link to Apache average request duration too long")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
rate(apache_duration_ms_total[5m]) / (rate(apache_accesses_total[5m]) > 0) > 1000
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the access\_log LogFormat includes %D (microsecond duration), then run awk '{print $NF, $7}' access\_log | sort -rn | head -20 to find the slowest URLs;
2. If the slow URLs are dynamic requests, move on to the backend (PHP-FPM slowlog, application logs, database slow queries);
3. If static assets are slow, check disk IO and whether sendfile or caching was accidentally disabled;
4. While investigating, apply mod\_ratelimit or degrade that URL so workers are not held indefinitely.

### Apache restarted recently[​](#apache-restarted-recently "Direct link to Apache restarted recently")

S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
apache_uptime_seconds_total < 300
```

Runbook:

1. First confirm whether this was a planned release by checking change records and shell history;
2. If unplanned, run journalctl -u httpd --since '-30min' and tail -200 error\_log to determine whether it was a segfault, an OOM, or a configuration error;
3. For an OOM kill, confirm with dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' and lower MaxRequestWorkers based on real per-worker memory;
4. For repeated crashes, keep core dumps (CoreDumpDirectory) and bisect by disabling third-party modules one at a time.

## Related[​](#related "Direct link to Related")

* [Apache template source](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/tree/main/integrations/Apache): the raw JSON for dashboards, rules and collector config. Pull requests welcome.
* [Categraf `apache` plugin docs](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/tree/main/inputs/apache): every config option and the full metric list.
* [Import dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)
* [Verify that metrics are stored](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md)
* [All integrations](https://n9e.github.io/integrations.md)

# Monitor AutoMQ with Nightingale

AutoMQ exposes metrics through an OTel Collector or its own Prometheus endpoint; templates cover cluster overview, brokers, topics, consumer groups and detail.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

AutoMQ is a Kafka-compatible messaging system with separated compute and storage. It sends metrics to an OTel Collector's Prometheus exporter or exposes Prometheus-format data on its own endpoint (8890 in the reference test). Scrape that with the Categraf `prometheus` input, using whatever port your deployment configures.

The template ships five dashboards (cluster overview, broker, topic, consumer group and detail) and metric descriptions for requests, throughput, latency, storage and object-store operations. The rules cover brokers going offline, request error rate, consumer lag and failed storage operations.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **5 dashboards**, 97 panels in total
* **12 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **59 metric descriptions**
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.prometheus`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

These components expose Prometheus-format `/metrics` themselves, so the Categraf `prometheus` input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, [add it as a Nightingale data source](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md) and the templates work as they are.

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.prometheus/采集OTEL-COLLECTOR的样例.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.prometheus started` once the plugin is loaded.

   ```
   interval = 15



   [[instances]]

   urls = [

        "http://<automq-or-otel-collector>:8890/metrics"

   ]



   # AutoMQ metrics already contain an instance label; do not overwrite it.

   url_label_key = "otel_collector"

   url_label_value = "{{.Host}}"

   labels = { source = "automq" }
   ```

2. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find AutoMQ, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.

3. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled dashboards[​](#bundled-dashboards "Direct link to Bundled dashboards")

| Dashboard        | Panels |
| ---------------- | ------ |
| Broker Metrics   | 13     |
| Cluster Overview | 12     |
| Detailed Metrics | 60     |
| Group Metrics    | 2      |
| Topic Metrics    | 10     |

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

12 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### Kafka active controller count abnormal[​](#kafka-active-controller-count-abnormal "Direct link to Kafka active controller count abnormal")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(kafka_controller_active_count) by (job) != 1
```

Runbook:

1. On each broker confirm the process is alive and can reach the controller quorum;
2. In KRaft mode run kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server \<broker> describe --status to check the quorum;
3. When the count is 0, restore the failed controller nodes first — the cluster elects automatically once the majority is back;
4. When it is above 1, investigate the network partition and then stop the minority side so the cluster reconverges.

### Kafka broker has too many connections[​](#kafka-broker-has-too-many-connections "Direct link to Kafka broker has too many connections")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(kafka_server_connection_count) by (job, instance) > 1000
```

Runbook:

1. Run ss -tn state established '( sport = :9092 )' | awk '{print $5}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to see which clients the connections come from;
2. Tell more client instances apart from a connection leak (producers/consumers not being reused);
3. As an emergency measure raise the broker's file handle limit;
4. For the root cause, make clients reuse connections and confirm there is no short-lived reconnect pattern.

### Kafka fetch request latency high[​](#kafka-fetch-request-latency-high "Direct link to Kafka fetch request latency high")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
kafka_request_time_99p_milliseconds{type="Fetch"} > 1000
```

Runbook:

1. Check broker disk IO and page cache hit rate — slow Fetch usually means cold data being read from disk;
2. Check whether a consumer is replaying from a very old offset and pulling large amounts of cold data;
3. Check whether network bandwidth is saturated;
4. If it persists, add brokers or memory to raise the page cache hit rate.

### Kafka partition count too high[​](#kafka-partition-count-too-high "Direct link to Kafka partition count too high")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
kafka_partition_count > 5000
```

Runbook:

1. Run kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server \<broker> --describe to count partitions per topic and find the ones that are clearly oversized;
2. Check whether the partition count matches actual throughput — many topics are sized by guesswork;
3. Partitions can only be added, never removed, so shrinking means creating a new topic and migrating;
4. Delete long-idle abandoned topics — that is the quickest win.

### Kafka produce request latency high[​](#kafka-produce-request-latency-high "Direct link to Kafka produce request latency high")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
kafka_request_time_99p_milliseconds{type="Produce"} > 100
```

Runbook:

1. Check broker disk write latency and whether network bandwidth is saturated;
2. Check the acks setting — with acks=all latency follows the slowest replica, so look for lagging replicas;
3. Run kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions to confirm replication is healthy;
4. If the storage side is clearly the bottleneck, add brokers or move to faster disks.

### Kafka fetch requests exceed 1000 per second[​](#kafka-fetch-requests-exceed-1000-per-second "Direct link to Kafka fetch requests exceed 1000 per second")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(rate(kafka_request_count_total{type="Fetch"}[1m])) by (job, instance) > 1000
```

Runbook:

1. Check the consumer count together with fetch.min.bytes / fetch.max.wait.ms — values that are too small cause busy high-frequency polling;
2. Raising fetch.min.bytes makes consumers batch their fetches and significantly reduces request count;
3. Check whether consumers are spinning (polling frequently with no data);
4. Combine with broker CPU to judge whether to scale out.

### Kafka produce requests exceed 1000 per second[​](#kafka-produce-requests-exceed-1000-per-second "Direct link to Kafka produce requests exceed 1000 per second")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(rate(kafka_request_count_total{type="Produce"}[1m])) by (job, instance) > 1000
```

Runbook:

1. Check the producer's batch.size and linger.ms — values that are too small mean one request per message;
2. Raising linger.ms lets the producer batch and dramatically reduces the request count;
3. Check whether producers have compression enabled (compression.type);
4. Combine with broker CPU to judge whether to scale out.

### Kafka consumer lag high[​](#kafka-consumer-lag-high "Direct link to Kafka consumer lag high")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(max(kafka_log_end_offset) by (job, topic, partition)) by (job, topic)

- on (topic) group_left (consumer_group)

sum(max(kafka_group_commit_offset) by (job, consumer_group, topic, partition)) by (job, consumer_group, topic) > 10000
```

Runbook:

1. Take topic and consumer\_group from the alert labels and run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group \<group> to see the LAG distribution per partition;
2. Lag concentrated on a few partitions means data skew — check the producer's partition key;
3. Evenly spread lag means slow consumers: check the consumer logs for abnormal retries, then add consumer instances (never beyond the partition count);
4. Confirm the consumers have not all dropped out.

### Kafka S3 request failure rate high[​](#kafka-s3-request-failure-rate-high "Direct link to Kafka S3 request failure rate high")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(rate(kafka_stream_operation_latency_count{operation_type="S3Request", status="failed"}[1m])) by (job, operation_name) > 0.1
```

Runbook:

1. Take operation\_name from the alert labels to identify which operation is failing (upload, download, delete);
2. Find the matching S3 error code in the broker log and separate permissions (403), throttling (503 SlowDown) and network timeouts;
3. For throttling, ask the object storage side to raise the quota or reduce write concurrency;
4. For permissions, verify the AK/SK and bucket policy; for network issues, check connectivity and bandwidth to the object store.

### Kafka request error rate too high[​](#kafka-request-error-rate-too-high "Direct link to Kafka request error rate too high")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(rate(kafka_request_error_count_total{error!="NONE"}[1m])) by (job, instance, error) > 0.1
```

Runbook:

1. Take the error field from the alert labels to identify the error type;
2. NOT\_LEADER\_OR\_FOLLOWER usually means partition leaders are moving — check whether the cluster is rebalancing;
3. For REQUEST\_TIMED\_OUT, check broker load and disk IO;
4. For authentication/authorization errors, verify the client's ACLs and credentials.

### Kafka cluster inbound network traffic high[​](#kafka-cluster-inbound-network-traffic-high "Direct link to Kafka cluster inbound network traffic high")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(rate(kafka_broker_network_io_bytes_total{direction="in"}[1m])) by (job) > 50 * 1024 * 1024



sum(rate(kafka_broker_network_io_bytes_total{direction="in"}[1m])) by (job) > 20 * 1024 * 1024
```

Runbook:

1. Use kafka-topics.sh together with per-topic traffic metrics to find the highest-traffic topic;
2. Determine whether it is natural growth or a client resending abnormally;
3. If producers have no compression, enable compression.type=lz4/zstd — that usually cuts bandwidth immediately;
4. Once confirmed, add brokers or NIC bandwidth as needed.

### Kafka cluster outbound network traffic high[​](#kafka-cluster-outbound-network-traffic-high "Direct link to Kafka cluster outbound network traffic high")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(rate(kafka_broker_network_io_bytes_total{direction="out"}[1m])) by (job) > 50 * 1024 * 1024



sum(rate(kafka_broker_network_io_bytes_total{direction="out"}[1m])) by (job) > 20 * 1024 * 1024
```

Runbook:

1. Identify the topics and consumer groups with the highest consume traffic;
2. Check whether a consumer group is doing a full replay from the beginning — this is the most common cause of an outbound traffic spike;
3. Check whether there are far more consumers than needed, and whether groups consuming the same topic can be merged;
4. Add brokers or NIC bandwidth as needed.

| `sum by (job) (kafka_group_stable_count)`                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Sum of the number of steady-state Consumer Groups                           | count   |
| `sum by (job) (kafka_group_empty_count)`                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Sum number of empty Consumer Groups                                         | count   |
| `kafka_server_connection_count`                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Number of connections currently established by the node                     | count   |
| `kafka_broker_fenced_count`                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Number of Brokers fenced                                                    | count   |
| `sum by (job) (rate(kafka_request_error_count_total[1m]))`                                                                                                                                                                                 | Request error count sum                                                     | count   |
| `rate(kafka_request_error_count_total[1m])`                                                                                                                                                                                                | Request error count rate                                                    | count   |
| `sum by(job, instance) (rate(kafka_request_error_count_total[1m]))`                                                                                                                                                                        | Request error count rate (per instance)                                     | req/s   |
| `kafka_topic_count`                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Total number of cluster topics                                              | count   |
| `kafka_partition_total_count`                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Total number of cluster partitions                                          | count   |

# Monitor Azure Monitor with Nightingale

Pulls metrics per resource type through the Azure Monitor API, authenticating with a service principal that only needs the Monitoring Reader role.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

The Azure input calls the Azure Monitor metrics API and pulls metrics by subscription, resource group or resource type (virtual machines, storage accounts, SQL databases, App Service and so on). The config lets you name the metrics and aggregations to collect per resource type.

Register a service principal, grant it the `Monitoring Reader` role, and put the tenant ID, client ID, secret and subscription ID into the config. The Azure API allows 12,000 reads per hour, so keep the interval and metric count within that budget.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **Categraf collector config**: `input.azure`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.azure/azure.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.azure started` once the plugin is loaded.

   # 每2m查询一次azure monitor, 查询时间范围也为2m

   [[instances]]

   # can be found under Overview->Essentials in the Azure portal for your application/service

   subscription_id = ""

   # can be obtained by registering an application under Azure Active Directory

   client_id = ""

   # can be obtained by registering an application under Azure Active Directory.

   # If not specified Default Azure Credentials chain will be attempted:

   # - Environment credentials (AZURE_*)

   # - Workload Identity in Kubernetes cluster

   # - Managed Identity

   # - Azure CLI auth

   # - Developer Azure CLI auth

   client_secret = ""

   # can be found under Azure Active Directory->Properties

   tenant_id = ""

   # Define the optional Azure cloud option e.g. AzureChina, AzureGovernment or AzurePublic. The default is AzurePublic.

   # cloud_option = "AzurePublic"



   # 聚合粒度

   # 比如我采集周期是10m, 指标上报周期是30s, 那么在10m内会有20个原始点

   # 经过该参数的聚合处理后，比如聚合粒度是1m, 那么就会获取到10个点

   # 注意，最小值是1m

   # 支持的值为1m,5m,15m,30m,1h,6h,12h,1d

   # 且aggregation_interval不能大于interval

   aggregation_interval = "1m"



   ## 以下为采集目标配置，有三种方式，分别是指定资源、指定资源组、指定订阅

   ## 三种方法可同时使用

   # 方式一：指定具体的资源, 比如某台具体的主机

   # the metric names to collect

   # metrics aggregation type value to collect

   # # resource group target #1 to collect metrics from resources under it with resource type

   # [[instances.resource_group_target]]

   # resource_group = "flashcat"

   # resource_type = "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines"

   # metrics = [ "<<METRIC>>", "<<METRIC>>" ]

   # # subscription target #1 to collect metrics from resources under it with resource type

# Monitor BIND DNS with Nightingale

Collects query counts, response codes, cache and memory contexts from BIND's statistics channel (XML v3); rules watch rising SERVFAIL and unreachable servers.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

The BIND input is ported from Telegraf and reads the statistics channel of named (`http://localhost:8053/xml/v3` by default): incoming queries by type, responses by rcode, recursive clients, socket and network counters, cache state per view and memory context usage.

Configure `statistics-channels` in `named.conf` and restrict who can reach it. The rules cover rising SERVFAIL and REFUSED ratios, recursive clients near the limit, query volume dropping and named being unreachable.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **5 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.bind`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.bind/bind.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.bind started` once the plugin is loaded.

   ```
   [[instances]]

   urls = [

       # "http://localhost:8053/xml/v3",

   ]

   gather_memory_contexts = true

   gather_views = true

   timeout = "5s"

   # labels={app="bind"}
   ```

2. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Bind, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.

3. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### BIND SERVFAIL response ratio too high[​](#bind-servfail-response-ratio-too-high "Direct link to BIND SERVFAIL response ratio too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_SERVFAIL[5m])) / (sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_Response[5m])) > 0) * 100 > 5
```

Runbook:

1. Run rndc querylog to turn on query logging (remember to run it again to turn it off afterwards) and find the domains that dominate the errors in the named log;
2. Run dig +trace @127.0.0.1 \<domain> against that domain to tell whether the upstream authoritative server is unreachable, DNSSEC validation is failing, or a forwarder is broken;
3. For DNSSEC failures, verify with dig +cd first, then fix the trust anchor or temporarily add a negative-trust-anchor for that zone;
4. For forwarder problems, check that the servers in forwarders are reachable and switch to a backup DNS server.

### BIND recursive clients approaching the limit[​](#bind-recursive-clients-approaching-the-limit "Direct link to BIND recursive clients approaching the limit")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
sum without (type) (bind_counter_RecursClients) > 900
```

Runbook:

1. Run rndc status to see the live recursive client count and the configured limit;
2. Spot-check a few slow domains with dig +trace to determine whether a slow upstream authoritative server is causing recursive requests to pile up;
3. Once confirmed, raise recursive-clients in options (re-checking memory) and run rndc reload;
4. If malicious queries are filling the quota, configure response-rate-limit and tighten the source networks allowed by allow-recursion.

### BIND hit the recursive client limit and is dropping queries[​](#bind-hit-the-recursive-client-limit-and-is-dropping-queries "Direct link to BIND hit the recursive client limit and is dropping queries")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum without (type) (increase(bind_counter_RecLimitDropped[5m])) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run rndc status immediately to confirm recursive client usage;
2. Run rndc recursing to dump the queries currently being resolved and identify the domain or client consuming the quota;
3. As an emergency measure raise recursive-clients and run rndc reload to restore service;
4. Afterwards check the health of the upstream authoritative servers for the domain you identified, or restrict the offending source IPs with allow-recursion or RRL.

### BIND recursive query timeout ratio too high[​](#bind-recursive-query-timeout-ratio-too-high "Direct link to BIND recursive query timeout ratio too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_QueryTimeout[5m])) / ((sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_Queryv4[5m])) + sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_Queryv6[5m]))) > 0) * 100 > 10
```

Runbook:

1. Run rndc dumpdb -all and inspect the dump file for slow upstream servers;
2. From the BIND host run dig @\<authoritative IP> plus ping/mtr to separate an upstream outage from packet loss on this host's egress;
3. If IPv6 is unreachable and causing the timeouts, add -4 to the named start-up arguments or disable outbound IPv6 queries;
4. Longer term, add forwarders and enable forward first to reduce the share of queries recursed directly to authoritative servers.

### BIND is dropping queries[​](#bind-is-dropping-queries "Direct link to BIND is dropping queries")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum without (type) (increase(bind_counter_QryDropped[5m])) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Look for client-related dropped entries in the named log and identify the source IPs and query names being dropped;
2. If the source is a legitimate business network, check whether the allow-query / allow-recursion ACLs are missing that range;
3. If the sources are scattered and the query names look random, treat it as a random-subdomain attack: enable response-rate-limit and consider adding a fetches-per-zone limit;
4. After changing the configuration, validate it with named-checkconf before running rndc reload.

## Related[​](#related "Direct link to Related")

* [Bind template source](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/tree/main/integrations/Bind): the raw JSON for dashboards, rules and collector config. Pull requests welcome.
* [Categraf `bind` plugin docs](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/tree/main/inputs/bind): every config option and the full metric list.
* [Import dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md)

# Monitor cAdvisor with Nightingale

Scrapes the cAdvisor built into kubelet or a standalone one for per-container CPU, memory, filesystem and network metrics; in kubelet mode it can attach Pod labels and annotations.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

The cAdvisor input collects the `container_*` metrics that cAdvisor exposes: per-container CPU usage and throttling, memory working set and OOM events, filesystem reads and writes, network traffic and drops. Two ways to connect: `type = "kubelet"` scrapes the kubelet's `/metrics/cadvisor` (port 10250, authenticated) and can attach Pod labels and annotations to the metrics; `type = "cadvisor"` scrapes a standalone cAdvisor (port 8080 by default).

The dashboard shows resource usage per container and the metric reference explains each `container_*` metric. The rules cover CPU throttling, memory near the limit, OOM kills and network drops.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **6 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **45 metric descriptions**

   # # collect interval

   # url = "https://1.2.3.4:10250"

   # type = "kubelet"

   ## url = "http://1.2.3.4:8080/metrics"

   ## type = "cadvisor"



   # url_label_key = "instance"

   # url_label_value = "{{.Host}}"

   # bearer_token_string = "eyJlonglongxxxx.eyJlonglongyyyy.oQsXlonglongZZZ"

   ## bearer_token_file = "/path/to/token/file"



   # ignore_label_keys = ["id","name", "container_label*"]

   ## choose_label_keys = ["id"]



   # timeout = "3s"

| --------- | ------ |
| cAdvisor  | 5      |

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

6 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### Container memory approaching its limit[​](#container-memory-approaching-its-limit "Direct link to Container memory approaching its limit")

S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
container_memory_working_set_bytes{name!=""} / (container_spec_memory_limit_bytes{name!=""} > 0) * 100 > 90
```

Runbook:

1. Take name from the alert labels and run docker stats \<name> or kubectl top pod to confirm live usage;
2. Use the application's own memory analysis inside the container (jmap -histo:live for Java, pprof heap for Go) to separate normal growth from a leak;
3. If the limit is simply too small, raise it and redeploy, adjusting the application's own heap ceiling to match (-Xmx must leave room for off-heap memory);
4. If it is a leak, estimate the remaining runway from the growth rate and add an automatic restart as a stopgap while you investigate the code.

### Container OOM killed[​](#container-oom-killed "Direct link to Container OOM killed")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
increase(container_oom_events_total{name!=""}[10m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Take name from the alert labels and confirm the OOMKilled state via the State.OOMKilled field in docker inspect \<name> output or with kubectl describe pod;
2. Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to find the killed process and its memory usage at the time;
3. Compare that usage against the limit and raise the limit if it is clearly too small;
4. If usage looks abnormal, investigate it as a memory leak; for Java, -Xmx must be smaller than the container limit with room for off-heap memory or an OOM is guaranteed.

### Container CPU heavily throttled[​](#container-cpu-heavily-throttled "Direct link to Container CPU heavily throttled")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{name!=""}[5m]) / (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{name!=""}[5m]) > 0) * 100 > 25
```

Runbook:

1. Take name from the alert labels and confirm the growth of nr\_throttled and throttled\_usec with cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat (cgroup v2);
2. Compare actual CPU usage against the limit; being throttled while below the limit usually means bursts are being sliced up by the 100 ms period, so raise the limit slightly or lower in-period concurrency;
3. A common trigger is a JVM or Go runtime sizing thread pools from the host core count; set GOMAXPROCS or -XX:ActiveProcessorCount to match the limit;
4. If more compute is genuinely needed, raise the CPU limit and watch the throttling ratio fall.

### Container filesystem usage too high[​](#container-filesystem-usage-too-high "Direct link to Container filesystem usage too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
container_fs_usage_bytes{name!=""} / (container_fs_limit_bytes{name!=""} > 0) * 100 > 85
```

Runbook:

1. Take name and device from the alert labels and run docker exec \<name> du -sh /\* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head to find the biggest consumers;
2. In the vast majority of cases application logs are not being rotated: configure logrotate or switch to writing to stdout and let the runtime rotate them;
3. If the writable layer is filling up, mount a volume for directories that need persistence rather than writing into the layer;
4. As an emergency measure run docker system prune to reclaim host space from unused images and stopped containers.

### Container restarting repeatedly[​](#container-restarting-repeatedly "Direct link to Container restarting repeatedly")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
changes(container_start_time_seconds{name!=""}[1h]) > 3
```

Runbook:

1. Take name from the alert labels and run docker logs --tail 200 \<name> or kubectl logs --previous to read the logs from before the last exit;
2. Run docker inspect \<name> and check State.ExitCode and State.OOMKilled in the output to distinguish an OOM, a deliberate application exit, and a failing health check;
3. Handle OOMKilled as a memory alert; for a non-zero exit code, find the start-up failure in the application logs (missing configuration, dependency not ready);
4. If a health check is the cause, confirm the probe's initial delay is longer than the real start-up time and raise the start period if needed.

### Container network receive packet drops[​](#container-network-receive-packet-drops "Direct link to Container network receive packet drops")

S3 Info · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
rate(container_network_receive_packets_dropped_total{name!=""}[5m]) > 1
```

Runbook:

1. Take name from the alert labels and run docker exec \<name> cat /proc/net/dev plus ss -s to check drops and queue state;
2. If the receive queue is overflowing, raise the kernel's net.core.netdev\_max\_backlog and the application's accept queue (somaxconn);
3. Check whether the host NIC is also dropping packets (ethtool -S \<nic> | grep -i drop); if the problem is at the host level, do not chase it inside the container;
4. If traffic genuinely exceeds the container's networking capacity, evaluate switching to host networking or raising the bandwidth allocation.

## Metric reference[​](#metric-reference "Direct link to Metric reference")

# Monitor Ceph with Nightingale

Enable Ceph's prometheus mgr module and scrape port 9283; templates cover cluster health, OSDs, PGs, pool capacity and IOPS.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Ceph's mgr ships a prometheus module: after `ceph mgr module enable prometheus`, `/metrics` is served on port 9283 and the Categraf `prometheus` input scrapes it without any dedicated plugin.

The dashboard covers cluster health, OSD availability and capacity, PG state distribution, usage and IOPS per pool, and MON quorum. The rules cover HEALTH\_WARN and HEALTH\_ERR, OSDs down, abnormal PGs, pools near capacity and loss of MON quorum.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **1 dashboard**, 57 panels in total
* **15 alert rules**, each with runbook steps

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

These components expose Prometheus-format `/metrics` themselves, so the Categraf `prometheus` input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, [add it as a Nightingale data source](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md) and the templates work as they are.

```
# conf/input.prometheus/ceph.toml

[[instances]]

urls = ["http://<ceph-mgr>:9283/metrics"]

labels = { service = "ceph", cluster = "ceph-cluster-001" }
```

1. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Ceph, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.
2. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled dashboards[​](#bundled-dashboards "Direct link to Bundled dashboards")

| Dashboard                  | Panels |
| -------------------------- | ------ |
| Ceph - Cluster By Categraf | 57     |

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

15 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### CephErrorState[​](#cepherrorstate "Direct link to CephErrorState")

Ceph is in Error state longer than 5m, please check status of pools and OSDs

S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_health_status > 1
```

Runbook:

1. Immediately run ceph health detail to see which ERR item it is;
2. Common ones are inactive/incomplete PGs, many down OSDs, or a full OSD forcing the cluster read-only;
3. Restore the down OSDs or free space on the full OSD first — this is the root cause of the vast majority of ERRs;
4. Do not scale or adjust the crush map during recovery, as it worsens data migration.

### CephOsdReweighted[​](#cephosdreweighted "Direct link to CephOsdReweighted")

OSD {{ $labels.ceph\_daemon}} on cluster {{ $labels.cluster}} was reweighted for too long. Please either create silent or fix that issue

S2 Warning · for 60 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_osd_weight < 1
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph osd tree to see which OSD is down-weighted and to what;
2. Determine whether it was a manual reweight or an automatic reweight-by-utilization;
3. If the fault is resolved, run ceph osd reweight \<id> 1.0 to restore the weight and let data backfill;
4. If it was down-weighted to balance capacity, consider using the balancer module instead.

### CephOSDUtilization[​](#cephosdutilization "Direct link to CephOSDUtilization")

Osd free space for {{ $labels.osd }} is higher tan 90%. Please validate why its so big, reweight or add storage

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_osd_utilization > 90
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph osd df to see the utilization spread and whether it is one OSD or the cluster as a whole;
2. For a single hot OSD, check ceph balancer status and run ceph balancer on if it is disabled;
3. If the cluster as a whole is near full you must add OSDs, or first delete unused pools/snapshots to free space;
4. Temporarily raising mon\_osd\_full\_ratio buys time but is a dangerous operation and must be paired with real expansion.

### CephPgActivating[​](#cephpgactivating "Direct link to CephPgActivating")

Some groups are activating for too long on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Those PGs are unavailable for too long!

S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_pg_activating > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph -s and ceph health detail for the overall state and the specific warnings;
2. Use ceph pg dump\_stuck and ceph pg \<pgid> query to locate the stuck PGs and why;
3. In most cases the root cause is a down OSD or a full disk — restore the OSD or free space and the PGs return to active+clean automatically;
4. Watch with ceph -w during recovery and avoid other operations that add load.

### CephPgBackfillTooFull[​](#cephpgbackfilltoofull "Direct link to CephPgBackfillTooFull")

Some groups are located on full OSD on cluster {{ $labels.cluster }}. Those PGs can be unavailable shortly. Please check OSDs, change weight or reconfigure CRUSH rules.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_pg_backfill_toofull > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph osd df to find the OSDs short on space;
2. Freeing space or adding OSDs is the real fix;
3. As an emergency measure raise osd\_backfill\_full\_ratio so backfill continues, but only if the disks genuinely have headroom;
4. Avoid taking further OSDs offline before backfill completes, or redundancy drops further.

### CephPgDown[​](#cephpgdown "Direct link to CephPgDown")

Some groups are down (unavailable) for too long on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Please ensure that all the data are available

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_pg_down > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph pg \<pgid> query to see why it is down, focusing on which OSDs blocked\_by points to;
2. Bringing those OSDs back online is the most direct fix — usually a disk or host failure;
3. If an OSD genuinely cannot be recovered, assess the data loss risk of an osd lost operation before running it;
4. Record every step: decisions involving data loss should be reviewed by a second person.

### CephPgIncomplete[​](#cephpgincomplete "Direct link to CephPgIncomplete")

Some groups are incomplete (unavailable) for too long on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Please ensure that all the data are available

S1 Critical · for 2 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_pg_incomplete > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph -s and ceph health detail for the overall state and the specific warnings;
2. Use ceph pg dump\_stuck and ceph pg \<pgid> query to locate the stuck PGs and why;
3. In most cases the root cause is a down OSD or a full disk — restore the OSD or free space and the PGs return to active+clean automatically;
4. Watch with ceph -w during recovery and avoid other operations that add load.

### CephPgInconsistent[​](#cephpginconsistent "Direct link to CephPgInconsistent")

Some groups are inconsistent for too long on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Data is available but inconsistent across nodes

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_pg_inconsistent > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Use ceph health detail to find the inconsistent PGs, then rados list-inconsistent-obj \<pgid> for the specific objects;
2. Run ceph pg repair \<pgid> to trigger repair — Ceph overwrites from the authoritative copy;
3. Before repairing, confirm which copy is bad: if the primary itself is corrupt, verify the authoritative copy is trustworthy first;
4. An OSD that repeatedly produces inconsistencies should have its SMART checked — it is usually bad sectors and the disk should be replaced.

### CephPgUnavailable[​](#cephpgunavailable "Direct link to CephPgUnavailable")

Some groups are unavailable on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Please check their detailed status and current configuration.

S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_pg_total - ceph_pg_active > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph -s and ceph health detail for the overall state and the specific warnings;
2. Use ceph pg dump\_stuck and ceph pg \<pgid> query to locate the stuck PGs and why;
3. In most cases the root cause is a down OSD or a full disk — restore the OSD or free space and the PGs return to active+clean automatically;
4. Watch with ceph -w during recovery and avoid other operations that add load.

### CephTargetDown[​](#cephtargetdown "Direct link to CephTargetDown")

CEPH target down for more than 2m, please check - it could be a either exporter crash or a whole cluster crash

S1 Critical · for 10 min · Trigger:

```
up{job="ceph"} == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Confirm the node running ceph exporter / mgr is alive and the process is running;
2. Run ceph -s on any mon node to confirm by hand whether the cluster itself is healthy;
3. A failed mgr causes many metrics to disappear — run ceph mgr fail to switch to the standby mgr;
4. After collection resumes, note the data gap and remember there were no alerts during the blind window.

### CephWarnState[​](#cephwarnstate "Direct link to CephWarnState")

Ceph is in Warn state longer than 30m, please check status of pools and OSDs

S2 Warning · for 30 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_health_status == 1
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph health detail to see exactly which WARN items are present;
2. Common ones are a single down OSD, PGs not clean, clock skew and pools without pg\_autoscale;
3. Work through them following the guidance — Ceph's health detail usually gives explicit instructions;
4. Once done, confirm ceph -s returns to HEALTH\_OK.

### MonitorAvailableStorage[​](#monitoravailablestorage "Direct link to MonitorAvailableStorage")

Monitor storage for {{ $labels.monitor }} less than 30% - please check why its too high

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_monitor_avail_percent < 30
```

Runbook:

1. Run df -h to check the free space on the partition holding /var/lib/ceph/mon;
2. The most common reason the mon directory grows is a cluster that has been unclean for a long time, preventing osdmap trimming — fix the cluster health first;
3. Run ceph tell mon.\<id> compact to trigger rocksdb compaction and reclaim space;
4. Longer term, give mon its own larger disk.

### MonitorClockSkewTooHigh[​](#monitorclockskewtoohigh "Direct link to MonitorClockSkewTooHigh")

Monitor clock skew detected on {{ $labels.monitor }} - please check ntp and hardware clock settings

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
abs(ceph_monitor_clock_skew_seconds) > 0.1
```

Runbook:

1. On each mon node run chronyc tracking to check the offset and upstream source state;
2. Confirm every mon node uses the same set of NTP sources;
3. Start chronyd where it is not running and enable it at boot; where the offset is large, use chronyc makestep to step the clock;
4. After correcting the time, confirm with ceph -s that the clock skew warning is gone.

### OsdApplyLatencyTooHigh[​](#osdapplylatencytoohigh "Direct link to OsdApplyLatencyTooHigh")

OSD latency for {{ $labels.osd }} is too high. Please check if it doesn't stuck in weird state

S2 Warning · for 90s · Trigger:

```
ceph_osd_perf_apply_latency_seconds > 10
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph osd perf to see commit/apply latency per OSD and whether it is isolated or widespread;
2. For a single slow OSD, go to that node and use iostat -x 1 and smartctl to check disk health and saturation;
3. If it is widespread, check whether a large recovery/backfill is running and lower osd\_max\_backfills to reduce the impact;
4. For a failing disk, follow the replacement procedure.

### OsdDown[​](#osddown "Direct link to OsdDown")

OSD is down longer than 30 min, please check what's the status

S2 Warning · for 30 min · Trigger:

```
ceph_osd_up == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run ceph osd tree to identify the OSD and its node;
2. On that node use systemctl status ceph-osd@\<id> and its logs to find the cause (disk failure, OOM, process crash);
3. If the disk is fine, just start the OSD; if the disk failed, follow the replacement procedure and ceph osd out to migrate data away;
4. Watch recovery progress with ceph -s and avoid taking more OSDs offline.

# Monitor ClickHouse with Nightingale

Reads system.metrics, system.events and system.asynchronous\_metrics over HTTP; queries, merges, replication queues and memory all come with metric descriptions.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

The ClickHouse input queries the system tables over HTTP (port 8123 by default): `system.metrics`, `system.events`, `system.asynchronous_metrics`, `system.parts` and others. That yields concurrent queries, merges and mutations, replication queue and lag, memory and caches, part counts and ZooKeeper sessions. Verified against a real ClickHouse 24.8 workload.

The two dashboards use different metric families and are not interchangeable: `ClickHouse_Categraf` expects this input, `ClickHouse_Exporter` expects the `clickhouse_*` metrics from ClickHouse's built-in Prometheus endpoint. The rules cover query backlog, replication lag, too many parts, memory near the limit and lost ZooKeeper sessions.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **2 dashboards**, 26 panels in total
* **10 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **81 metric descriptions**
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.clickhouse`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.clickhouse/clickhouse.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.clickhouse started` once the plugin is loaded.

   ```
   # # collect interval

   # interval = 15



   # Read metrics from one or many ClickHouse servers

   [[instances]]

     ## Username for authorization on ClickHouse server

     username = "default"



     ## Password for authorization on ClickHouse server

     # password = ""



     ## HTTP(s) timeout while getting metrics values

     ## The timeout includes connection time, any redirects, and reading the

     ## response body.

     # timeout = 5



     ## List of servers for metrics scraping

     ## metrics scrape via HTTP(s) clickhouse interface

     ## https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/interfaces/http/

     # servers = ["http://127.0.0.1:8123"]



     ## If "auto_discovery"" is "true" plugin tries to connect to all servers

     ## available in the cluster with using same "user:password" described in

     ## "user" and "password" parameters and get this server hostname list from

     ## "system.clusters" table. See

     ## - https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/operations/system_tables/#system-clusters

     ## - https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/operations/server_settings/settings/#server_settings_remote_servers

     ## - https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/operations/table_engines/distributed/

     ## - https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/operations/table_engines/replication/#creating-replicated-tables

     # auto_discovery = true



     ## Filter cluster names in "system.clusters" when "auto_discovery" is "true"

     ## when this filter present then "WHERE cluster IN (...)" filter will apply

     ## please use only full cluster names here, regexp and glob filters is not

     ## allowed for "/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/remote.xml"

     ## <yandex>

     ##  <remote_servers>

     ##    <my-own-cluster>

     ##        <shard>

     ##          <replica><host>clickhouse-ru-1.local</host><port>9000</port></replica>

     ##          <replica><host>clickhouse-ru-2.local</host><port>9000</port></replica>

     ##        </shard>

     ##        <shard>

     ##          <replica><host>clickhouse-eu-1.local</host><port>9000</port></replica>

     ##          <replica><host>clickhouse-eu-2.local</host><port>9000</port></replica>

     ##        </shard>

     ##    </my-own-cluster>

     ##  </remote_servers>

     ##

     ## </yandex>

     ##

     ## example: cluster_include = ["my-own-cluster"]

     # cluster_include = []



     ## Filter cluster names in "system.clusters" when "auto_discovery" is

     ## "true" when this filter present then "WHERE cluster NOT IN (...)"

     ## filter will apply

     ##    example: cluster_exclude = ["my-internal-not-discovered-cluster"]

     # cluster_exclude = []



     ## Optional TLS Config

     # tls_ca = "/etc/telegraf/ca.pem"

     # tls_cert = "/etc/telegraf/cert.pem"

     # tls_key = "/etc/telegraf/key.pem"

     ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification

     # insecure_skip_verify = false



       # [[instances.metrics]]

       # measurement = "sessions"

       # metric_fields = [ "value" ]

       # timeout = "3s"

       # request = '''

       # SELECT count() AS value FROM system.processes

       # '''
   ```

2. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find ClickHouse, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.

3. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled dashboards[​](#bundled-dashboards "Direct link to Bundled dashboards")
