# Monitor SMART with Nightingale

Runs smartctl to read S.M.A.R.T. health attributes from HDDs, SSDs and NVMe drives, so you see reallocated sectors, temperature and wear before a disk actually dies.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

S.M.A.R.T. is the self-monitoring built into hard drives and SSDs. The Categraf smart input runs `smartctl` (and the `nvme` tool for NVMe devices) and emits `smart_device` for overall health plus `smart_attribute` for individual attributes: reallocated sectors, pending sectors, temperature, power-on hours, SSD wear and more.

The bundled rules watch the precursors of data loss: failed health checks, growing reallocated-sector counts and high temperature. The host needs smartmontools installed and Categraf needs permission to run smartctl, usually via passwordless sudo.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **1 dashboard**, 20 panels in total
* **6 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **14 metric descriptions**
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.smart`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.smart/smart.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.smart started` once the plugin is loaded.

   ```
   # Read metrics from storage devices supporting S.M.A.R.T.

   [[instances]]

       ## Optionally specify the path to the smartctl executable

       # path_smartctl = "/usr/bin/smartctl"



       ## Optionally specify the path to the nvme-cli executable

       # path_nvme = "/usr/bin/nvme"



       ## Optionally specify if vendor specific attributes should be propagated for NVMe disk case

       ## ["auto-on"] - automatically find and enable additional vendor specific disk info

       ## ["vendor1", "vendor2", ...] - e.g. "Intel" enable additional Intel specific disk info

       #  enable_extensions = ["auto-on"]



       ## On most platforms used cli utilities requires root access.

       ## Setting 'use_sudo' to true will make use of sudo to run smartctl or nvme-cli.

       ## Sudo must be configured to allow the telegraf user to run smartctl or nvme-cli

       ## without a password.

       # use_sudo = true



       ## Skip checking disks in this power mode. Defaults to

       ## "standby" to not wake up disks that have stopped rotating.

       ## See --nocheck in the man pages for smartctl.

       ## smartctl version 5.41 and 5.42 have faulty detection of

       ## power mode and might require changing this value to

       ## "never" depending on your disks.

       # nocheck = "standby"



       ## Gather all returned S.M.A.R.T. attribute metrics and the detailed

       ## information from each drive into the 'smart_attribute' measurement.

       # attributes = true



       ## Optionally specify devices to exclude from reporting if disks auto-discovery is performed.

       # excludes = [ "/dev/pass6" ]



       ## Optionally specify devices and device type, if unset

       ## a scan (smartctl --scan and smartctl --scan -d nvme) for S.M.A.R.T. devices will be done

       ## and all found will be included except for the excluded in excludes.

       # devices = [ "/dev/ada0 -d atacam", "/dev/nvme0"]

       # devices = ["dev/nvme0 -d nvme", "/dev/nvme0"]



       ## Timeout for the cli command to complete.

         timeout = "30s"



       ## Optionally call smartctl and nvme-cli with a specific concurrency policy.

       ## By default, smartctl and nvme-cli are called in separate threads (goroutines) to gather disk attributes.

       ## Some devices (e.g. disks in RAID arrays) may have access limitations that require sequential reading of

       ## SMART data - one individual array drive at the time. In such case please set this configuration option

       ## to "sequential" to get readings for all drives.

       ## valid options: concurrent, sequential

       # read_method = "concurrent"
   ```

2. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find SMART, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.

3. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled dashboards[​](#bundled-dashboards "Direct link to Bundled dashboards")

| Dashboard           | Panels |
| ------------------- | ------ |
| S.M.A.R.T Dashboard | 20     |

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

6 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### SMART device health status abnormal[​](#smart-device-health-status-abnormal "Direct link to SMART device health status abnormal")

Disk self-assessed overall health is FAILED, serious failure risk, handle immediately

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
smart_device_health_ok == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX for the full attribute list, focusing on Reallocated\_Sector\_Ct, Current\_Pending\_Sector and Offline\_Uncorrectable;
2. Immediately confirm the data on this disk has a replica or backup — this is the highest priority action;
3. In a RAID array, check the array state and let it evict this disk and rebuild onto a hot spare;
4. Schedule downtime to replace the disk and stop writing to it.

### SSD media wearout >= 90%[​](#ssd-media-wearout--90 "Direct link to SSD media wearout >= 90%")

SSD flash wearout is nearly exhausted and may fail at any time; back up data and replace the drive immediately

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
smart_attribute_media_wear_percentage >= 90
```

Runbook:

1. Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and check Media\_Wearout\_Indicator / Percentage\_Used together with Total\_LBAs\_Written;
2. Combine with the write rate to estimate remaining life and plan the replacement window;
3. Confirm the data on this disk has a replica and prepare the migration plan in advance;
4. Review the source of write amplification (log level, frequent small writes, no TRIM) so the replacement does not repeat it.

### Disk temperature exceeds 65 Celsius[​](#disk-temperature-exceeds-65-celsius "Direct link to Disk temperature exceeds 65 Celsius")

Disk operating temperature too high, which accelerates aging or causes outright failure; check cooling immediately

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
smart_device_temp_c > 65
```

Runbook:

1. Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and compare the temperature against the vendor's rated maximum;
2. Check chassis airflow, fan speeds and dust in the filters, plus the room's ambient temperature;
3. Check whether the bay layout is too dense and whether neighbouring disks are equally hot;
4. Short term, reduce IO pressure on this disk (shift backups off peak, move hot data) to buy time.

### CRC error count keeps growing within 1 hour[​](#crc-error-count-keeps-growing-within-1-hour "Direct link to CRC error count keeps growing within 1 hour")

Growing CRC failures on the data link, a possible precursor of interface, cable or disk controller failure

S1 Critical · for 60 min · Trigger:

```
increase(smart_attribute_crc_error_count[1h]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and check how fast UDMA\_CRC\_Error\_Count is growing;
2. Take the machine down, reseat the SATA/SAS data and power cables, and preferably just replace the cable;
3. After replacing the cable, watch whether the counter stops growing — SMART counters never reset, so judge by the delta, not the absolute value;
4. If a new cable does not help, suspect the backplane or HBA and swap them one at a time.

### SSD erase fail count growing[​](#ssd-erase-fail-count-growing "Direct link to SSD erase fail count growing")

SSD flash block erase failures indicate aging flash chips and a risk of write failures

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
increase(smart_attribute_erase_fail_count[1h]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and check Erase\_Fail\_Count together with the remaining Reallocated/Available\_Reservd\_Space;
2. A shrinking spare block pool means the disk is near end of life — confirm the data has a replica immediately;
3. Schedule a replacement rather than waiting for writes to fail outright;
4. Reduce write pressure on the disk beforehand so it does not degrade faster.

### SSD program fail count growing[​](#ssd-program-fail-count-growing "Direct link to SSD program fail count growing")

SSD flash block program failures; flash chip health is degrading rapidly, back up data immediately

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
increase(smart_attribute_program_fail_count[1h]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and check Program\_Fail\_Count together with the remaining spare block ratio;
2. Immediately confirm the data on this disk has a replica or backup — this is the highest priority action;
3. Schedule a replacement soon: program failures often come with a risk of silent data corruption;
4. Before replacing it, make the disk read-only or move hot data off to stop further writes.

## Metric reference[​](#metric-reference "Direct link to Metric reference")

14 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on.

| Metric                                             | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Unit |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---- |
| `smart_attribute_crc_error_count`                  | SMART CRC Error Count — The number of Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) failures during hard disk data transmission, reflecting the reliability of the data transmission link.                                                           |      |
| `smart_attribute_end_to_end_error_detection_count` | SMART End-to-End Error Detection Count — The number of end-to-end verification failures in internal hard disk data transmission, associated with the health of hard disk firmware or physical storage units.                         |      |
| `smart_attribute_erase_fail_count`                 | SMART Erase Fail Count — The number of failures when a Solid State Drive (SSD) erases flash memory blocks; an excessive number may indicate flash chip aging or an increase in bad blocks.                                           |      |
| `smart_attribute_host_reads`                       | SMART Host Reads Count — The total number of times the operating system reads data from the hard disk, which is a statistical indicator of hard disk usage with no direct fault warning significance.                                |      |
| `smart_attribute_media_wear_percentage`            | SMART Media Wear Percentage — A core indicator dedicated to Solid State Drives (SSDs) that reflects the wear level of flash memory chips; the closer the value is to 100%, the shorter the lifespan.                                 | %    |
| `smart_attribute_pll_lock_loss_count`              | SMART PLL Lock Loss Count — The number of times the hard disk clock synchronization module (Phase-Locked Loop, PLL) loses lock, which can cause data transmission timing errors.                                                     |      |
| `smart_attribute_program_fail_count`               | SMART Program Fail Count — The number of failures when a Solid State Drive (SSD) writes data (program operation) to flash memory blocks, which is a core indicator of flash memory health.                                           |      |
| `smart_attribute_retry_buffer_overflow_count`      | SMART Retry Buffer Overflow Count — The number of times the data buffer overflows when the hard disk automatically retries after a read/write failure, indicating a decline in hard disk read/write performance or hardware failure. |      |
| `smart_attribute_thermal_throttle_status`          | SMART Thermal Throttle Status — The state where the hard disk triggers automatic speed reduction protection due to high temperature (1=triggered, 0=not triggered), which will cause slow read/write speeds after triggering.        |      |
| `smart_attribute_timed_workload_timer`             | SMART Timed Workload Timer — Accumulates the operating time of the hard disk in a preset load mode, used to evaluate the long-term working intensity of the hard disk and assist in judging the wear rate.                           | s    |
| `smart_attribute_wear_leveling_count`              | SMART Wear Leveling Count — An indicator dedicated to Solid State Drives (SSDs) that records the number of executions of the wear leveling algorithm to ensure uniform wear of flash memory blocks and extend lifespan.              |      |
| `smart_device_exit_status`                         | SMART Device Exit Status — The exit status code of the hard disk SMART self-test; 0 means the self-test is completed normally, and a non-zero value indicates self-test interruption or abnormality.                                 |      |
| `smart_device_health_ok`                           | SMART Device Health Status — The overall health status identifier of the hard disk; 1=healthy (no fault warning), 0=unhealthy (potential faults exist).                                                                              |      |
| `smart_device_temp_c`                              | SMART Device Temperature — The current operating temperature of the hard disk (in ℃); the safe operating range for mainstream hard disks is 0-60℃, and prolonged overheating will accelerate hardware aging.                         | ℃    |

# Monitor network devices over SNMP with Nightingale

Collect any network device by listing OIDs, with OID values usable as labels; the template ships Cisco, Juniper and generic switch dashboards and dozens of rules.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Categraf has included Telegraf's snmp input since v0.2.13. The idea is simple: list the OIDs for the metrics you want. `[[instances.field]]` reads single values, `[[instances.table]]` walks a table into multiple rows, and selected OIDs in a table (interface names, say) can become labels. Generic OIDs for interface traffic, errors and state work on almost every device; vendor-specific OIDs for CPU and memory are configured per vendor and model.

The template ships dashboards for a generic switch overview, device traffic, access switches, and Cisco and Juniper device detail. The rules cover interfaces going down, traffic near bandwidth, errors and discards, high CPU and memory, and unreachable devices. The `Cisco.toml` in the template directory is a starting point for per-model configs.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **9 dashboards**, 74 panels in total
* **37 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **5 metric descriptions**
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.snmp`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md) and enable the plugins you need. Each config goes in its own `conf/input.<plugin>/` directory; fill in addresses and credentials, then restart Categraf.

   `conf/input.snmp/Cisco.toml`

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

37 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

Rules are grouped by collector; import the group that matches how you collect.

### Collected by Categraf (25)[​](#collected-by-categraf-25 "Direct link to Collected by Categraf (25)")

#### H3C power supply state abnormal[​](#h3c-power-supply-state-abnormal "Direct link to H3C power supply state abnormal")

Normal state is 2 alert after 3 consecutive checks != 2

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
snmp_system_power_status{Brand='H3C'} != 2
```

Runbook:

1. Log in and run display power to identify the faulty power slot;
2. On site, check the power module indicator, the supply line and the PDU output;
3. If the line is fine, treat it as a power module hardware fault and start the replacement process;
4. Before replacing, confirm the other feed is healthy so the device does not lose power mid-operation.

#### H3C device CPU usage exceeds 70%[​](#h3c-device-cpu-usage-exceeds-70 "Direct link to H3C device CPU usage exceeds 70%")

CPU usage above 70% for 10 consecutive minutes

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger:

```
snmp_system_cpuuse{Brand='H3C'}>70
```

Runbook:

1. Log in and run display cpu-usage (Huawei/H3C) or show system processes (Juniper) to see which process is busy;
2. Common root causes are route flapping, an ARP/broadcast storm, an excessive number of ACL rules, or being scanned;
3. Use display interface brief to spot abnormal port traffic and capture packets to find the broadcast storm source;
4. Isolate the offending port or tune the configuration; if load stays high, evaluate whether the device has hit its capacity limit.

#### H3C device memory usage exceeds 70%[​](#h3c-device-memory-usage-exceeds-70 "Direct link to H3C device memory usage exceeds 70%")

Memory usage above 70% for 2 consecutive minutes

S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger:

```
snmp_system_memuse{Brand='H3C'}>70
```

Runbook:

1. Log in and run display memory-usage to see the memory breakdown;
2. Check whether the routing table or ARP table has grown abnormally (display ip routing-table statistics, display arp statistics);
3. Common root causes are route leaks, ARP attacks, or fragmentation on a device that has not been restarted for a long time;
4. Improve route aggregation and ARP ageing, and schedule a maintenance window restart if needed.

#### H3C device fan state abnormal[​](#h3c-device-fan-state-abnormal "Direct link to H3C device fan state abnormal")

Normal state is 2 alert after 3 consecutive checks != 2

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
snmp_system_fan_status{Brand='H3C'} != 2
```

Runbook:

1. Log in and run display fan to identify the faulty fan slot;
2. At the same time run display temperature to confirm whether temperature has already risen;
3. On site, check whether the fan is seized and whether the filter is clogged; clean and retest;
4. Replace the fan module promptly once a hardware fault is confirmed; if temperature is already high, reduce device load or improve room cooling first.

#### ICMP timeout[​](#icmp-timeout "Direct link to ICMP timeout")

0 = no response 1 = responding If all requests within 1 minute get no response, the device is considered lost

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
max_over_time(snmp_icmp_up{}[1m]) == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Ping again from another subnet to rule out a single-path problem, and use traceroute to find where it breaks;
2. Try SSH/Telnet to the device — if you can log in, ICMP is being blocked by policy rather than the device being down;
3. If it is completely unreachable, go on site and check the power and indicator lights;
4. Confirm whether the services behind it have failed over to a redundant path, and restore traffic first if not.

#### Incoming bandwidth usage high[​](#incoming-bandwidth-usage-high "Direct link to Incoming bandwidth usage high")

snmp\_interface\_incoming is the cumulative inbound traffic in bytes per second; rate(snmp\_interface\_incoming{}\[1m]) \* 8 gives inbound traffic per second in bit/s snmp\_interface\_speed is the maximum transmission rate of the interface

This condition means actual inbound traffic exceeds 90% of the bandwidth

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
(rate(snmp_interface_incoming{}[1m]) * 8 / 10^9) > ((snmp_interface_speed{}/ 10^3) *0.9) and snmp_interface_speed >0
```

Runbook:

1. Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface \<port> to confirm the actual rate and peak;
2. Use NetFlow/sFlow or capture traffic on the upstream device to find which sources/destinations consume the bandwidth;
3. Determine whether it is normal growth, a backup job, or abnormal traffic (attack, loop);
4. For genuine growth, upgrade the link or use link aggregation; for abnormal traffic, rate limit or isolate it first.

#### Interface Down[​](#interface-down "Direct link to Interface Down")

SNMP metric notes: snmp\_interface\_admin\_status: up = 1, down = 2, testing = 3 Alert rule: latest snmp\_interface\_admin\_status == up was up at least once in the last 14 days (offset 1h avoids alerting right at the down-to-up transition) latest ostatus != 1 checked every 60s, alert after 3 consecutive matches

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
snmp_interface_admin_status{ifname!~'^(vlan|Vlanif|VLAN|V|irb|gr-).*'} == 1 and min_over_time(snmp_interface_ostatus{ifname!~'^(vlan|Vlanif|VLAN|V|irb|gr-).*'}[14d] offset 1h)  == 1 and snmp_interface_ostatus{ifname!~'^(vlan|Vlanif|VLAN|V|irb|gr-).*'} != 1
```

Runbook:

1. Take the device and ifname from the alert labels, log in and run display interface \<port> for the down reason and error counters;
2. On site, check whether the cable or optical module is loose — for optics use display transceiver to read the TX/RX power;
3. Confirm the port state on the peer device as well: only when both sides are down can you tell a link fault from a one-sided fault;
4. Confirm whether a redundant link has taken over, and restore first if there is none.

#### Inbound CRC errors[​](#inbound-crc-errors "Direct link to Inbound CRC errors")

incoming\_errors: cumulative port error packets, incoming\_ucastpkts: cumulative port packets

1. 1-minute delta of incoming\_errors above 100
2. 1-minute delta of incoming\_errors divided by 1-minute delta of incoming\_ucastpkts above 1%
3. checked every 60s, alert after 5 consecutive matches

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
rate(snmp_interface_incoming_errors{}[2m]) > 100 and rate(snmp_interface_incoming_errors{}[2m]) / rate(snmp_interface_incoming_ucastpkts{}[2m]) > 0.01
```

Runbook:

1. Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface \<port> to see how fast CRC/errors are growing;
2. Check the cable and optical module; for optical ports use display transceiver to confirm TX/RX power is within spec;
3. Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match on both ends — a mismatch is the classic source of errors;
4. After replacing the cable or module, clear the counters (reset counters interface) and retest.

#### Outbound CRC errors[​](#outbound-crc-errors "Direct link to Outbound CRC errors")

outgoing\_errors: cumulative port error packets, outgoing\_ucastpkts: cumulative port packets

1. 1-minute delta of outgoing\_errors above 100
2. 1-minute delta of outgoing\_errors divided by 1-minute delta of outgoing\_ucastpkts above 1%
3. checked every 60s, alert after 5 consecutive matches

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
rate(snmp_interface_outgoing_errors{}[2m]) > 100 and rate(snmp_interface_outgoing_errors{}[2m]) / rate(snmp_interface_outgoing_ucastpkts{}[2m]) > 0.01
```

Runbook:

1. Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface \<port> to see how fast CRC/errors are growing;

3. Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match on both ends — a mismatch is the classic source of errors;
4. After replacing the cable or module, clear the counters (reset counters interface) and retest.

#### Device interrupted[​](#device-interrupted "Direct link to Device interrupted")

snmp\_uptime is the device uptime in units of 10ms

delta(snmp\_uptime{}/100 \[2m]) means the device has not updated its uptime within 2 minutes

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
delta(snmp_uptime{}/100 [2m]) == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run an snmpwalk of the device's sysUpTime by hand to confirm whether it is still responding;
2. If it responds, the problem is on the collector side — check categraf's snmp configuration, community string and timeouts;
3. If it does not respond, treat it as a device outage and check power and the management network;
4. After recovery, note the data gap — there were no alerts during the blind window.

#### Device lost connection[​](#device-lost-connection "Direct link to Device lost connection")

no response == 0, responding == 1 checked every 60s; alert when both snmp and icmp are 0 for 3 consecutive checks if not recovered, the alert repeats after 24h

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
max_over_time(snmp_icmp_up{}[3m]) == 0 and max_over_time(snmp_up{}[3m]) == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Immediately confirm whether the services behind the device have failed over to redundant equipment, and handle traffic first if not;
2. On site, check the device power, indicators and whether the console produces output;
3. If you can reach the console, check whether it is rebooting or in an abnormal state and collect logs;
4. For a hardware fault, start the replacement process and keep traffic on the redundant path meanwhile.

#### Device rebooted[​](#device-rebooted "Direct link to Device rebooted")

Alert when device uptime is below 600.00 seconds

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
resets(snmp_uptime{}[10m]) == 1 and resets(snmp_enginetime{}[10m]) == 1
```

Runbook:

1. Log in and run display version for the uptime, and display logbuffer or display trapbuffer for the restart reason;
2. Separate a manual restart, a power loss and an abnormal reset (memory exhaustion, software defect);
3. For an abnormal reset, collect logs, contact the vendor and consider a firmware upgrade;
4. Confirm all interfaces and routing neighbours recovered after the restart.

#### Bgp Down[​](#bgp-down "Direct link to Bgp Down")

1. the 2nd latest peer\_status = 6 (established)
2. peer\_status changed within the last 5 minutes
3. admin\_status == 2 (up)

S3 Info · Trigger:

```
snmp_juniper_bgp_prefix_peer_status offset 1m == 6 and delta(snmp_juniper_bgp_prefix_peer_status[5m]) != 0 and snmp_juniper_bgp_prefix_admin_status == 2
```

Runbook:

1. Log in and run show bgp neighbor \<peer> for the session state and the last disconnect reason;
2. Check layer-3 connectivity to the neighbour (ping/traceroute) and whether TCP 179 is reachable;
3. If the network is fine, verify the AS numbers, authentication password and prefix limits on both sides (exceeding the limit disconnects deliberately);
4. Confirm whether the traffic is already carried by another neighbour, and restore it first if not.

#### Bgp peer flap[​](#bgp-peer-flap "Direct link to Bgp peer flap")

1.

S3 Info · Trigger:

```
delta(snmp_juniper_bgp_prefix_peer_up_count[1h]) >= 3
```

Runbook:

1. Run show bgp neighbor \<peer> to see the reasons for previous disconnects;
2. For link-layer instability, check interface errors and optical power;
3. For repeated disconnects caused by exceeding the prefix limit, adjust maximum-prefix or aggregate routes on the peer side;
4. Check whether BGP damping is configured to suppress flapping, and evaluate enabling it if not.

#### SNMP probe failed (device online)[​](#snmp-probe-failed-device-online "Direct link to SNMP probe failed (device online)")

The device is reachable by ICMP but the SNMP probe keeps failing. This means the device is not down: SNMP is not enabled, an ACL is blocking it, UDP 161 is unreachable, or the credentials (community string / v3 authentication) are wrong.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
max_over_time(snmp_icmp_up{}[3m]) == 1 and max_over_time(snmp_up{}[3m]) == 0
```

Runbook:

1. On the device, confirm SNMP is enabled and the community string / v3 user is configured correctly;
2. Check whether the device ACL and any firewall in between allow UDP 161 from the collector to the device;
3. On the collector host, verify the credentials by hand with snmpwalk;
4. If the credentials changed recently, update the SNMP authentication settings of this device on the platform as well and verify with Test on the page.

#### SNMP collection interrupted (previously had data)[​](#snmp-collection-interrupted-previously-had-data "Direct link to SNMP collection interrupted (previously had data)")

The SNMP probe of this device succeeded at some point in the last hour, but there has been no snmp\_up sample in the last 10 minutes. Common causes: the collection agent is offline or its configuration was removed, the device was disabled, or the network is down. Unlike a probe failure, this means the collection link as a whole produces no data at all.

S2 Warning · Trigger:

```
max_over_time(snmp_up{}[1h]) == 1 unless max_over_time(snmp_up{}[10m])
```

Runbook:

1. Open the network device list and read the Health column of this device to tell an unreachable collection agent from a failed device probe;
2. Confirm the configured collection agent (categraf) process and heartbeat are healthy;
3. Confirm collection is not disabled for the device and the collect templates are still attached;
4. On the device detail page, run Test to quickly verify the collection link.

#### Bandwidth Usage Too High[​](#bandwidth-usage-too-high "Direct link to Bandwidth Usage Too High")

1. traffic value: delta(snmp\_network\_status\_incoming \[1m]) #delta() computes the increment (difference) of the time series /8 unit conversion factor min\_over\_time(metric\_name \[3m]) 3 max\_over\_time(snmp\_network\_status\_speed \[30m])/1000 \* 0.7 \* 1024 \* 1024 \* 1024 alert at 70% and 90% of the physical port capacity

S3 Info · for 2 min · Trigger:

```
min_over_time(delta(snmp_network_status_incoming[3m]) * 8 / 180 / 1024 / 1024 [3m]) > snmp_network_status_speed / 1000 * 0.7 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024 and snmp_network_status_speed > 0



min_over_time(delta(snmp_network_status_incoming[3m]) * 8 / 180 / 1024 / 1024 [3m]) > snmp_network_status_speed / 1000 * 0.9 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024 and snmp_network_status_speed > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface \<port> to confirm the actual rate and peak;
2. Use NetFlow/sFlow or capture traffic on the upstream device to find which sources/destinations consume the bandwidth;
3. Determine whether it is normal growth, a backup job, or abnormal traffic (attack, loop);
4. For genuine growth, upgrade the link or use link aggregation; for abnormal traffic, rate limit or isolate it first.

#### CRC Error[​](#crc-error "Direct link to CRC Error")

incoming\_errors: cumulative port error packets, incoming\_ucastpkts: cumulative port packets

1. delta of incoming\_errors\[1m] > 100
2. delta of incoming\_errors\[1m] divided by delta of incoming\_ucastpkts\[1m] > 0.001

S3 Info · for 2 min · Trigger:

```
delta(snmp_network_status_incoming_errors[1m]) > 100 and delta(snmp_network_status_incoming_errors[1m]) / delta(snmp_network_status_incoming_ucastpkts[1m]) > 0.001



delta(snmp_network_status_incoming_errors[1m]) > 100 and delta(snmp_network_status_incoming_errors[1m]) / delta(snmp_network_status_incoming_ucastpkts[1m]) > 0.01
```

Runbook:

1. Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface \<port> to see how fast CRC/errors are growing;
2. Check the cable and optical module; for optical ports use display transceiver to confirm TX/RX power is within spec;
3. Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match on both ends — a mismatch is the classic source of errors;
4. After replacing the cable or module, clear the counters (reset counters interface) and retest.

#### Interface Down[​](#interface-down-1 "Direct link to Interface Down")

1. admin == 1
2. ops status was 2 (down) for the last 3 checks and 1 (up) on the 4th latest

S3 Info · for 2 min · Trigger:

```
snmp_network_status_admin_status == 1 and snmp_network_status_ostatus offset 4m == 1 and min_over_time(snmp_network_status_ostatus[3m]) == 2
```

Runbook:

1. Take the device and ifname from the alert labels, log in and run display interface \<port> for the down reason and error counters;
2. On site, check whether the cable or optical module is loose — for optics use display transceiver to read the TX/RX power;
3. Confirm the port state on the peer device as well: only when both sides are down can you tell a link fault from a one-sided fault;
4. Confirm whether a redundant link has taken over, and restore first if there is none.

## Metric reference[​](#metric-reference "Direct link to Metric reference")

5 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on.

| Metric                              | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Unit  |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| `snmp_interface_admin_status`       | SNMP Interface Admin Status — SNMP interface administrative status, MIB name is ifAdminStatus. up(1): The interface is administratively enabled, the device is configured to allow the interface to operate. down(2): The interface is administratively disabled, the device is configured to prevent data transmission or operation. testing(3): The interface is in testing mode. Rarely seen in practice but exists in standard definitions. |       |
| `snmp_interface_ostatus`            | SNMP Interface Operational Status — Interface operational status up(1): The interface is currently in normal working state and can send/receive data. down(2): The interface is currently unable to work, possibly due to physical link disconnection, configuration issues, or hardware failure. testing(3): The interface is in testing mode and temporarily not processing normal data flow, generally rare.                                 |       |
| `snmp_interface_outgoing_ucastpkts` | Total Unicast Packets Sent by Interface — The total number of unicast packets sent by the interface in the outgoing direction.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |       |
| `snmp_interface_outgoing_errors`    | Total Outgoing Errors on Interface — The number of errors that occurred during data transmission on the interface. These errors typically include network layer or link layer issues, such as packet corruption, checksum errors, or other reasons that prevent normal data transmission.                                                                                                                                                       |       |
| `snmp_interface_speed`              | Interface Bandwidth — snmp\_interface\_speed is an object in SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) used to represent the speed or bandwidth of a network interface, typically in bits per second (bps). It indicates the maximum data transfer rate of the network interface, i.e., the maximum traffic the interface can handle under ideal conditions.                                                                                    | bit/s |

# Monitor Spring Boot applications with Nightingale

Add Actuator and micrometer-registry-prometheus and the application exposes /actuator/prometheus itself; the template ships JVM dashboards split by application name.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Spring Boot applications need no external agent. Add the `spring-boot-starter-actuator` and `micrometer-registry-prometheus` dependencies, expose the prometheus endpoint, and the application serves JVM, HTTP request, datasource pool, executor and custom metrics on `/actuator/prometheus`. Actuator is built on Micrometer underneath.

The two JVM dashboards are written against Actuator metric names (`jvm_memory_used_bytes`, `http_server_requests_seconds` and so on); one of them separates services by the `application` label. The rules cover heap near the limit, long GC pauses, rising HTTP 5xx and abnormal thread counts.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **2 dashboards**, 71 panels in total
* **5 alert rules**, each with runbook steps

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

For Spring Boot 3.x, add to `application.properties`:

```
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus

management.endpoint.prometheus.enabled=true

management.prometheus.metrics.export.enabled=true
```

On 2.x the last line is `management.metrics.export.prometheus.enabled=true`. Check that `http://localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus` responds, then scrape it with the Categraf `prometheus` input and set an `application` label to the service name. Do not set `exposure.include` to `*`.

1. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find SpringBoot, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.
2. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled dashboards[​](#bundled-dashboards "Direct link to Bundled dashboards")

| Dashboard                            | Panels |
| ------------------------------------ | ------ |
| JVM (Actuator) with application name | 37     |
| JVM Dashboard                        | 34     |

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### SpringBoot heap memory usage above 85%[​](#springboot-heap-memory-usage-above-85 "Direct link to SpringBoot heap memory usage above 85%")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"}) * 100 / sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="heap"}) > 85
```

Runbook:

1. Check jvm\_gc\_pause\_seconds to see whether full GC became more frequent and how long the pauses are;
2. Capture a heap with jmap -histo:live \<pid> or the arthas heapdump, then sort by object count to find the abnormally growing classes;
3. Tell traffic growth (raise -Xmx) apart from a memory leak (must be fixed in code — a bigger heap only postpones it);
4. You can restart the instance to recover, but capture the heap snapshot first or you lose the evidence.

### SpringBoot HTTP request latency exceeds 10s[​](#springboot-http-request-latency-exceeds-10s "Direct link to SpringBoot HTTP request latency exceeds 10s")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
max by (instance, uri) (http_server_requests_seconds_max{status!~"5.."}) > 10
```

Runbook:

1. Take uri from the alert labels to identify the endpoint;
2. Use arthas trace or APM distributed tracing to see which segment consumes the time (database, downstream RPC, or local computation);
3. For a slow database, follow the slow-query path and add indexes; for a slow downstream, check its state and add a circuit breaker or fallback;
4. Check whether the thread pool is saturated by slow requests and amplifying the queue — isolate the pool if so.

### SpringBoot HTTP errors[​](#springboot-http-errors "Direct link to SpringBoot HTTP errors")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum by (instance, uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Take uri from the alert labels to identify the endpoint, then search the application log for stack traces on that path;
2. Tell total failure from partial failure — partial failure usually means one bad downstream instance or a data edge case;
3. If it lines up with a recent release, roll back rather than keep investigating;
4. Check whether downstream dependencies (database, cache, third-party APIs) are failing at the same time.

### SpringBoot non-heap memory usage above 85%[​](#springboot-non-heap-memory-usage-above-85 "Direct link to SpringBoot non-heap memory usage above 85%")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="nonheap"}) > 0 and sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="nonheap"}) * 100 / sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="nonheap"}) > 85
```

Runbook:

1. Run jcmd \<pid> VM.native\_memory summary (requires NativeMemoryTracking) or the arthas memory command to see each region's usage;
2. Steadily growing Metaspace usually means a class loader leak — common with repeated hot deploys, dynamic proxies and script engines;
3. As an emergency measure raise -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize and restart;
4. For the root cause, look for a custom ClassLoader that is never released, and check jmap -clstats for an abnormal class loader count.

### SpringBoot event errors[​](#springboot-event-errors "Direct link to SpringBoot event errors")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum by (instance) (increase(logback_events_total{level="error"}[5m])) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Take instance from the alert labels, then search your log system for ERROR-level stack traces in that time window;
2. Group by exception type to tell an intermittent problem (downstream jitter, timeout retries) from a reproducible one (code bug, misconfiguration);
3. Fix reproducible ones in code; for intermittent ones confirm retry and fallback logic actually works;
4. If the ERROR volume spiked in line with a release, roll back first.

# Monitor SQLServer with Nightingale

Collects connections, waits, buffer pool, log usage and database state from DMVs and performance counters; VIEW SERVER STATE is all the permission it needs.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

The SQL Server input is based on the Telegraf plugin of the same name and reads dynamic management views (DMVs) and performance counters: connections and requests, wait statistics, buffer cache hit ratio, page life expectancy, transaction log usage, database state and size, and Always On availability group health. It has been verified against SQL Server 2022.

Create a login in master and grant `VIEW SERVER STATE` and `VIEW ANY DEFINITION`; on 2022 and later add `VIEW SERVER PERFORMANCE STATE`. The rules cover blocking, deadlocks, log space, falling cache hit ratio and databases going offline.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **1 dashboard**, 10 panels in total
* **11 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.sqlserver`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

   ```

   # interval = 15



   [[instances]]



   ## Specify instances to monitor with a list of connection strings.

   ## All connection parameters are optional.

   ## By default, the host is localhost, listening on default port, TCP 1433.

   ##   for Windows, the user is the currently running AD user (SSO).

   ##   See https://github.com/denisenkom/go-mssqldb for detailed connection

   # servers = [ ]

   ## "database_type" enables a specific set of queries depending on the database type. If specified, it replaces azuredb = true/false and query_version = 2

   ## In the config file, the sql server plugin section should be repeated each with a set of servers for a specific database_type.

   ## Possible values for database_type are - "SQLServer" or "AzureSQLDB" or "AzureSQLManagedInstance" or "AzureSQLPool"



   database_type = "SQLServer"

   # health_metric = false

| Dashboard | Panels |

| SQLServer | 10     |

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

11 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### SQL Server instance unreachable[​](#sql-server-instance-unreachable "Direct link to SQL Server instance unreachable")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sqlserver_up == 0
```

Runbook:

1. On the database host run systemctl status mssql-server (Linux) or Get-Service MSSQLSERVER (Windows) to check the service;
2. If the service is running, connect by hand with sqlcmd -S \<host>,1433 -U \<user> to separate a network problem, a port not listening, and a locked account;
3. If the service is down, check /var/opt/mssql/log/errorlog (Linux) or the SQL Server error log; a full disk, tempdb creation failure, or an expired certificate are common causes;
4. After recovery run SELECT name, state\_desc FROM sys.databases to confirm every database is back ONLINE.

### SQL Server has a database in SUSPECT state[​](#sql-server-has-a-database-in-suspect-state "Direct link to SQL Server has a database in SUSPECT state")

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sqlserver_server_properties_db_suspect > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run SELECT name, state\_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE state\_desc <> 'ONLINE' to identify the database;
2. Look for the most recent errors for that database in the SQL Server error log to tell an IO error from log corruption;
3. Restoring from the most recent good backup (RESTORE DATABASE) is the path with the least data loss and should be preferred;
4. Only if no backup exists should you use EMERGENCY mode plus DBCC CHECKDB(..., REPAIR\_ALLOW\_DATA\_LOSS); that operation loses data, so take a file-level snapshot first.

### SQL Server has a database in OFFLINE state[​](#sql-server-has-a-database-in-offline-state "Direct link to SQL Server has a database in OFFLINE state")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
sqlserver_server_properties_db_offline > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run SELECT name, state\_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE state\_desc = 'OFFLINE' to list the offline databases;
2. Confirm against the change record whether this is planned maintenance or a migration;
3. If unplanned, try ALTER DATABASE \[db] SET ONLINE and read the error log for the exact reason if it fails;
4. Once online run DBCC CHECKDB(\[db]) WITH NO\_INFOMSGS to confirm data consistency.

### SQL Server data volume free space low[​](#sql-server-data-volume-free-space-low "Direct link to SQL Server data volume free space low")

S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
sqlserver_volume_space_available_space_bytes / (sqlserver_volume_space_total_space_bytes > 0) * 100 < 10
```

Runbook:

1. Take volume\_mount\_point from the alert labels and run SELECT DB\_NAME(database\_id), name, size\*8/1024 AS size\_mb FROM sys.master\_files ORDER BY size DESC to find the largest files;
2. For an oversized log file, run BACKUP LOG to truncate it first and then DBCC SHRINKFILE; under the full recovery model it cannot shrink without a log backup;
3. If the data files genuinely need that space, clean up historical partitions or archive cold data;
4. As an emergency measure move tempdb or backup files to another volume, but plan a disk expansion.

### SQL Server transaction log usage too high[​](#sql-server-transaction-log-usage-too-high "Direct link to SQL Server transaction log usage too high")

S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Percent Log Used", instance!="_Total", instance!="Total"} > 85
```

Runbook:

1. Take instance (the database name) from the alert labels and run SELECT name, log\_reuse\_wait\_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE name = '\<db>' to see why the log cannot be reused;
2. For LOG\_BACKUP, run BACKUP LOG \[db] TO DISK='...' immediately; this is by far the most common cause;
3. For ACTIVE\_TRANSACTION, run DBCC OPENTRAN to find the long transaction and decide whether to KILL it;
4. For REPLICATION or AVAILABILITY\_REPLICA, investigate whether replication/AlwaysOn synchronisation is stuck and repair the replication link first.

### SQL Server page life expectancy too low[​](#sql-server-page-life-expectancy-too-low "Direct link to SQL Server page life expectancy too low")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Page life expectancy", object="SQLServer:Buffer Manager"} < 300
```

Runbook:

1. Run SELECT \* FROM sys.dm\_os\_performance\_counters WHERE counter\_name LIKE '%Page life%' to confirm the live value;
2. Run SELECT TOP 20 \* FROM sys.dm\_exec\_query\_stats ORDER BY total\_logical\_reads DESC to find the statements with the highest logical reads, usually full scans caused by missing indexes;
3. Take the suggestions from sys.dm\_db\_missing\_index\_details, review them, and create the indexes; this pays off faster than adding memory;
4. If queries are already optimised and it is still low, check whether max server memory is set too small or is being squeezed by other processes before adding RAM.

### SQL Server has queries waiting for memory grants[​](#sql-server-has-queries-waiting-for-memory-grants "Direct link to SQL Server has queries waiting for memory grants")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Memory Grants Pending"} > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run SELECT session\_id, requested\_memory\_kb, granted\_memory\_kb, wait\_time\_ms FROM sys.dm\_exec\_query\_memory\_grants to see who is waiting and who is holding;
2. For sessions with huge grants, pull the statement with sys.dm\_exec\_sql\_text; it is usually a large sort or hash join, and a missing index amplifies the memory requirement significantly;
3. As an emergency measure KILL the largest consumer to release memory;
4. Longer term add the indexes suggested by dm\_db\_missing\_index\_details, split large queries, or raise max server memory.

### SQL Server blocked process count too high[​](#sql-server-blocked-process-count-too-high "Direct link to SQL Server blocked process count too high")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Processes blocked"} > 5
```

Runbook:

1. Run SELECT blocking\_session\_id, session\_id, wait\_type, wait\_time, wait\_resource FROM sys.dm\_exec\_requests WHERE blocking\_session\_id <> 0 to find the head of the blocking chain;
2. For the head session use DBCC INPUTBUFFER(\<spid>) or sys.dm\_exec\_sql\_text to see what it is running;
3. Once confirmed as a runaway long transaction, run KILL \<spid> to stop the bleeding;
4. Afterwards check whether that transaction lacks an index (widening the lock range) or the application forgot to commit, and consider enabling READ\_COMMITTED\_SNAPSHOT to reduce reader/writer conflict.

### SQL Server deadlock occurred[​](#sql-server-deadlock-occurred "Direct link to SQL Server deadlock occurred")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
increase(sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Number of Deadlocks/sec"}[10m]) > 0
```

Runbook:

1. Query the system\_health extended event session for the deadlock graph: SELECT XEvent.query('.') FROM (SELECT CAST(target\_data AS XML) AS TargetData FROM sys.dm\_xe\_session\_targets ...) and extract xml\_deadlock\_report;
2. Read the lock acquisition order and the indexes involved from the graph;
3. The usual fix is to make multi-table updates follow the same order everywhere in the application code, plus indexes on the participating queries to narrow the lock range;
4. In the short term the application can retry on error 1205, but that does not replace fixing the root cause.

### SQL Server data file read latency too high[​](#sql-server-data-file-read-latency-too-high "Direct link to SQL Server data file read latency too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
rate(sqlserver_database_io_read_latency_ms[5m]) / (rate(sqlserver_database_io_reads[5m]) > 0) > 50
```

Runbook:

1. Take database\_name and logical\_filename from the alert labels to identify the slow file;
2. On the host run iostat -x 1 (Linux) or watch Avg. Disk sec/Read in Performance Monitor to tell slow storage from read amplification inside SQL Server;
3. If the storage is fine, optimise queries and add indexes as for page life expectancy to reduce physical reads;
4. If the storage really is slow, consider moving the file to SSD, splitting filegroups to spread IO, or checking whether backup jobs overlap the business peak.

### SQL Server data file write latency too high[​](#sql-server-data-file-write-latency-too-high "Direct link to SQL Server data file write latency too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
rate(sqlserver_database_io_write_latency_ms[5m]) / (rate(sqlserver_database_io_writes[5m]) > 0) > 50
```

Runbook:

1. Take database\_name and file\_type from the alert labels and handle file\_type=LOG first, since slow log writes stall every commit;
2. On the host run iostat -x 1 and check that disk's await and %util to see whether it is saturated;
3. If the log file shares a disk with the data files, move the log to a dedicated low-latency disk;
4. Check whether backups, DBCC CHECKDB, or index rebuilds overlap the business peak and move them to off-peak hours.

# Monitor switches with zero config (Switch Legacy) in Nightingale

Give it a list of IPs and it detects the device model and collects CPU, memory and per-port traffic, errors and state; SNMP v2c only.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

The switch\_legacy input is forked from swcollector and targets the "just get the switches in quickly" case. List IPs in the config (single addresses, subnets or ranges), and the input detects the device model and uses generic OIDs to collect CPU and memory usage plus traffic, packets, errors, discards and up/down state for every port. No OIDs to write.

It supports SNMP v2c only, so authentication is a single community string. Set `switch_id_label` to `ident` and each switch appears in Nightingale's host list keyed by its IP. For custom OIDs or SNMP v3, use the [SNMP integration](https://n9e.github.io/integrations/snmp.md) instead. The rules cover ports going down, traffic near bandwidth, rising errors and unreachable devices.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **1 dashboard**, 14 panels in total
* **7 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.switch_legacy`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.switch_legacy/switch_legacy.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.switch_legacy started` once the plugin is loaded.

   ```
   # # collect interval

   # interval = "300s"



   switch_id_label = "ip"



   [mappings]

   "192.168.88.160" = "switch001.bj"

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

7 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### Switch unreachable[​](#switch-unreachable "Direct link to Switch unreachable")

S1 Critical · for 2 min · Trigger:

```
switch_legacy_ping_up == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Take the device identifier from the alert labels and double-check with ping and traceroute from a different machine to rule out a problem on the collector side;
2. If it does ping from elsewhere, the problem is on the path from the collector; check the intermediate links and ACLs;
3. If it does not ping at all, ask the data centre to check the power and status LEDs and try logging in over the console port;
4. Once the device is confirmed failed, switch to the redundant link (check whether stacking/VRRP already failed over) and arrange a replacement.

### Switch CPU utilization too high[​](#switch-cpu-utilization-too-high "Direct link to Switch CPU utilization too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
switch_legacy_cpu_util > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Log in to the device and run display cpu-usage (Huawei) or show processes cpu sorted (Cisco) to see which process is consuming CPU;
2. High usage is commonly an ARP or broadcast storm, or heavy punting of packets to the CPU; check with display cpu-defend statistics;
3. For a broadcast storm, locate the source port and configure storm-control, and check for a loop at the same time (STP state);
4. If a protocol process is the consumer, check the routing table size and neighbour count and apply route summarisation if needed.

### Switch memory utilization too high[​](#switch-memory-utilization-too-high "Direct link to Switch memory utilization too high")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
switch_legacy_mem_util > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Log in to the device and run display memory-usage or show memory statistics to see the breakdown;
2. Check whether the MAC table, ARP table, and routing table sizes are approaching the device's specification limits;
3. If entries are growing abnormally, check for a MAC flooding attack and configure port security to cap MAC learning per port;
4. If this is genuine business growth, evaluate whether the device model needs upgrading and clean up unused configuration and ACLs.

### Switch port flapping[​](#switch-port-flapping "Direct link to Switch port flapping")

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
changes(switch_legacy_if_oper_status[10m]) > 2
```

Runbook:

1. Take the port identifier from the alert labels, log in to the device, and run display interface \<port> to see the up/down count and the last transition time;
2. Suspect the physical layer first: check whether the optical module's transmit and receive power (display transceiver diagnosis) are within thresholds and whether the fibre and connectors are loose;
3. For copper ports, check cable quality and whether speed/duplex negotiation matches on both ends;
4. Once physical problems are ruled out, check whether the peer device is restarting repeatedly, and shut down the port if necessary to stop it triggering network-wide reconvergence.

### Switch port inbound errors[​](#switch-port-inbound-errors "Direct link to Switch port inbound errors")

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger:

```
rate(switch_legacy_if_in_errors[5m]) > 1
```

Runbook:

1. Take the port identifier from the alert labels and run display interface \<port> to see the detailed CRC, Frame, and Giants error counters;
2. Predominantly CRC errors are essentially always physical: replace the cable or fibre, clean the optical connectors, and confirm the cable length is within spec;
3. Check that speed and duplex negotiation match on both ends, since a half/full duplex mismatch produces large numbers of collision errors;
4. After replacing the cable, clear the counters with reset counters interface \<port> and confirm they stop growing.

### Switch port inbound bandwidth utilization too high[​](#switch-port-inbound-bandwidth-utilization-too-high "Direct link to Switch port inbound bandwidth utilization too high")

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger:

```
switch_legacy_if_in_speed_percent > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Take the port identifier from the alert labels and run display interface \<port> to confirm the live rate against the negotiated port speed;
2. Use NetFlow/sFlow, or capture on the server side, to identify which workloads generate the traffic and rule out anomalies (backup jobs or data sync running in the wrong window);
3. If this is genuine business growth, evaluate link aggregation (Eth-Trunk / port-channel) to add capacity;
4. In the short term apply QoS rate limiting to non-critical traffic to protect the important flows.

### Switch port outbound bandwidth utilization too high[​](#switch-port-outbound-bandwidth-utilization-too-high "Direct link to Switch port outbound bandwidth utilization too high")

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger:

```
switch_legacy_if_out_speed_percent > 80
```

Runbook:

1. Take the port identifier from the alert labels and run display interface \<port> to see the outbound rate and queue drop counters;
2. For a saturated uplink, link aggregation is the most direct fix;
3. Use traffic analysis to confirm whether high-volume workloads should be taking a different path, and adjust routing or apply traffic engineering if so;
4. Before adding capacity, apply QoS queue rate limiting to secondary traffic to protect the critical business.

# Monitor Systemd with Nightingale

Reads systemd unit state, restart counts and startup time over D-Bus, so failed or flapping services page you right away.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

The systemd input talks to systemd over D-Bus and collects each unit's active state, enabled flag, restart count, task count and startup time. Unlike a plain process check, it tells "the service exists but is failed" apart from "the service keeps getting restarted".

All units are collected by default, minus the noisy automount, device, mount, scope and slice types. In production, narrow it down with `unit_include` to the services you actually care about. Requires Linux with systemd 212 or newer.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **1 dashboard**, 7 panels in total
* **3 alert rules**, each with runbook steps
* **12 metric descriptions**
* **Categraf collector config**: `input.systemd`

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

1. [Install Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md), put the config below in `conf/input.systemd/systemd.toml`, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints `input: local.systemd started` once the plugin is loaded.

   ```
   # # collect interval

   # interval = 15



   # 是否启用 systemd 插件

   enable = true



   # 包含的 unit 正则表达式，默认为 ".+"（所有unit）

   unit_include = '''.+'''



   # 排除的 unit 正则表达式，默认排除 automount、device、mount、scope、slice 类型

   unit_exclude = '''.+\.(automount|device|mount|scope|slice)'''



   # 是否采集 service unit 的启动时间信息（单位：秒）

   enable_start_time_metrics = true



   # 是否采集 service unit task 的 metrics

   enable_task_metrics = true



   # 是否采集 service unit 重启次数信息

   enable_restarts_metrics = true



   # 是否使用私有 systemd 连接

   systemd_private = true
   ```

2. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Systemd, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.

3. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled dashboards[​](#bundled-dashboards "Direct link to Bundled dashboards")

| Dashboard                    | Panels |
| ---------------------------- | ------ |
| Systemd Monitoring Dashboard | 7      |

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

3 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### Service state abnormal[​](#service-state-abnormal "Direct link to Service state abnormal")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
systemd_unit_state{state!="active"} == 1
```

Runbook:

1. Run systemctl --failed to list every failed unit, then systemctl status \<unit> for its state and recent logs;
2. Use journalctl -u \<unit> -n 100 --no-pager to find the exit reason;
3. For configuration problems, fix the config before systemctl restart \<unit>;
4. For repeated failures, check systemctl show \<unit> -p NRestarts for a restart loop and find the root cause before restarting again.

### Service restarting frequently[​](#service-restarting-frequently "Direct link to Service restarting frequently")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
increase(systemd_service_restart_total[5m]) > 3
```

Runbook:

1. Run journalctl -u \<unit> -n 200 --no-pager to see the error before each exit;
2. Check the exit code and whether it was OOM-killed (dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process');
3. If an unready dependency is the cause (cannot reach the database, mount not finished), add After=/Requires= to the unit and fix the dependency;
4. While investigating you can systemctl stop the service so it does not flood the disk with logs.

### System state abnormal[​](#system-state-abnormal "Direct link to System state abnormal")

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger:

```
systemd_system_running == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Run systemctl status for the overall state, then systemctl --failed to list the failed units;
2. Use journalctl -u \<unit> on each to find and fix the failure;
3. Confirm whether the failed units affect critical services — some are unrelated one-shot jobs whose state can be cleared with systemctl reset-failed;
4. After fixing, confirm systemctl is-system-running returns running.

## Metric reference[​](#metric-reference "Direct link to Metric reference")

12 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on.

| Metric                                      | Meaning                                                                                                                             | Unit |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---- |

| `systemd_socket_accepted_connections_total` | Total Accepted Socket Connections                                                                                                   |      |
| `systemd_socket_current_connections`        | Current Socket Connections                                                                                                          |      |
| `systemd_socket_refused_connections_total`  | Total Refused Socket Connections                                                                                                    |      |

| `systemd_unit_start_time_seconds`           | Unit Start Timestamp — Unix timestamp                                                                                               | ms   |

# Monitor Tencent Cloud with Nightingale

Scrape Cloud Monitor metrics converted to Prometheus format by the tencentcloud-exporter; templates cover CVM, CKafka, PostgreSQL, Redis, TDSQL-C and load balancers.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Tencent Cloud metrics come from its Cloud Monitor service. The `tencentcloud-exporter` maintained by Tencent Cloud converts them per product into Prometheus metrics named `qce_<product>_<metric>`, which the Categraf `prometheus` input scrapes.

The templates ship one dashboard per product: CVM instances, CKafka, Cloud PostgreSQL, Redis (memory edition), TDSQL-C for MySQL, and public and private load balancers. The metric reference further down lists Tencent Cloud's monitoring metrics per product with meaning, unit and dimensions.

```
# conf/input.prometheus/tencentcloud.toml

interval = 60



[[instances]]

urls = ["http://<exporter>:9123/metrics"]

labels = { job = "tencentcloud" }
```

# Monitor TiDB with Nightingale

TiDB, PD and TiKV all expose Prometheus metrics on /metrics; the templates cover SQL latency, Region scheduling, storage and node health.

Last reviewed 2026-10-31

Every TiDB component ships a Prometheus endpoint: TiDB Server on 10080, PD on 2379, TiKV on 20180, with TiFlash and TiCDC on whatever ports they are configured with. Scrape them with the Categraf `prometheus` input, or add the Prometheus that TiUP deploys as a Nightingale data source.

The dashboards depend on four labels: `k8s_cluster`, `tidb_cluster`, `job` and `instance`. Give the first two fixed values even outside Kubernetes. The rules cover failed and slow queries on TiDB, Region anomalies on PD, storage and Raft latency on TiKV, and components going down.

## What's in the template[​](#whats-in-the-template "Direct link to What's in the template")

* **1 dashboard**, 58 panels in total
* **28 alert rules**, each with runbook steps

## How to connect[​](#how-to-connect "Direct link to How to connect")

These components expose Prometheus-format `/metrics` themselves, so the Categraf `prometheus` input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, [add it as a Nightingale data source](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md) and the templates work as they are.

```
# conf/input.prometheus/tidb.toml

interval = 15



[[instances]]

urls = ["http://<tidb>:10080/metrics"]

labels = { job = "tidb", k8s_cluster = "", tidb_cluster = "prod" }



[[instances]]

urls = ["http://<pd>:2379/metrics"]

labels = { job = "pd", k8s_cluster = "", tidb_cluster = "prod" }



[[instances]]

urls = ["http://<tikv>:20180/metrics"]

labels = { job = "tikv", k8s_cluster = "", tidb_cluster = "prod" }
```

1. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find TiDB, and [import the dashboards and alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md) into a business group.
2. Imported rules start disabled. [Check that the metrics are arriving](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md) first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

## Bundled dashboards[​](#bundled-dashboards "Direct link to Bundled dashboards")

| Dashboard     | Panels |
| ------------- | ------ |
| tidb-Overview | 58     |

## Bundled alert rules[​](#bundled-alert-rules "Direct link to Bundled alert rules")

28 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

### TiDB - CPU usage exceeds 80%[​](#tidb---cpu-usage-exceeds-80 "Direct link to TiDB - CPU usage exceeds 80%")

TiDB (Control Plane)

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
avg(irate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) by(instance) * 100 <= 20
```

Runbook:

1. Run top -H to see whether tidb-server, tikv-server or something else is busy;
2. High TiKV CPU usually means too many coprocessor requests — use the TiDB slow log to find SQL scanning large ranges;
3. High TiDB CPU usually means complex computation or many small queries — check the Grafana TiDB Query Summary;
4. If it stays high after SQL tuning, add nodes.

### TiDB-Node\_exporter\_is\_down[​](#tidb-node_exporter_is_down "Direct link to TiDB-Node_exporter_is_down")

TiDB (Control Plane)

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
probe_success{group="node_exporter"} == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh;
2. On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM;
3. If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall;
4. Run tiup cluster display \<cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

### TiDB - PD disk write latency exceeds 1s; slow leader writes cause leader switches[​](#tidb---pd-disk-write-latency-exceeds-1s-slow-leader-writes-cause-leader-switches "Direct link to TiDB - PD disk write latency exceeds 1s; slow leader writes cause leader switches")

TiDB (Control Plane)

S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (instance,job,le) ) > 1
```

Runbook:

1. On the PD node run iostat -x 1 to check disk util and await — PD requires SSDs;
2. Confirm the PD data directory does not share a disk with TiKV data;
3. Check whether another process is competing for that disk's IO;
4. If disk performance is genuinely insufficient, moving PD to a dedicated SSD is the only real fix.

### TiDB - PD has no leader[​](#tidb---pd-has-no-leader "Direct link to TiDB - PD has no leader")

TiDB (Control Plane)

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
sum(etcd_server_is_leader) !=1
```

Runbook:

1. Run pd-ctl member to check each PD member's state and whether the surviving nodes still form a majority;
2. Without a majority, restore the failed PD nodes immediately;
3. If all nodes are alive but no leader is elected, check connectivity and clock skew between PDs;
4. Check each PD's log for the election failure reason and follow the official PD recovery procedure if needed.

### TiDB - network latency between PD nodes exceeds 1s[​](#tidb---network-latency-between-pd-nodes-exceeds-1s "Direct link to TiDB - network latency between PD nodes exceeds 1s")

TiDB (Control Plane)

S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(etcd_network_peer_round_trip_time_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (To,instance,job,le) ) > 1
```

Runbook:

1. Run mtr between PD nodes to find where latency and loss appear;
2. Confirm PD nodes are not spread across data centres — PD is very sensitive to network latency and should be co-located;
3. Check the NIC for errors and drops and whether bandwidth is saturated;
4. Involve the network team, and avoid large data migrations meanwhile.

### TiDB - TCP connections exceed 50000[​](#tidb---tcp-connections-exceed-50000 "Direct link to TiDB - TCP connections exceed 50000")

TiDB (Control Plane)

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
node_netstat_Tcp_CurrEstab > 50000
```

Runbook:

1. Run ss -s to see the connection state distribution and whether ESTABLISHED or TIME\_WAIT dominates;
2. Run ss -tan | awk '{print $5}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to locate the sources;
3. If the application does not reuse connections, switch to a connection pool;
4. If TIME\_WAIT dominates, enable tcp\_tw\_reuse and widen the port range.

### TiDB-TiDB\_server\_is\_down[​](#tidb-tidb_server_is_down "Direct link to TiDB-TiDB_server_is_down")

TiDB (Control Plane)

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
probe_success{group="tidb"} == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh;
2. On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM;
3. If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall;
4. Run tiup cluster display \<cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

### TiDB-blackbox\_is\_down[​](#tidb-blackbox_is_down "Direct link to TiDB-blackbox_is_down")

TiDB (Control Plane)

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger:

```
probe_success{group="blackbox_exporter"} == 0
```

Runbook:

1. Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh;

### TiDB-grafana\_is\_down[​](#tidb-grafana_is_down "Direct link to TiDB-grafana_is_down")
